Macroscopic fluctuation theory

Abstract

Stationary non-equilibrium states describe steady flows through macroscopic systems. Although they represent the simplest generalization of equilibrium states, they exhibit a variety of new phenomena. Within a statistical mechanics approach, these states have been the subject of several theoretical investigations, both analytic and numerical. The macroscopic fluctuation theory, based on a formula for the probability of joint space-time fluctuations of thermodynamic variables and currents, provides a unified macroscopic treatment of such states for driven diffusive systems. We give a detailed review of this theory including its main predictions and most relevant applications.

I Introduction

Far from equilibrium behavior is ubiquitous. Indeed, most of the processes that characterize energy flow occur far from equilibrium; so do typical biological phenomena, and significant processes in molecules, solids, earth sciences, astrophysics. Classical thermodynamics does not cover such processes. It is a phenomenological theory which deals with states of matter which either do not change in time (equilibrium) or change very slowly so that they can be described by a sequence of equilibrium states.

For systems out of equilibrium it does not exist yet a macroscopic description of a scope comparable with equilibrium thermodynamics. In non-equilibrium one has to cope with a variety of phenomena much greater than in equilibrium. From a conceptual point of view the non-equilibrium situations closest to equilibrium are the stationary non-equilibrium states which describe a steady flow through some system. Simple examples are the heat flow in an iron rod whose endpoints are thermostated at different temperatures or the stationary flow of electrical current in a given potential difference. For such states the fluctuations exhibit novel and rich features with respect to the equilibrium situation. For example, as experimentally observed [53], the space correlations of the density extend to macroscopic distances.

Previous formulations of non-equilibrium thermodynamics, notably Onsager’s theory [109, 111], mostly refer to situations near equilibrium where some kind of expansion can be made. Over the last ten years, a general approach to non-equilibrium diffusive systems known as Macroscopic Fluctuation Theory (MFT) [12, 16, 43], making some progress in far from equilibrium processes and improving on near equilibrium linear approximations, has been developed. This theory has been inspired by stochastic models of interacting particles (stochastic lattice gases). It is based on the study of rare fluctuations of macroscopic variables in stationary states and leads to a consistent definition of non-equilibrium thermodynamic functionals as well as to significant new results and predictions.

The MFT can be seen as the next stage beyond Onsager theory which postulates simplified evolution equations. In particular, in Onsager theory the space dependence is neglected and the time derivative of thermodynamic variables are directly identified with the associated currents. The currents are assumed to be proportional to the thermodynamic forces that are identified with the derivatives of the equilibrium entropy with respect to the thermodynamic variables. The entropy is expanded around an equilibrium (maximum) value up to second order leading to linear evolution equations. Within Onsager theory the fluctuations are modeled by Gaussian processes. The near equilibrium theory has been developed further by Kubo [94].

With respect to Onsager theory, the MFT removes two restrictions. On one hand the systems considered may admit nonlinear hydrodynamic equations. In the second place the external driving, like the potential difference, is not assumed small so that stationary states far from equilibrium are possible. In general, the fluctuations are not Gaussian. The main source of new phenomena is the non-linearity of the underlying evolution equations.

In the context of driven diffusive systems, characterized by an applied external field and contact with boundary reservoirs, the MFT allows to define a non-equilibrium functional which plays a role analogous to the entropy in the Onsager theory. The current can be expressed as the sum of two terms. The first is linear in the thermodynamic force, here identified with the derivative of this functional, while the second, absent in equilibrium, plays the role of an effective field and is orthogonal to the thermodynamic force.

In equilibrium statistical mechanics, the connection between thermodynamic functionals and fluctuations is provided by the Einstein theory [56] of equilibrium fluctuations. Consider a system in contact with an environment; a fluctuation is a deviation of a thermodynamic variable, e.g. the density, from its equilibrium value. In the notation of [96], the probability of a fluctuation is given by

P≍e−Rminκ​T0,P\asymp e^{-{\frac{R_{\mathrm{min}}}{\kappa T_{0}}}}, (1)

where κ\kappa is the Boltzmann constant and

Rmin=Δ​U−T0​Δ​S+P0​Δ​VR_{\mathrm{min}}=\Delta U-T_{0}\Delta S+P_{0}\Delta V (2)

is the minimal work necessary to produce the fluctuation with a reversible transformation. Δ​U\Delta U, Δ​S\Delta S, Δ​V\Delta V are the corresponding variations of energy, entropy, volume, and T0T_{0}, P0P_{0} are the temperature and pressure of the environment. The exponent RminR_{\mathrm{min}} depends both on the environment and the state of the system and, with the opposite sign, is equal to the variation of the availability, see e.g. [115]. The Boltzmann-Einstein formula (1) is, we believe, the first example in physics of a large deviation estimate as it is called in modern probabilistic language. It is derived simply by inverting Boltzmann relationship between entropy and probability. In a non-equilibrium situation, like the case of a system in contact with reservoirs, we may expect a more complex entanglement between the variables describing the system and those related to the environment so that it is unlikely that quantities like U,S,…U,S,... can be simply defined. However, as we shall see, the MFT allows to establish a formula like (1), thus generalizing the notion of availability.

Dynamics plays a major role out of equilibrium. In fact what distinguishes non-equilibrium is the presence of currents flowing through the system which have to be considered together with the usual thermodynamic variables. The systems considered by the MFT are connected to several reservoirs (the environment), possibly distributed continuously on the boundary surface, characterized by their chemical potentials. The reservoirs are assumed to be much larger than the system so that their state will be essentially constant in time. When the system is put in contact with the environment, after an initial stage we expect that a description in terms of diffusive processes may apply for a wide class of microscopic dynamics. We admit also external fields such that linear response is valid. On the basis of a local equilibrium assumption, on macroscopic scale it is possible to define thermodynamic variables like the density of mass, electric charge, energy and the corresponding currents, which vary smoothly on the same scale. Microscopically, this implies that the system reaches a local equilibrium in a time which is short compared to the times typical of macroscopic evolution. So what characterizes situations in which this description can be applied is a separation of scales both in space and time. Furthermore, we assume that the system is Markovian. Namely, the currents at time tt depend on the thermodynamic variables at the same time tt. These assumptions are clearly discussed in [36, 61] and are behind the near equilibrium theories.

The proposed theory is based on the following formula for the probability of joint space-time fluctuations, at constant temperature T0T_{0}, of thermodynamic variables and currents

ℙ≍exp{−1κ​T014∫dt∫dx(j−J(ρ))⋅χ(ρ)−1(j−J(ρ))},{\mathbb{P}}\asymp\exp\Big\{-{\frac{1}{\kappa T_{0}}}\frac{1}{4}\int\!dt\!\int\!dx\,\big(j-J(\rho)\big)\cdot\chi(\rho)^{-1}\big(j-J(\rho)\big)\Big\}, (3)

where ρ\rho is the thermodynamic variable, e.g., the local density, jj is the actual value of the current, which is connected to ρ\rho by the continuity equation ∂tρ+∇⋅j=0\partial_{t}\rho+\nabla\cdot j=0, while J⁡(ρ)J(\rho) is the hydrodynamic current for the given value of ρ\rho, and χ\chi is the mobility. Formula (3) depends only on the relationship between the thermodynamic variable ρ\rho and the associated hydrodynamic current J⁡(ρ)J(\rho), that is on the constitutive equations of the system. With slight modifications, (3) can be applied also to fluctuations of the energy as in the heat conduction case. Its structure and interpretation is otherwise universal.

According to the reductionist point of view of statistical mechanics, in the realm of classical physics, (3) should be derived starting from molecules interacting with realistic forces and evolving with Newtonian dynamics. This is beyond the reach of present day mathematical tools and much simpler models have to be adopted in the reasonable hope that some essential features are adequately captured. Formula (3) can be proven, as discussed in Section VIII.8, for a wide class of stochastic interacting particle systems.

The exponent on the right hand side of (3) is proportional to the energy dissipated by the extra current j−J⁡(ρ)j-J(\rho). This can be understood relying on an active interpretation of the fluctuations. Namely, given a fluctuation, we perturb the original system by adding a (deterministic) external field for which the prescribed fluctuation becomes the trajectory followed by the system. For the fluctuation (ρ,j)(\rho,j) such external field is F=χ​(ρ)−1​(j−J⁡(ρ))F=\chi(\rho)^{-1}\big(j-J(\rho)\big). Hence, the exponent in the right hand side of (3) is proportional to ∫d​t​∫d​x​F⋅χ⁡(ρ)​F\int\!dt\int\!dx\,F\cdot\chi(\rho)F. In the case of an electric circuit χ−1\chi^{-1} is the resistance, FF is the electric field, and the above integral is the energy dissipated by the extra current j−J⁡(ρ)j-J(\rho) according to Ohm’s law.

Within the scheme of fluctuating hydrodynamics [74, 97, 124], it is possible to provide an alternative justification of (3). Namely, one postulates j=J⁡(ρ)+αj=J(\rho)+\alpha, where, conditionally on ρ\rho, α\alpha is a Gaussian random term with variance

⟨αi​(t,x),αj​(t′,x′)⟩=2​κ​T0​χi​j​(ρ)​δ​(t−t′)​δ​(x−x′)\langle\alpha_{i}(t,x),\alpha_{j}(t^{\prime},x^{\prime})\rangle=2\kappa T_{0}\,\chi_{ij}(\rho)\,\delta(t-t^{\prime})\delta(x-x^{\prime})

where the indices i,ji,j label the space directions. Formula (3) can be inferred from the Gaussian distribution of the stochastic field α\alpha. However, mathematically the random noise α\alpha is singular and induces, through the non-linear terms in the equation, ultraviolet divergences that should be properly renormalized. For Landau–Ginzburg models with constant mobility, this renormalization has been carried out in [40]. In our setting ultraviolet divergences are not relevant as formula (3) is an asymptotic expression for fluctuations of macroscopic variables defined through coarse–graining. The role of lattice gases, in particular exactly solvable models, is important similarly to what happened in the theory of critical phenomena where special models have provided explicit illustrations of the more general but often heuristic renormalization group calculations.

As the Boltzmann-Einstein formula (1), the fundamental formula (3) provides a quantitative relation between the probabilities computed in the microscopic ensemble and macroscopic variables. With respect to the theory of equilibrium thermodynamic fluctuations, formula (3) is an important generalization that holds both in equilibrium and non-equilibrium. Note the difference in notation between formulas (1) and (3): in (1) PP represents the ensemble over the space of configurations, while in (3) ℙ{\mathbb{P}} represents the ensemble over space-time trajectories. We will use this same distinction throughout the paper, both for probabilities and expectation values. The Boltzmann-Einstein formula (1) and its non-equilibrium analogue will be derived from (3).

The fundamental formula (3) leads to the prediction of rather surprising properties of diffusive systems such as the existence of phase transitions not permitted in equilibrium, the possibility of states spontaneously breaking the time translation invariance in the fluctuations of the current, the universality of the cumulants of the current. Furthermore it predicts generic long range correlations in stationary non-equilibrium states.

The behavior of the fundamental formula (3) under time reversal plays a crucial role in the MFT. As well known, in the near equilibrium Onsager theory the symmetry of the transport coefficients is deduced form a statistical form of time reversal invariance of the underlying microscopic dynamics [109]. Of course in presence of inhomogeneous boundary conditions and/or external fields, this time reversal invariance is lost. However in the systems considered, we assume that given a microscopic path it is possible, by adding a suitable field, to modify the dynamics in such a way that the corresponding evolution is given by the time reversed path. At the level of stationary ensembles over space-time trajectories, the time reversed ensemble is then defined by assigning to a backward path the probability of the forward path under the original ensemble. In particular, the stationary macroscopic currents are inverted under the time reversal operation. For stochastic lattice gases the microscopic dynamics is Markovian and the previous definition can be directly implemented.

The splitting of the hydrodynamic current into two orthogonal terms discussed before is derived as a simple consequence of the transformation properties of (3) under time reversal. The even part of the current is connected with the work of thermodynamic forces active within the system in the relaxation or creation of a non-stationary state while the odd part is connected with the dissipation necessary to keep the system in a non-equilibrium state.

For the convenience of the reader we summarize the main achievements of the MFT.

From the fundamental formula (3) for space-time fluctuations we derive a dynamical variational principle which expresses the probability of density fluctuations of the stationary ensemble. This leads naturally to the definition of a thermodynamic functional called in the following the quasi-potential and denoted V⁡(ρ)V(\rho). The argument ρ\rho represents generic thermodynamic variables like the densities of the different types of matter composing the system. The quasi-potential is the natural extension to non-equilibrium of the availability of classical thermodynamics. In the context of finite dimensional diffusion processes, the quasi potential was first introduced by Freidlin and Wentzell, [62]. A related analysis, motivated by applications to optics, can be found in [70].

The quasi-potential satisfies an infinite dimensional Hamilton-Jacobi equation which is equivalent to the splitting of the current. The density correlation functions can be computed by expanding the Hamilton-Jacobi equation around the stationary density and exhibit, generically, long range behavior. In non-equilibrium the quasi-potential VV may have singularities not permitted in equilibrium. These singularities do occur in a model with external field and inhomogeneous boundary conditions, [18].

The splitting of the current is relevant in the analysis of non-equilibrium thermodynamic transformations. Consider a slow (quasi static) transformation leading from a stationary state to another one. Since to maintain a non-equilibrium stationary state it is necessary to dissipate a positive amount of energy per unit time, the work associated to the odd part of the current will diverge when the time diverges. The equation expressing the energy balance between the system and the environment becomes then meaningless. To obtain equations in finite terms one can subtract the divergent part and define a renormalized work. It turns out that the renormalized work satisfies a Clausius type inequality with respect to which quasi-static transformations are optimal. The idea of renormalizing the work involved in a non-equilibrium transformation goes back to [112].

The MFT allows a detailed mathematical description of quasi-static thermodynamic transformations that in textbooks are discussed only in words. This is achieved through an expansion of the energy balance and of the macroscopic evolution (hydrodynamic) equations in terms of the inverse duration of the transformation. In this expansion the diverging terms cancel and we obtain new relations among finite quantities which in principle can be tested experimentally.

One of the most interesting topic in the MFT is provided by current fluctuations. From the fundamental formula (3) it is possible to derive the rate function describing the behavior of the average current over a long time interval TT, namely

ℙ≍exp⁡{−β​T​Φ​(J)},\mathbb{P}\asymp\exp\big\{-\beta T\Phi(J)\big\}, (4)

where ℙ\mathbb{P} is the probability of the fluctuation JJ of the averaged current and β=1/(κ​T0)\beta=1/(\kappa T_{0}). The temperature of the environment T0T_{0} (not to be confused with the time TT) will be mostly considered constant. The functional Φ\Phi, first introduced in [14], is defined by a variational principle and it is a genuine (convex) thermodynamic functional. As pointed out in the same paper, the singularities of Φ\Phi correspond to dynamical phase transitions. For some models it has then been shown [15, 25] that for suitable values of JJ these transitions corresponds to a spontaneous breaking of the time translation invariance.

In the general context of non-equilibrium processes, an important role is played by the so-called Fluctuation Theorems [81, 39, 67, 100, 76, 95, 58, 98]. This topic will appear only marginally in this paper and we refer the interested reader to the reviews [66, 102, 31]. There are other relevant topics not covered as each of them would require an extended review. Among these topics we mention the so-called stochastic thermodynamics [121], the general approach to non–equilibrium developed in [114], path integral approaches [85], algebraic techniques for microscopic dynamics [120], the analysis of rare fluctuations in finite dimensional dynamical systems, with the related discussion on current fluctuations [103], and in reaction–population systems [127].

Reader’s guide

The aim of this review is to present the MFT as an effective macroscopic theory, providing a working knowledge of the theory rather than a chronological exposition of its main results. For this reason, some computations are detailed when useful.

The general framework of driven diffusive systems and the basic principles are illustrated in Section II.

Part of the material in Section III, which deals with thermodynamic transformations between non–equilibrium states, is presented here for the first time. We discuss quantitatively the interplay between fluctuations and thermodynamics. This section is not however used in the sequel and can be omitted on first reading.

Section IV contains the core of the MFT, deducing the statistics of density and current from the fundamental formula.

Section V discusses few models where the quasi-potential can be computed (almost) explicitly. While we use the terminology of underlying microscopic models, we emphasize that the computations are macroscopic and require only the knowledge of the transport coefficients.

Section VI develops one of the most relevant consequences of the MFT by deriving the statistics of the time averaged current.

Section VII contains more specialized material related to hyperbolic conservation laws. Although these are not diffusive systems, the fluctuation formula can be obtained from the MFT by a singular limit procedure. This section can be omitted on first reading.

Finally, Section VIII describes microscopic models of stochastic lattice gases, showing how the general principles of the MFT can be analytically derived. This Section can be read independently of the others and can be anticipated if the reader wishes to do so.

II Basics of the macroscopic fluctuation theory

We introduce the hydrodynamic description of out of equilibrium driven diffusive systems which are characterized by conservation laws. We then introduce the fundamental formula of the MFT and discuss its behavior under time-reversal together with its main implications. We restrict to the case of a single conservation law, e.g., the conservation of the mass.

II.1 Hydrodynamic description

We denote by Λ⊂ℝd\Lambda\subset{\mathbb{R}}^{d} the bounded region occupied by the system, by ∂Λ\partial\Lambda the boundary of Λ\Lambda, by xx the macroscopic space coordinates and by tt the macroscopic time. The system is in contact with boundary reservoirs, characterized by their chemical potential λ⁡(t,x)\lambda(t,x), and under the action of an external field E⁡(t,x)E(t,x).

At the macroscopic level the system is completely described by the local density ρ⁡(t,x)\rho(t,x) and the local current j⁡(t,x)j(t,x). Their evolution is given by the continuity equation together with the constitutive equation which expresses the current as a function of the density. Namely,

{∂tρ⁡(t)+∇⋅j⁡(t)=0,j⁡(t)=J⁡(t,ρ⁡(t)),\begin{cases}\partial_{t}\rho(t)+\nabla\cdot j(t)=0,\\ j(t)=J(t,\rho(t)),\end{cases} (5)

where we omit the explicit dependence on the space variable x∈Λx\in\Lambda. For driven diffusive systems the constitutive equation takes the form

J(t,ρ)=−D(ρ)∇ρ+χ(ρ)E(t),J(t,\rho)=-D(\rho)\nabla\rho+\chi(\rho)\,E(t), (6)

where the diffusion coefficient D⁡(ρ)D(\rho) and the mobility χ⁡(ρ)\chi(\rho) are d×dd\times d symmetric and positive definite matrices. Equation (6) relies on the diffusive approximation and on the linear response to the external field. The evolution of the density is thus given by the driven diffusive equation

∂tρ(t)+∇⋅(χ(ρ)E(t))=∇⋅(D(ρ)∇ρ).\partial_{t}\rho(t)+\nabla\cdot\big(\chi(\rho)E(t)\big)=\nabla\cdot\big(D(\rho)\nabla\rho\big). (7)

We emphasize that the diffusion coefficient and the mobility do depend on the value of the local density. Accordingly, equation (7) is nonlinear and this is the source of interesting phenomena. In contrast, the near equilibrium approximation can be obtained by expanding ρ\rho around some (constant) equilibrium value so that (7) becomes linear.

The transport coefficients DD and χ\chi are not arbitrary matrices. The characterization of equilibrium states implies (see Section V.1) that they satisfy the local Einstein relation

D⁡(ρ)=χ⁡(ρ)​f′′​(ρ),D(\rho)=\chi(\rho)\,f^{\prime\prime}(\rho), (8)

where ff is the equilibrium free energy per unit volume.

Equations (5)–(6) have to be supplemented by the appropriate boundary condition on ∂Λ\partial\Lambda due to the interaction with the external reservoirs. If λ⁡(t,x)\lambda(t,x), x∈∂Λx\in\partial\Lambda, is the chemical potential of the external reservoirs, the boundary condition reads

f′​(ρ⁡(t,x))=λ⁡(t,x),x∈∂Λ.f^{\prime}\big(\rho(t,x)\big)=\lambda(t,x),\qquad x\in\partial\Lambda. (9)

While in the near equilibrium approximation the variation of λ\lambda on ∂Λ\partial\Lambda is required to be small, we shall not restrict to this case.

One of the achievements of mathematical physics is the derivation of the hydrodynamic equations (5)–(9) as laws of large numbers from an underlying microscopic stochastic dynamics in the diffusive scaling limit [60, 124, 87]. This means taking the limit of infinitely many degrees of freedom and rescaling space and time keeping x2/tx^{2}/t fixed.

We now restrict the discussion to time-independent chemical potential λ⁡(x)\lambda(x) and external field E⁡(x)E(x). We denote by ρ¯=ρ¯λ,E\bar{\rho}=\bar{\rho}_{\lambda,E} the stationary solution of (7),(9),

{∇⋅J(ρ¯)=∇⋅(−D(ρ¯)∇ρ¯+χ(ρ¯)E)=0,f′(ρ¯(x))=λ(x),x∈∂Λ.\begin{cases}\nabla\cdot J(\bar{\rho})=\nabla\cdot\big(-D(\bar{\rho})\nabla\bar{\rho}+\chi(\bar{\rho})\,E\big)=0,\\ f^{\prime}(\bar{\rho}(x))=\lambda(x),\qquad x\in\partial\Lambda.\end{cases} (10)

We will assume that this stationary solution is unique. The stationary density profile ρ¯\bar{\rho} is characterized by the vanishing of the divergence of the associated current, ∇⋅J⁡(ρ¯)=0\nabla\cdot J(\bar{\rho})=0. A special situation is when the current itself vanishes, J⁡(ρ¯)=0J(\bar{\rho})=0; if this is the case we say that the system is in an equilibrium state. Uniqueness to (10) can be proven in one dimension when the external field EE is constant in space. It can also be proven in general, by a perturbation argument, near equilibrium. In the case of several conserved quantities, i.e. when ρ\rho is not a scalar, uniqueness may fail.

Homogeneous equilibrium states correspond to the case in which the external field vanishes and the chemical potential is constant. The stationary solution is then constant and satisfies f′​(ρ¯λ,0)=λf^{\prime}(\bar{\rho}_{\lambda,0})=\lambda. Inhomogeneous equilibrium states correspond to the case in which the external field is gradient, E=−∇UE=-\nabla U, and it is possible to choose the arbitrary constant in the definition of UU such that U⁡(x)=−λ⁡(x)U(x)=-\lambda(x), x∈∂Λx\in\partial\Lambda. By the Einstein relation (8), the stationary solution satisfies −f′​(ρ¯λ,E​(x))=U⁡(x)-f^{\prime}\big(\bar{\rho}_{\lambda,E}(x)\big)=U(x) and the stationary current vanishes, J⁡(ρ¯λ,E)=0J(\bar{\rho}_{\lambda,E})=0. Examples of inhomogeneous equilibrium states in presence of an external field are provided by a still atmosphere in the gravitational field or by sedimentation in a centrifuge.

II.2 Fundamental formula

In the context of equilibrium systems, the Einstein theory of thermodynamic fluctuations establishes a connection between the thermodynamic functionals and the probability of observing a fluctuation. The extension of this theory to non-equilibrium stationary states is provided by the fundamental formula (3), describing the joint fluctuations of thermodynamic variables and currents at the level of space-time paths.

Let ℙρ0{\mathbb{P}}_{\rho_{0}} be the statistical ensemble on microscopic trajectories such that at time t=T0t=T_{0} the density profile is ρ0\rho_{0}. Consider a path (ρ,j)(\rho,j) satisfying the continuity equation in (5), the boundary condition (9), and ρ⁡(T0)=ρ0\rho(T_{0})=\rho_{0}. The fundamental formula (3) can be written in detail as

ℙρ0​((ρε​(t),jε​(t))≈(ρ⁡(t),j⁡(t)),t∈[T0,T1])≍exp⁡{−ε−d​ℐ[T0,T1]​(ρ,j)}\begin{split}&{\mathbb{P}}_{\rho_{0}}\big((\rho_{\varepsilon}(t),j_{\varepsilon}(t))\approx(\rho(t),j(t))\,,\,t\in[T_{0},T_{1}]\,\big)\\ &\quad\asymp\exp\big\{-\varepsilon^{-d}\,\mathcal{I}_{[{T_{0}},{T_{1}}]}(\rho,j)\big\}\end{split} (11)

where the rate functional ℐ\mathcal{I} is

ℐ[T0,T1]​(ρ,j)=14​∫T0T1d​t​∫Λd​x​[j−J⁡(t,ρ)]⋅χ​(ρ)−1​[j−J⁡(t,ρ)].\begin{split}&\mathcal{I}_{[{T_{0}},{T_{1}}]}(\rho,j)\\ &\quad=\frac{1}{4}\int_{{T_{0}}}^{{T_{1}}}\!\!dt\int_{\Lambda}\!dx\,[j-J(t,\rho)]\cdot\chi(\rho)^{-1}[j-J(t,\rho)].\end{split} (12)

In (11) ε≪1\varepsilon\ll 1 is a dimensionless scaling factor, e.g., the ratio between the microscopic length scale (say the typical inter-molecular distance) and the macroscopic one, and the symbol ≍\asymp denotes logarithmic equivalence as ε→0\varepsilon\to 0. We denote by ρε\rho_{\varepsilon} the empirical density, that is, ρε​(x)\rho_{\varepsilon}(x) is the density of particles in a macroscopically small volume around xx. Analogously, jεj_{\varepsilon} denotes the empirical current, that is jε​(t,x)⋅n^​d​σ​d​tj_{\varepsilon}(t,x)\cdot\hat{n}d\sigma dt is the flow of mass across a macroscopically small surface d​σd\sigma centered at xx and orthogonal to the unit vector n^\hat{n} in the macroscopic time interval [t,t+d​t][t,t+dt]. The factor ε−d\varepsilon^{-d} is proportional to the number of particles in the macroscopic volume. It plays the role of Avogadro’s number (implicit in the Boltzmann constant) in (3).

The interpretation of (11)–(12) is quite intuitive and already discussed in the Introduction. In Section VIII these formulas will be derived from an underlying microscopic dynamics in the case of stochastic lattice gases.

Assume that the external drivings do not depend on time and let PP be the stationary ensemble, that is the invariant measure of the underlying microscopic dynamics. Note that PP is an ensemble on the configuration space. The probability of observing a fluctuation ρ\rho of the density profile can be written in the form

P⁡(ρε≈ρ)≍exp⁡{−ε−d​V​(ρ)}.P(\rho_{\varepsilon}\approx\rho)\asymp\exp\big\{-\varepsilon^{-d}\,V(\rho)\big\}. (13)

While for equilibrium states VV is given by the Boltzmann-Einstein formula (1)-(2), in non–equilibrium we do not have a general formula for VV. In the following VV will be called the quasi–potential, according to the terminology of [62]. As we show in the following sections, the MFT provides characterizations of the quasi-potential that can be used either for exact computations or for perturbation expansions.

Let ℙ{\mathbb{P}} be the stationary process, that is the ensemble on paths for which the initial conditions are sampled according to the stationary ensemble PP. If we make a Markovian assumption on the microscopic dynamics, combining (13) and (11), the fluctuation formula for the stationary process ℙ{\mathbb{P}} is

ℙ⁡((ρε​(t),jε​(t))≈(ρ⁡(t),j⁡(t)),t∈[T0,T1])≍exp⁡{−ε−d​ℛ[T0,T1]​(ρ,j)},\begin{split}&{\mathbb{P}}\big((\rho_{\varepsilon}(t),j_{\varepsilon}(t))\approx(\rho(t),j(t))\,,\,t\in[T_{0},T_{1}]\,\big)\\ &\quad\asymp\exp\big\{-\varepsilon^{-d}\,{\mathcal{R}}_{[{T_{0}},{T_{1}}]}(\rho,j)\big\},\end{split} (14)

where

ℛ[T0,T1]​(ρ,j)=V⁡(ρ⁡(T0))+ℐ[T0,T1]​(ρ,j).{\mathcal{R}}_{[{T_{0}},{T_{1}}]}(\rho,j)=V(\rho(T_{0}))+\mathcal{I}_{[{T_{0}},{T_{1}}]}(\rho,j)\,. (15)

Formula (15) states that at time T0T_{0} the density profile ρ⁡(T0)\rho(T_{0}) is sampled according to the stationary ensemble and the corresponding asymptotic probability is given by (13). Then, the probability of following the path (ρ,j)(\rho,j) in the time interval [T0,T1][T_{0},T_{1}] with initial condition ρ⁡(T0)\rho(T_{0}) is given by (11). We point out that (15) may hold also when the microscopic dynamics is not Markovian provided the Markov property is recovered at the macroscopic level.

II.3 Time reversal and its consequences

We analyze the behavior of the fundamental formula (14)–(15) under time reversal and deduce, in particular, the orthogonal decomposition of the hydrodynamic current.

The time reversal operator θ\theta on density and current paths is defined as [θ​ρ]​(t)=ρ​(−t)[\theta\rho](t)=\rho(-t), [θ​j]​(t)=−j​(−t)[\theta j](t)=-j(-t). Denote by ℙ∗{\mathbb{P}}^{*} the time reversal of ℙ{\mathbb{P}}, that is ℙ∗=ℙ∘θ−1{\mathbb{P}}^{*}={\mathbb{P}}\circ\theta^{-1}. In words, ℙ∗{\mathbb{P}}^{*} is defined by assigning to a backward path the probability of the forward path under ℙ{\mathbb{P}}.

Then ℙ∗{\mathbb{P}}^{*} is the stationary processes associated to some dynamics that we call adjoint. When ℙ{\mathbb{P}} is Markov then ℙ∗{\mathbb{P}}^{*} is also Markov and has the same stationary ensemble. By definition,

ℙ⁡(ρε≈ρ,jε≈j,t∈[T0,T1])=ℙ∗​(ρε≈θ​ρ,jε≈θ​j,t∈[−T1,−T0]).\begin{split}&{\mathbb{P}}\Big(\rho_{\varepsilon}\approx\rho\,,\,j_{\varepsilon}\approx j\,,\,t\in[T_{0},T_{1}]\Big)\\ &\qquad={\mathbb{P}}^{*}\Big(\rho_{\varepsilon}\approx\theta\rho\,,\,j_{\varepsilon}\approx\theta j\,,\,t\in[-T_{1},-T_{0}]\Big).\end{split} (16)

At the level of large deviations the identity (16) implies

ℛ[T0,T1]​(ρ,j)=ℛ[−T1,−T0]∗​(θ​ρ,θ​j),{\mathcal{R}}_{[T_{0},T_{1}]}(\rho,j)={\mathcal{R}}^{*}_{[-T_{1},-T_{0}]}(\theta\rho,\theta j), (17)

where ℛ∗{\mathcal{R}}^{*} is the large deviation functional for the stationary adjoint process.

Since the stationary ensembles of process and its time reversal coincide, the functional ℛ∗{\mathcal{R}}^{*} can be written as

ℛ[T0,T1]∗​(ρ,j)=V⁡(ρ⁡(T0))+ℐ[T0,T1]∗​(ρ,j).{\mathcal{R}}^{*}_{[T_{0},T_{1}]}(\rho,j)\;=\;V(\rho(T_{0}))+\mathcal{I}^{*}_{[T_{0},T_{1}]}(\rho,j). (18)

From equations (15), (17) and (18), we have

V⁡(ρ⁡(T0))+ℐ[T0,T1]​(ρ,j)=V⁡(ρ⁡(T1))+ℐ[−T1,−T0]∗​(θ​ρ,θ​j).V(\rho(T_{0}))+\mathcal{I}_{[T_{0},T_{1}]}(\rho,j)=V(\rho(T_{1}))+\mathcal{I}_{[-T_{1},-T_{0}]}^{*}(\theta\rho,\theta j). (19)

We now assume that the adjoint dynamics admits a hydrodynamic description of the form (5)–(9) with a suitable external field. This assumption is very natural from the physical point of view. It expresses the fact that empirically by acting on a system with suitable external fields we can invert the evolution of a process. For example, we can arrange the action on the system in such a way that heat flows from a lower temperature to a higher temperature reservoir. In view of this assumption, the adjoint process satisfies a dynamical large deviations principle of the same form as (11) with ℙ\mathbb{P} replaced by ℙ∗\mathbb{P}^{*} and ℐ\mathcal{I} replaced by ℐ∗\mathcal{I}^{*} where

ℐ[T0,T1]∗​(ρ,j)=14​∫T0T1d​t​∫Λd​x​[j−J∗​(ρ)]⋅χ​(ρ)−1​[j−J∗​(ρ)]\mathcal{I}^{*}_{[T_{0},T_{1}]}(\rho,j)=\frac{1}{4}\int_{T_{0}}^{T_{1}}\!dt\int_{\Lambda}\!dx\,[j-J^{*}(\rho)]\cdot\chi(\rho)^{-1}[j-J^{*}(\rho)] (20)

in which J∗​(ρ)J^{*}(\rho) expresses the constitutive relationship of the adjoint hydrodynamics.

Relation (19) has far reaching consequences. By choosing [T0,T1]=[−T,T][T_{0},T_{1}]=[-T,T], dividing both sides by 2​T2T, and taking the limit T→0T\rightarrow 0, we find

∫Λdxδ​Vδ​ρ∇⋅j=12∫Λdx[J(ρ)+J∗(ρ)]⋅χ(ρ)−1j−14∫Λdx[J(ρ)+J∗(ρ)]⋅χ(ρ)−1[J(ρ)−J∗(ρ)],\begin{split}&\int_{\Lambda}dx\,\frac{\delta V}{\delta\rho}\nabla\cdot j=\frac{1}{2}\int_{\Lambda}dx\,[J(\rho)+J^{*}(\rho)]\cdot\chi(\rho)^{-1}j\\ &\quad-\frac{1}{4}\int_{\Lambda}dx\,[J(\rho)+J^{*}(\rho)]\cdot\chi(\rho)^{-1}[J(\rho)-J^{*}(\rho)],\end{split} (21)

which has to be satisfied for any ρ\rho and jj. Since the path ρ⁡(t)\rho(t) satisfies the boundary condition (9), in (21) we can restrict to profiles ρ\rho satisfying (9). For such profiles δ​V/δ​ρ\delta V/\delta\rho vanishes at the boundary (see Section IV.1), integrating by parts the left hand side of (21) we obtain that

{J(ρ)+J∗(ρ)=−2χ(ρ)∇δ​Vδ​ρ∫Λd​x​J​(ρ)⋅χ​(ρ)−1​J​(ρ)=∫Λd​x​J∗​(ρ)⋅χ​(ρ)−1​J∗​(ρ).\left\{\begin{split}&J(\rho)+J^{*}(\rho)=-2\chi(\rho)\nabla\frac{\delta V}{\delta\rho}\\ &\int_{\Lambda}dx\,J(\rho)\cdot\chi(\rho)^{-1}J(\rho)=\int_{\Lambda}dx\,J^{*}(\rho)\cdot\chi(\rho)^{-1}J^{*}(\rho).\end{split}\right. (22)

These two equations are symmetric in JJ and J∗J^{*}. The first equation may be considered as a fluctuation–dissipation relation for the currents.

We now define the symmetric current JSJ_{S} by

JS(ρ)=−χ(ρ)∇δ​Vδ​ρ.J_{S}(\rho)=-\chi(\rho)\nabla\frac{\delta V}{\delta\rho}. (23)

Since the stationary density ρ¯\bar{\rho} is a minimum for VV, then (δ​V/δ​ρ)​(ρ¯)=0(\delta V/\delta\rho)(\bar{\rho})=0. The symmetric current thus vanishes at the stationary profile,

JS​(ρ¯)= 0.J_{S}(\bar{\rho})\;=\;0. (24)

We rewrite the hydrodynamic current as

J⁡(ρ)=JS​(ρ)+JA​(ρ),J(\rho)=J_{S}(\rho)+J_{A}(\rho), (25)

which defines the antisymmetric current JAJ_{A}.

In view of these definitions, equations (22) become

{J∗​(ρ)=JS​(ρ)−JA​(ρ),∫Λd​x​JS​(ρ)⋅χ​(ρ)−1​JA​(ρ)=0.\left\{\begin{split}&J^{*}(\rho)\;=\;J_{S}(\rho)-J_{A}(\rho)\;,\\ &\int_{\Lambda}dx\,J_{S}(\rho)\cdot\chi(\rho)^{-1}J_{A}(\rho)=0.\end{split}\right. (26)

In this way we see that the splitting of the currents and the orthogonality property are a consequence of the existence of a time reversed dynamics admitting an hydrodynamic behavior. Moreover, inserting the first of the two equations (22) into the second we obtain the equation for VV

∫Λdx∇δ​Vδ​ρ⋅χ(ρ)∇δ​Vδ​ρ−∫Λdxδ​Vδ​ρ∇⋅J(ρ)=0.\int_{\Lambda}dx\,\nabla\frac{\delta V}{\delta\rho}\cdot\chi(\rho)\nabla\frac{\delta V}{\delta\rho}-\int_{\Lambda}dx\,\frac{\delta V}{\delta\rho}\nabla\cdot J(\rho)=0\,. (27)

This will be interpreted as a Hamilton-Jacobi equation. As shown in [12], VV is the maximal positive solution to (27) which vanishes when ρ=ρ¯\rho=\bar{\rho}. Since J⁡(ρ)J(\rho) and J∗​(ρ)J^{*}(\rho) play a symmetric role in (22), the Hamilton-Jacobi equation (27) holds replacing J⁡(ρ)J(\rho) with J∗​(ρ)J^{*}(\rho).

In view of the fluctuation-dissipation relation (22), we may write the hydrodynamic equation and the adjoint hydrodynamic equation as

∂tρ=∇⋅(χ(ρ)∇δ​Vδ​ρ)−∇⋅JA(ρ),∂tρ=∇⋅(χ(ρ)∇δ​Vδ​ρ)+∇⋅JA(ρ)\begin{split}\partial_{t}\rho&=\nabla\cdot\Big(\chi(\rho)\nabla\frac{\delta V}{\delta\rho}\Big)-\nabla\cdot J_{A}(\rho),\\ \partial_{t}\rho&=\nabla\cdot\Big(\chi(\rho)\nabla\frac{\delta V}{\delta\rho}\Big)+\nabla\cdot J_{A}(\rho)\end{split}

respectively. Another way of writing the adjoint hydrodynamic equation is

∂tρ=−∇⋅D(ρ)∇ρ+∇⋅χ(ρ)(E+2∇δ​Vδ​ρ).\partial_{t}\rho=-\nabla\cdot D(\rho)\nabla\rho+\nabla\cdot\chi(\rho)\,\Big(E+2\nabla\frac{\delta V}{\delta\rho}\Big). (28)

In spite of its appearance, the forward evolution of this equation is well posed. Indeed, the added external field 2∇(δV/δρ)2\nabla(\delta V/\delta\rho) produces a second order term which makes the equation of parabolic type. In the case of equilibrium states the adjoint hydrodynamics coincides with the original one.

We illustrate the decomposition of the current by giving three simple examples.

Equilibrium states. Equilibrium states, homogeneous and inhomogeneous, are characterized by J⁡(ρ¯)=0J(\bar{\rho})=0. In this case the quasi-potential VV is given by (see Section V.1)

V⁡(ρ)=∫Λd​x​[f⁡(ρ)−f⁡(ρ¯)−f′​(ρ¯)​(ρ−ρ¯)].V(\rho)=\int_{\Lambda}\!dx\,\big[f(\rho)-f(\bar{\rho})-f^{\prime}(\bar{\rho})(\rho-\bar{\rho})\big]. (29)

Observe that, due to the convexity of ff, VV is convex, positive and is minimal on the stationary density profile ρ¯\bar{\rho}. The Einstein relation (8) and J⁡(ρ¯)=0J(\bar{\rho})=0 imply that

J(ρ)=−χ(ρ)∇δ​Vδ​ρ.J(\rho)=-\chi(\rho)\nabla\frac{\delta V}{\delta\rho}. (30)

Hence, the antisymmetric current vanishes, JA=0J_{A}=0, and the current, as in Onsager theory, is proportional to the thermodynamic force. In geometrical terms, the hydrodynamic evolution can thus be viewed as the flow along the steepest descent of VV with an intensity given by the mobility.

Circulation of a fluid in a ring. In absence of an external field, we have an equilibrium state that fits in the scheme just discussed: the density ρ¯\bar{\rho} is constant, and the current J⁡(ρ¯)J(\bar{\rho}) is zero. Moreover, if we start with an arbitrary density profile ρ\rho, the system evolves to the equilibrium according to the hydrodynamic equation

∂tρ=−∇⋅J(ρ)=∇⋅(χ(ρ)∇δ​Vδ​ρ),\partial_{t}\rho=-\nabla\cdot J(\rho)=\nabla\cdot\Big(\chi(\rho)\nabla\frac{\delta V}{\delta\rho}\Big),

where V⁡(ρ)V(\rho) is given by (29). In this case, by conservation of mass, the expression (29) simplifies since the last term does not contribute.

When we switch on a constant weak driving field EE tangent to the ring, in the stationary regime the particle density ρ¯\bar{\rho} is still constant, but there is a non-zero current J⁡(ρ¯)=χ⁡(ρ¯)​EJ(\bar{\rho})=\chi(\bar{\rho})E. The corresponding hydrodynamic equation is

∂tρ=−∇⋅J(ρ)=∇⋅(χ(ρ)∇δ​Vδ​ρ−χ(ρ)E).\partial_{t}\rho=-\nabla\cdot J(\rho)=\nabla\cdot\Big(\chi(\rho)\nabla\frac{\delta V}{\delta\rho}-\chi(\rho)E\Big). (31)

The stationary non-equilibrium situation, with density ρ¯\bar{\rho} and current J⁡(ρ¯)J(\bar{\rho}), is not invariant under time reversal. In fact, time reversal corresponds to inverting the current, namely to changing EE with −E-E. Therefore, the hydrodynamic equation for the time reversed system will be

∂tρ=−∇⋅J∗(ρ)=∇⋅(χ(ρ)∇δ​Vδ​ρ+χ(ρ)E),\partial_{t}\rho=-\nabla\cdot J^{*}(\rho)=\nabla\cdot\Big(\chi(\rho)\nabla\frac{\delta V}{\delta\rho}+\chi(\rho)E\Big), (32)

which corresponds to

JS(ρ)=−χ(ρ)∇δ​Vδ​ρ,JA(ρ)=χ(ρ)E.J_{S}(\rho)=-\chi(\rho)\nabla\frac{\delta V}{\delta\rho}\,\,,\,\,\,\,J_{A}(\rho)=\chi(\rho)E\,. (33)

A simple computation shows that these two components satisfy the orthogonality condition in (26).

Rarefied gas with boundary reservoirs. For simplicity we consider again to the one-dimensional case. When we can neglect the interaction among the particles the transport coefficients are D⁡(ρ)=D0D(\rho)=D_{0}, χ⁡(ρ)=χ0​ρ\chi(\rho)=\chi_{0}\rho where D0,χ0D_{0},\chi_{0} are constants, and the equilibrium free energy per unit volume is given by f⁡(ρ)=(D0/χ0)​ρ​log⁡ρf(\rho)=(D_{0}/\chi_{0})\rho\log\rho. The quasi-potential V⁡(ρ)V(\rho) is again given by (29).

Letting Λ=(0,L)\Lambda=(0,L), λ⁡(0)=λ0\lambda(0)=\lambda_{0}, λ⁡(L)=λ1\lambda(L)=\lambda_{1}, the stationary density profile is ρ¯​(x)=ρ0​(1−x/L)+ρ1​x/L\bar{\rho}(x)=\rho_{0}(1-x/L)+\rho_{1}x/L where ρ0\rho_{0} and ρ1\rho_{1} are the densities associated to λ0\lambda_{0} and λ1\lambda_{1} by (9). In particular, (∇ρ¯)​(x)=(ρ1−ρ0)/L(\nabla\bar{\rho})(x)=(\rho_{1}-\rho_{0})/L. In this case the hydrodynamic equation reduces to the heat equation and the constitutive equation to

J(ρ)=−D0∇ρ=−χ(ρ)∇δ​Vδ​ρ−D0∇ρ¯ρ¯ρ.J(\rho)\,=\,-D_{0}\nabla\rho\;=\;-\,\chi(\rho)\nabla\frac{\delta V}{\delta\rho}\,-\,D_{0}\frac{\nabla\bar{\rho}}{\bar{\rho}}\,\rho\;.

To reverse the current in the stationary state we have to add a suitable external field. The unique expression for the adjoint current such that J∗​(ρ¯)=−J⁡(ρ¯)J^{*}(\bar{\rho})=-J(\bar{\rho}) is

J∗​(ρ)=−D0∇ρ+ 2D0∇ρ¯ρ¯ρ,\begin{split}J^{*}(\rho)\,&=\,-D_{0}\nabla\rho\;+\;2D_{0}\frac{\nabla\bar{\rho}}{\bar{\rho}}\,\rho,\end{split}

which corresponds to

JS​(ρ)=D0​(∇ρ¯ρ¯​ρ−∇ρ),JA​(ρ)=−D0​∇ρ¯ρ¯​ρ,J_{S}(\rho)=D_{0}\Big(\frac{\nabla\bar{\rho}}{\bar{\rho}}\,\rho-\nabla\rho\Big),\,\,\,\,\,\,J_{A}(\rho)=-D_{0}\,\frac{\nabla\bar{\rho}}{\bar{\rho}}\,\rho, (34)

which satisfy the orthogonality in (26).

The decomposition (25) of the current is entirely general for driven diffusive systems. It depends on the chemical potential λ\lambda and the external field EE and can not be inferred by inspection as in the simple examples discussed above. We mention the general approach to non-equilibrium introduced in [114] that is based on a separation of the evolution equations into dissipative and conservative terms which may remind this decomposition.

III Thermodynamic transformations

As clearly stated in classical textbooks, e.g. [36, 96], in a transformation between equilibrium states a system necessarily goes through deviations from equilibrium which are small if the transformation is quasi-static. Classical thermodynamics is unable to describe this intrinsically dynamic aspect. The aim of this section is to develop a coherent dynamical approach to thermodynamic transformations covering both equilibrium and non-equilibrium states [20, 21].

III.1 Non-Equilibrium Clausius inequality

The second law of thermodynamics can be expressed as follows. Consider a system in an equilibrium state in thermal contact with an environment at a given temperature. The system then undergoes an isothermal transformation to a final state. By denoting with WW the mechanical work done on the system,

W≥Δ​FW\geq\Delta F (35)

where Δ​F\Delta F is the difference of the free energy between the final and the initial state. If equality holds the transformation is said to be reversible. It can be implemented by performing very slow variations so that the system goes through a sequence of equilibrium states. With a slight abuse of terminology, we shall refer to (35) as the Clausius inequality.

We present a dynamical derivation of the Clausius inequality based on the hydrodynamic description and the local Einstein relation (8). Consider a system in a time dependent environment, that is, EE and λ\lambda depend on time, as described in Section II.1. The work done by the environment on the system in the time interval [0,T][0,T] is

W[0,T]=∫0Td​t​{∫Λd​x​j​(t)⋅E⁡(t)−∫∂Λd​σ​λ​(t)​j​(t)⋅n^},\begin{split}W_{[0,T]}=&\int_{0}^{T}\!dt\,\Big\{\int_{\Lambda}\!dx\,j(t)\cdot E(t)-\int_{\partial\Lambda}\!d\sigma\,\lambda(t)\>j(t)\cdot\hat{n}\Big\},\end{split} (36)

where n^\hat{n} is the outer normal to ∂Λ\partial\Lambda and d​σd\sigma is the surface measure on ∂Λ\partial\Lambda. The first term on the right hand side is the energy provided by the external field while the second is the energy provided by the reservoirs.

Fix time dependent paths λ⁡(t)\lambda(t) of the chemical potential and E⁡(t)E(t) of the driving field. Given a density profile ρ0\rho_{0}, let ρ⁡(t)\rho(t), j⁡(t)j(t), t≥0t\geq 0, be the solution of (5)–(9) with initial condition ρ0\rho_{0}. By using the Einstein relation (8) and the boundary condition f′​(ρ⁡(t))=λ⁡(t)f^{\prime}(\rho(t))=\lambda(t), an application of the divergence theorem yields

W[0,T]=F⁡(ρ⁡(T))−F⁡(ρ⁡(0))+∫0Tdt∫Λdxj(t)⋅χ(ρ(t))−1j(t),\begin{split}W_{[0,T]}\,&=\,F(\rho(T))-F(\rho(0))\\ &+\,\int_{0}^{T}\!dt\int_{\Lambda}\!dx\;j(t)\cdot\chi(\rho(t))^{-1}j(t),\end{split} (37)

where FF is the equilibrium free energy functional,

F⁡(ρ)=∫Λd​x​f​(ρ⁡(x)).F(\rho)=\int_{\Lambda}\!dx\>f(\rho(x)). (38)

Equation (37) is not simply a rewriting of (36), as it depends on a physical principle, the local Einstein relationship.

Since the second term on the right hand side of (37) is positive, we deduce the Clausius inequality (35) with Δ​F=F⁡(ρ1)−F⁡(ρ0)\Delta F=F(\rho_{1})-F(\rho_{0}) for arbitrary density profiles ρ0=ρ⁡(0)\rho_{0}=\rho(0), ρ1=ρ⁡(T)\rho_{1}=\rho(T). Note that this derivation holds both for equilibrium and non-equilibrium systems.

For equilibrium states, the former dynamical derivation of Clausius inequality allows to discuss precisely in which sense quasi-static transformations approximate reversible transformations. We consider the simpler case of spatially homogeneous equilibrium states. As we mentioned before, such states are characterized by a vanishing external field EE and by a constant chemical potential λ\lambda. In this case the stationary solution ρ¯\bar{\rho} of the hydrodynamic equations (5)–(9) is the constant ρ¯\bar{\rho} satisfying f′​(ρ¯)=λf^{\prime}(\bar{\rho})=\lambda.

Fix two constant chemical potentials λ0\lambda_{0}, λ1\lambda_{1}. Consider a system initially in the state ρ¯0\bar{\rho}_{0} which is driven to a new state ρ¯1\bar{\rho}_{1} by changing the chemical potential in time in a way that λ⁡(t)=λ0\lambda(t)=\lambda_{0} for t≤0t\leq 0 and λ⁡(t)=λ1\lambda(t)=\lambda_{1} for t≥t0t\geq t_{0}, where t0t_{0} is some fixed positive time.

Let ρ⁡(t)\rho(t), j⁡(t)j(t), t≥0t\geq 0, be the solution of (5)–(9) with initial condition ρ¯0\bar{\rho}_{0}. Since the chemical potential is equal to λ1\lambda_{1} for t≥t0t\geq t_{0}, ρ⁡(t)→ρ¯1\rho(t)\to\bar{\rho}_{1} as t→∞t\to\infty. Moreover, as ρ¯1\bar{\rho}_{1} is an equilibrium state, the current j⁡(t)j(t) relaxes to J⁡(ρ¯1)=0J(\bar{\rho}_{1})=0. We deduce that the integral in (37) is finite as T→∞T\to\infty and that

W=F⁡(ρ¯1)−F⁡(ρ¯0)+∫0∞dt∫Λdxj(t)⋅χ(ρ(t))−1j(t),\begin{split}W\,&=\,F(\bar{\rho}_{1})-F(\bar{\rho}_{0})\\ &+\,\int_{0}^{\infty}\!dt\int_{\Lambda}\!dx\;j(t)\cdot\chi(\rho(t))^{-1}j(t)\;,\end{split} (39)

where W=limT→+∞W[0,T]W=\lim_{T\to+\infty}W_{[0,T]}.

It remains to show that in the quasi-static limit equality in (35) is achieved. For any fixed transformation the inequality (35) is strict because the second term on the right hand side of (39) cannot be identically zero. Therefore, reversible transformations cannot be achieved exactly. We can however exhibit a sequence of transformations for which the second term on the right hand side in (39) can be made arbitrarily small. This sequence of transformations is what we call a quasi-static transformation. Fix a smooth function λ⁡(t)\lambda(t) such that λ⁡(0)=λ0\lambda(0)=\lambda_{0} and λ⁡(t)=λ1\lambda(t)=\lambda_{1} for t≥t0t\geq t_{0}. Given τ>0\tau>0 we set λτ​(t)=λ⁡(t/τ)\lambda^{\tau}(t)=\lambda(t/\tau). Since E=0E=0, the last term on the right hand side of (39) is given by

∫0∞dt∫Λdx∇f′(ρτ(t))⋅χ(ρτ(t))∇f′(ρτ(t)),\int_{0}^{\infty}\!dt\int_{\Lambda}\!dx\,\nabla f^{\prime}(\rho^{\tau}(t))\cdot\chi(\rho^{\tau}(t))\nabla f^{\prime}(\rho^{\tau}(t)),

where ρτ\rho^{\tau} is the solution to (5)–(9) with initial condition ρ¯0\bar{\rho}_{0} and boundary conditions λτ​(t)\lambda^{\tau}(t). For each t≥0t\geq 0, let ρ¯λτ​(t)\bar{\rho}_{\lambda^{\tau}(t)} be the equilibrium state associated to the constant chemical potential λτ​(t)\lambda^{\tau}(t). Since ∇f′​(ρ¯λτ​(t))=0\nabla f^{\prime}(\bar{\rho}_{\lambda^{\tau}(t)})=0, we can rewrite the previous integral as

∫0∞dt∫Λdx∇[f′(ρτ(t))−f′(ρ¯λτ​(t))]⋅χ(ρτ(t))∇[f′(ρτ(t))−f′(ρ¯λτ​(t))].\begin{split}\int_{0}^{\infty}\!dt\int_{\Lambda}\!dx\,\nabla\big[&f^{\prime}(\rho^{\tau}(t))-f^{\prime}(\bar{\rho}_{\lambda^{\tau}(t)})\big]\\ &\cdot\chi(\rho^{\tau}(t))\nabla\big[f^{\prime}(\rho^{\tau}(t))-f^{\prime}(\bar{\rho}_{\lambda^{\tau}(t)})\big].\end{split}

The difference between the solution of the hydrodynamic equation ρτ​(t)\rho^{\tau}(t) and the stationary profile ρ¯λτ​(t)\bar{\rho}_{\lambda^{\tau}(t)} is of order 1/τ1/\tau uniformly in time, and so is the difference f′​(ρτ​(t))−f′​(ρ¯λτ​(t))f^{\prime}(\rho^{\tau}(t))-f^{\prime}(\bar{\rho}_{\lambda^{\tau}(t)}). As the integration over time essentially extends over an interval of length τ\tau, the previous expression vanishes for τ→∞\tau\to\infty. This implies that equality in (35) is achieved in this limit.

For non-equilibrium states, the inequality (35) does not carry any significant information when we consider transformations over long time intervals. In fact, as non-equilibrium stationary states support a non vanishing current, to maintain such a current one needs to dissipate a positive amount of energy per unit time. If we consider a transformation between non-equilibrium stationary states, the energy dissipated along such transformation will necessarily include the contribution needed to maintain such states and therefore the amount of energy exchanged in an unbounded time window is unbounded. In this case, the left hand side of (35) is infinite while the right hand side is finite.

To transform (35) into a meaningful inequality, by using the decomposition (25) of the current, we give a natural definition of renormalized work performed along any given transformation. This definition has been inspired by the point of view in [112] further developed in [119, 91]. We then show that the renormalized work satisfies a Clausius inequality and prove that equality is achieved in the quasi-static limit.

The idea to define a renormalized work is to subtract the energy needed to maintain the system out of equilibrium. For time independent drivings, by the orthogonal decomposition (25) and (24), J​(ρ¯)=JA​(ρ¯)J(\bar{\rho})=J_{\mathrm{A}}(\bar{\rho}) is the macroscopic current in the stationary state. In view of the general formula for the total work (37), the amount of energy per unit time needed to maintain the system in the stationary profile ρ¯\bar{\rho} is

∫Λd​x​JA​(ρ¯)⋅χ​(ρ¯)−1​JA​(ρ¯).\int_{\Lambda}\!dx\>J_{\mathrm{A}}(\bar{\rho})\cdot\chi(\bar{\rho})^{-1}J_{\mathrm{A}}(\bar{\rho}). (40)

Fix now T>0T>0, a density profile ρ0\rho_{0}, and space-time dependent chemical potentials λ⁡(t)\lambda(t) and external field E⁡(t)E(t), t∈[0,T]t\in[0,T]. Let (ρ⁡(t),j⁡(t))(\rho(t),j(t)) be the corresponding solution of (5)–(9) with initial condition ρ0\rho_{0}. We define the renormalized work W[0,T]renW^{\textrm{ren}}_{[0,T]} done by the reservoirs and the external field in the time interval [0,T][0,T] as

W[0,T]ren=W[0,T]−∫0Tdt∫ΛdxJA(t,ρ(t))⋅χ(ρ(t))−1JA(t,ρ(t))\begin{split}&W^{\textrm{ren}}_{[0,T]}=W_{[0,T]}\\ &\quad-\int_{0}^{T}\!dt\int_{\Lambda}\!dx\,J_{\mathrm{A}}(t,\rho(t))\,\cdot\chi(\rho(t))^{-1}J_{\mathrm{A}}(t,\rho(t))\end{split} (41)

where JA​(t,ρ)J_{\mathrm{A}}(t,\rho) is the antisymmetric current for the system with the time independent external driving obtained by freezing the time dependent chemical potential λ\lambda and external field EE at time tt. Observe that the definition of the renormalized work involves the antisymmetric current JA​(t)J_{\mathrm{A}}(t) computed not at density profile ρ¯λ⁡(t),E⁡(t)\bar{\rho}_{\lambda(t),E(t)} but at the solution ρ⁡(t)\rho(t) of the time dependent hydrodynamic equation. The definition (41) is natural within MFT and leads to a Clausius inequality.

In view of (37) and the orthogonality in (26) between the symmetric and the antisymmetric part of the current,

W[0,T]ren=F⁡(ρ⁡(T))−F⁡(ρ0)+∫0Tdt∫ΛdxJS(t,ρ(t))⋅χ(ρ(t))−1JS(t,ρ(t)).\begin{split}&W^{\textrm{ren}}_{[0,T]}=F(\rho(T))-F(\rho_{0})\\ &\quad+\int_{0}^{T}\!dt\int_{\Lambda}\!dx\,J_{\mathrm{S}}(t,\rho(t))\cdot\chi(\rho(t))^{-1}J_{\mathrm{S}}(t,\rho(t)).\end{split} (42)

Consider a space-time dependent chemical potential and external field (λ⁡(t),E⁡(t))(\lambda(t),E(t)), t≥0t\geq 0, with (λ⁡(0),E⁡(0))=(λ0,E0)(\lambda(0),E(0))=(\lambda_{0},E_{0}) and (λ⁡(∞),E⁡(∞))=(λ1,E1)(\lambda(\infty),E(\infty))=(\lambda_{1},E_{1}). Let ρ¯0=ρ¯λ0,E0\bar{\rho}_{0}=\bar{\rho}_{\lambda_{0},E_{0}}, ρ¯1=ρ¯λ1,E1\bar{\rho}_{1}=\bar{\rho}_{\lambda_{1},E_{1}} be the corresponding stationary profiles and let (ρ⁡(t),j⁡(t))(\rho(t),j(t)), t≥0t\geq 0 be the solution of (5)–(9) with initial condition ρ¯0\bar{\rho}_{0}. Since ρ⁡(T)\rho(T) converges to ρ¯1\bar{\rho}_{1}, the symmetric part of the current, JS​(ρ​(T))J_{\mathrm{S}}(\rho(T)), relaxes as T→+∞T\to+\infty to JS​(ρ¯1)=0J_{\mathrm{S}}(\bar{\rho}_{1})=0. By letting Wren=limT→∞W[0,T]renW^{\textrm{ren}}=\lim_{T\to\infty}W^{\textrm{ren}}_{[0,T]}, we thus get

Wren=F⁡(ρ¯1)−F⁡(ρ¯0)+∫0∞dt∫ΛdxJS(t,ρ(t))⋅χ(ρ(t))−1JS(t,ρ(t))\begin{split}&W^{\textrm{ren}}=F(\bar{\rho}_{1})-F(\bar{\rho}_{0})\\ &\quad+\int_{0}^{\infty}\!dt\int_{\Lambda}\!dx\>J_{\mathrm{S}}(t,\rho(t))\cdot\chi(\rho(t))^{-1}J_{\mathrm{S}}(t,\rho(t))\end{split} (43)

where FF is the equilibrium free energy functional (38). In particular,

Wren≥F⁡(ρ¯1)−F⁡(ρ¯0),W^{\textrm{ren}}\geq F(\bar{\rho}_{1})-F(\bar{\rho}_{0}), (44)

which is a meaningful version of the Clausius inequality for non-equilibrium states.

Arguing as in the equilibrium case, we can exhibit a sequence of transformations (λτ​(t),Eτ​(t))(\lambda^{\tau}(t),E^{\tau}(t)) which vary appreciably on a time scale τ\tau, such that in the quasi-static limit τ→∞\tau\to\infty equality in (44) is achieved,

Wren=F⁡(ρ¯1)−F⁡(ρ¯0).W^{\textrm{ren}}=F(\bar{\rho}_{1})-F(\bar{\rho}_{0}). (45)

III.2 Excess work

Consider a homogeneous equilibrium state with vanishing external field and constant chemical potential λ0\lambda_{0} and let ρ¯0\bar{\rho}_{0} be the corresponding homogeneous density, λ0=f′​(ρ¯0)\lambda_{0}=f^{\prime}(\bar{\rho}_{0}). The system is put in contact with a new environment with chemical potential λ1\lambda_{1}. In this case, recalling that ff is the free energy per unit volume and that the temperature of the system is the same of the environment, the availability per unit volume is defined by a=f⁡(ρ¯0)−λ1​ρ¯0a=f(\bar{\rho}_{0})-\lambda_{1}\bar{\rho}_{0}, [115, Ch. 7]. The function aa, which depends on the state of the system and on the environment, can be used to compute the maximal useful work that can be extracted from the system in the given environment. More precisely, by letting ρ¯1\bar{\rho}_{1} be such that f′​(ρ¯1)=λ1f^{\prime}(\bar{\rho}_{1})=\lambda_{1}, then

−Δ​a=f⁡(ρ¯0)−f⁡(ρ¯1)−λ1​(ρ¯0−ρ¯1)≥0-\Delta a=f(\bar{\rho}_{0})-f(\bar{\rho}_{1})-\lambda_{1}(\bar{\rho}_{0}-\bar{\rho}_{1})\geq 0 (46)

is the the maximal useful work per unit volume that can be extracted from the system in the given environment. Comparing −Δ​a-\Delta a with the large deviations functional VV in (29) which expresses the probability of density fluctuations in the equilibrium ensemble corresponding to the chemical potential λ1\lambda_{1}, we realize that

V⁡(ρ¯0)=−|Λ|​Δ​a.V(\bar{\rho}_{0})=-|\Lambda|\Delta a. (47)

An analogous relationship can be easily obtained for spatially inhomogeneous equilibrium states.

In order to discuss the thermodynamic role of the quasi-potential for non-equilibrium states, we introduce the excess work with respect to a quasi-static transformation. Consider a stationary non-equilibrium state with density profile ρ\rho for t≤0t\leq 0, while at time t=0t=0 the external driving is abruptly changed to new values (λ,E)(\lambda,E) so that for t>0t>0 the evolution is given by the hydrodynamic equation with initial condition ρ\rho and time independent driving (λ,E)(\lambda,E). We define the excess of work as the difference between the renormalized work and the renormalized work involved in a quasi-static transformation from ρ\rho to ρ¯λ,E\bar{\rho}_{\lambda,E}, namely Wex=Wren−min⁡WrenW_{\mathrm{ex}}=W^{\textrm{ren}}-\min W^{\textrm{ren}}. According to the discussion in Section III.1, the excess work is given by

Wex=Wren​(ρ)−[F⁡(ρ¯)−F⁡(ρ)]=∫0∞d​t​∫Λd​x​JS​(ρ⁡(t))⋅χ​(ρ⁡(t))−1​JS​(ρ⁡(t)),\begin{split}W_{\mathrm{ex}}&=W^{\textrm{ren}}(\rho)-\big[F(\bar{\rho})-F(\rho)\big]\\ &=\int_{0}^{\infty}\!dt\int_{\Lambda}\!dx\,J_{\mathrm{S}}(\rho(t))\,\cdot\chi(\rho(t))^{-1}J_{\mathrm{S}}(\rho(t)),\end{split} (48)

where ρ¯\bar{\rho} is the stationary density corresponding to (λ,E)(\lambda,E). By using the orthogonality in (26) and the formula (23) for the symmetric part of the current in terms of the quasi-potential, straightforward computations yield

Wex=Vλ,E​(ρ),W_{\mathrm{ex}}=V_{\lambda,E}(\rho), (49)

where we have made explicit the dependence of the quasi-potential on the driving. Therefore, while a definition of thermodynamic potentials, that is functionals of the state of the system (in this case of the density ρ\rho), does not appear possible in non-equilibrium thermodynamics, the quasi-potential is the natural extension of the availability.

III.3 Finite time thermodynamics

We next discuss the energy balance along slow transformations from a quantitative point of view taking into account that quasi-static transformations are an idealization and real transformations take place on a finite time window whose duration is denoted by τ\tau.

For s∈[0,1]s\in[0,1] a protocol is defined by a choice of the external drivings E⁡(s,x)E(s,x), x∈Λx\in\Lambda, and λ⁡(s,x)\lambda(s,x), x∈∂Λx\in\partial\Lambda. The slow transformation is then realized, for τ\tau large, by

{Eτ​(t)=E⁡(t/τ),λτ​(t)=λ⁡(t/τ),​t∈[0,τ].\left\{\begin{array}[]{l}E^{\tau}(t)=E\left(t/\tau\right),\\ \lambda^{\tau}(t)=\lambda\left(t/\tau\right),\end{array}\right.t\in[0,\tau].

Let ρτ​(t)\rho^{\tau}(t) and jτ​(t)j^{\tau}(t), 0≤t≤τ0\leq t\leq\tau, be the solution to the hydrodynamic equations with the slow external field EτE^{\tau} and chemical potential λτ\lambda^{\tau},

{∂tρτ+∇⋅J⁡(t/τ,ρτ​(t))=0,jτ​(t)=J⁡(t/τ,ρτ​(t))f′​(ρτ​(t))|∂Λ=λτ​(t)ρτ​(0)=ρ¯​(0)\left\{\begin{array}[]{l}\partial_{t}\rho^{\tau}+\nabla\cdot J(t/\tau,\rho^{\tau}(t))=0,\\ j^{\tau}(t)=J(t/\tau,\rho^{\tau}(t))\\ f^{\prime}(\rho^{\tau}(t))\big|_{\partial\Lambda}=\lambda^{\tau}(t)\\ \rho^{\tau}(0)=\bar{\rho}(0)\end{array}\right. (50)

where we recall that J(t,ρ)=−D(ρ)∇ρ+χ(ρ)E(t)J(t,\rho)=-D(\rho)\nabla\rho+\chi(\rho)E\left(t\right).

For s∈[0,1]s\in[0,1], let ρ¯​(s)\bar{\rho}(s) be the unique stationary solution of the hydrodynamics with external field E⁡(s)E(s) and chemical potential λ⁡(s)\lambda(s). When τ\tau is large the solution (ρτ,jτ)(\rho^{\tau},j^{\tau}) has an expansion of the type (recall s∈[0,1]s\in[0,1])

ρτ​(τ​s)=ρ¯​(s)+1τ​r​(s)+o⁡(1τ),jτ​(τ​s)=J⁡(s,ρ¯​(s))+1τ​g​(s)+o⁡(1τ).\begin{array}[]{l}\displaystyle{\rho^{\tau}(\tau s)=\bar{\rho}(s)+\tfrac{1}{\tau}\,r(s)+o\big(\tfrac{1}{\tau}\big)\,,}\\ \displaystyle{j^{\tau}(\tau s)=J(s,\bar{\rho}(s))+\tfrac{1}{\tau}\,g(s)+o\big(\tfrac{1}{\tau}\big)\,.}\end{array} (51)

By (50) we get the corresponding linear evolution equations for the first order corrections (r,g)(r,g),

{∂sρ¯​(s)+∇⋅g⁡(s)=0g(s)=−[D(ρ¯(s))∇r(s)+r(s)D′(ρ¯(s))∇ρ¯(s)]+r⁡(s)​χ′​(ρ¯​(s))​E​(s)r⁡(s,x)=0,x∈∂Λ\left\{\begin{array}[]{l}\partial_{s}\bar{\rho}(s)+\nabla\cdot g(s)=0\\ g(s)=-\Big[D(\bar{\rho}(s))\nabla r(s)+r(s)D^{\prime}(\bar{\rho}(s))\nabla\bar{\rho}(s)\Big]\\ \phantom{g(s)=}+r(s)\chi^{\prime}(\bar{\rho}(s))E(s)\\ r(s,x)=0,\;x\in\partial\Lambda\end{array}\right. (52)

which has the form of a Poisson equation for r⁡(s)r(s).

Evaluating equations (37) along the transformation (ρτ,jτ)(\rho^{\tau},j^{\tau}), we obtain

F⁡(ρτ​(τ))−F⁡(ρ¯​(0))=τ​∫01d​s​∫Λd​x​jτ​(τ​s)⋅E⁡(s)−τ∫01ds∫∂Λdσλ(s)jτ(τs)⋅n^−τ∫01ds∫Λdxjτ(τs)⋅χ(ρτ(τs))−1jτ(τs).\begin{split}&F\big(\rho^{\tau}(\tau)\big)-F\big(\bar{\rho}(0)\big)=\tau\int_{0}^{1}\!ds\int_{\Lambda}\!dx\,j^{\tau}(\tau s)\cdot E(s)\\ &-\tau\int_{0}^{1}\!ds\int_{\partial\Lambda}\!d\sigma\,\lambda(s)j^{\tau}(\tau s)\cdot\hat{n}\\ &\;\;-\tau\int_{0}^{1}\!ds\int_{\Lambda}\!dx\,j^{\tau}(\tau s)\cdot\chi\big(\rho^{\tau}(\tau s)\big)^{-1}j^{\tau}(\tau s).\end{split} (53)

We can analyze this equation at the different orders in 1/τ1/\tau, obtaining an identity for each order. Direct computations yield that at order τ\tau the right hand side of (53) vanishes, while at order 11 we get the first non trivial equation,

F​(ρ¯​(1))−F​(ρ¯​(0))=∫01d​s​∫Λd​x​E​(s)⋅g⁡(s)−∫01d​s​∫∂Λd​σ​λ​(s)​g​(s)⋅n^+∫01ds∫Λdxr(s)J(s,ρ¯(s))⋅(χ−1)′(ρ¯(s))J(s,ρ¯(s)).\begin{split}&F\big(\bar{\rho}(1)\big)-F\big(\bar{\rho}(0)\big)\\ &\;=\int_{0}^{1}\!ds\int_{\Lambda}\!dx\,E(s)\cdot g(s)-\int_{0}^{1}\!ds\int_{\partial\Lambda}\!d\sigma\,\lambda(s)g(s)\cdot\hat{n}\\ &\;\;+\int_{0}^{1}\!ds\int_{\Lambda}\!dx\,r(s)J(s,\bar{\rho}(s))\cdot(\chi^{-1})^{\prime}\big(\bar{\rho}(s)\big)J(s,\bar{\rho}(s)).\end{split} (54)

This is an interesting relationship as it connects the variation of the free energy to the first order corrections in a real transformation. It also carries relevant information for transformations among equilibrium states, but it cannot be derived within the framework of classical thermodynamics. If we consider transformations among equilibrium states, the second line on the right hand side of (54) vanishes when the intermediate states are also of equilibrium so that J​(s,ρ¯​(s))=0J(s,\bar{\rho}(s))=0 for any ss. However the transformation can go through non-equilibrium intermediate states.

As a further application of the expansion (51), consider the equation (42) which expresses the energy balance in the time interval [0,τ][0,\tau]. Recalling that we have already shown that the last term vanishes in the quasi-static limit, we now estimate this term when the transformation is given in term of a protocol and τ\tau is large but finite.

We thus want to estimate, for large τ\tau

∫0τd​t​∫Λd​x​JS​(t/τ,ρτ​(t))⋅χ​(ρτ​(t))−1​JS​(t/τ,ρτ​(t)).\int_{0}^{\tau}\!dt\int_{\Lambda}\!dx\,J_{S}(t/\tau,\rho^{\tau}(t))\cdot\chi(\rho^{\tau}(t))^{-1}J_{S}(t/\tau,\rho^{\tau}(t)). (55)

Recalling (33), the symmetric part of the current is

JS(s,ρ)=−χ(ρ)∇δ​Vλ⁡(s),E⁡(s)​(ρ)δ​ρJ_{S}(s,\rho)=-\chi(\rho)\nabla\frac{\delta V_{\lambda(s),E(s)}(\rho)}{\delta\rho} (56)

where Vλ⁡(s),E⁡(s)V_{\lambda(s),E(s)} is the quasi-potential associated to (λ⁡(s),E⁡(s))(\lambda(s),E(s)) (we regard ss here as a fixed parameter).

By (51), the symmetric current has the expansion

JS(s,ρτ(τs))=−1τχ(ρ¯(s))∇(Cs−1⋆r(s))+o(1τ).J_{S}(s,\rho^{\tau}(\tau s))=-\frac{1}{\tau}\chi(\bar{\rho}(s))\nabla\left(C^{-1}_{s}\star r(s)\right)+o\big(\tfrac{1}{\tau}\big). (57)

where ⋆\star denotes convolution and

Cs−1​(x,y)=δ2​Vλ⁡(s),E⁡(s)​(ρ¯​(s))δ​ρ​(x)​δ​ρ​(y).C^{-1}_{s}(x,y)=\frac{\delta^{2}V_{\lambda(s),E(s)}(\bar{\rho}(s))}{\delta\rho(x)\delta\rho(y)}.

Hence, for slow transformations we get that (55) has the form 1τ​B+o⁡(1τ)\frac{1}{\tau}\,B+o\big(\tfrac{1}{\tau}\big), where

B=∫01ds∫Λdx∇(Cs−1⋆r(s))⋅χ(ρ¯(s))∇(Cs−1⋆r(s)).B=\int_{0}^{1}\!ds\!\int_{\Lambda}\!dx\,\nabla\big(C_{s}^{-1}\star r(s)\big)\cdot\chi(\bar{\rho}(s))\nabla\big(C_{s}^{-1}\star r(s)\big). (58)

To illustrate the meaning of BB, consider a transformation between and through equilibrium states. Then, up to terms of order 1/τ21/\tau^{2}, the work done in the (finite time) transformation is

W[0,τ]=Δ​F+1τ​BW_{[0,\tau]}=\Delta F+\frac{1}{\tau}\,B

so that the inequality B≥0B\geq 0 is a restatement of the second principle. In general, BB quantifies the additional energy dissipated in the given transformation. As we have shown, in the limit τ→∞\tau\to\infty, all protocols realize the equality W=Δ​FW=\Delta F. On the other hand, for finite time τ\tau, this identity cannot be achieved and we can select the optimal protocol by minimizing BB.

For transformations between and through equilibrium states, the quasi-potential is given by (29) so that BB has an explicit expression. In particular, we can compute explicitly the optimal protocol for transformations through homogeneous equilibrium states. Namely, we assume that the external field vanishes and that the chemical potential does not depend on the space variable. The protocol is thus defined by a real function λ⁡(s)\lambda(s), s∈[0,1]s\in[0,1]. The associated stationary solution ρ¯​(s)\bar{\rho}(s) is also constant in space and solves λ⁡(s)=f′​(ρ¯​(s))\lambda(s)=f^{\prime}(\bar{\rho}(s)). For simplicity we also assume that the diffusion coefficient is a multiple of the identity; in this case the equation (52) reduces the the classical Poisson equation

{∂sρ¯​(s)=D⁡(ρ¯​(s))​Δ​r​(s)r⁡(s,x)=0,x∈∂Λ\begin{cases}\partial_{s}\bar{\rho}(s)=D(\bar{\rho}(s))\Delta r(s)\\ r(s,x)=0,\quad x\in\partial\Lambda\end{cases} (59)

whose solution is given by

r⁡(s,x)=∂sρ¯​(s)D​(ρ¯​(s))​∫Λd​y​G0​(x,y)r(s,x)=\frac{\partial_{s}\bar{\rho}(s)}{D(\bar{\rho}(s))}\int_{\Lambda}\!dy\,G_{0}(x,y) (60)

where G0G_{0} is the Green function of the Dirichlet Laplacian on Λ\Lambda. Since

δ2​Vλ⁡(s),E⁡(s)​(ρ¯​(s))δ​ρ​(x)​δ​ρ​(y)=D​(ρ¯​(s))χ​(ρ¯​(s))​δ​(x−y),\frac{\delta^{2}V_{\lambda(s),E(s)}(\bar{\rho}(s))}{\delta\rho(x)\delta\rho(y)}=\frac{D(\bar{\rho}(s))}{\chi(\bar{\rho}(s))}\,\delta(x-y), (61)

then

B=∫Λdx|∇∫ΛdyG0(x,y)|2∫01ds[∂sρ¯​(s)]2χ​(ρ¯​(s)).B=\int_{\Lambda}\!dx\Big|\,\nabla\!\int_{\Lambda}\!dy\,G_{0}(x,y)\Big|^{2}\,\int_{0}^{1}\!ds\,\frac{[\partial_{s}\bar{\rho}(s)]^{2}}{\chi(\bar{\rho}(s))}. (62)

The dependence on space factorizes in the pre–factor which depends only on the geometry of the domain. It is now straightforward to minimize BB with respect to ρ¯​(s)\bar{\rho}(s) with the constraints ρ¯​(0)=ρ¯0\bar{\rho}(0)=\bar{\rho}_{0}, ρ¯​(1)=ρ¯1\bar{\rho}(1)=\bar{\rho}_{1}. The minimizer is the unique function satisfying the constraints such that

∂sρ¯χ⁡(ρ¯)=const.\frac{\partial_{s}\bar{\rho}}{\sqrt{\chi(\bar{\rho})}}=\mathrm{const.} (63)

The optimal protocol is then obtained by the relationship λ=f′​(ρ¯)\lambda=f^{\prime}(\bar{\rho}). This protocol does not correspond to a constant rate as one could naively expect. In fact, (63) shows that this rate has to be adjusted to the response properties of the system.

III.4 Dissipation

The infinitesimal version of (37) gives the instantaneous energy balance which reads

W˙=∫Λd​x​[f′​(ρ)​ρ˙+j⋅χ​(ρ)−1​j]\begin{split}\dot{W}&=\int_{\Lambda}\!dx\,\big[f^{\prime}(\rho)\dot{\rho}+j\cdot\chi(\rho)^{-1}j\big]\end{split} (64)

where W˙\dot{W} is the power injected by the reservoirs and external field in the system. Accordingly, f′​(ρ)​ρ˙f^{\prime}(\rho)\dot{\rho} represents the rate of change of the density of free energy while j⋅χ​(ρ)−1​jj\cdot\chi(\rho)^{-1}j is the dissipated power per unit volume. For equilibrium states, the stationary density profile is characterized by the vanishing of the current and therefore it minimizes the dissipation. This is not the case for non-equilibrium stationary states. Recalling (24), the non-equilibrium stationary density profile is characterized by the vanishing of the symmetric current and this does not imply that the dissipation is minimal. In view of the orthogonal decomposition (25),

∫Λd​x​J​(ρ)⋅χ​(ρ)−1​J​(ρ)=∫Λd​x​JS​(ρ)⋅χ​(ρ)−1​JS​(ρ)+∫ΛdxJA(ρ)⋅χ(ρ)−1JA(ρ).\begin{split}\int_{\Lambda}\!dx\,J(\rho)\cdot\chi(\rho)^{-1}J(\rho)&=\int_{\Lambda}\!dx\,J_{\mathrm{S}}(\rho)\cdot\chi(\rho)^{-1}J_{\mathrm{S}}(\rho)\\ &+\int_{\Lambda}\!dx\,J_{\mathrm{A}}(\rho)\cdot\chi(\rho)^{-1}J_{\mathrm{A}}(\rho).\end{split}

The minimization of the left hand side is not achieved by making the first term on the the right hand side equal to zero. Indeed, in the simple case of a one dimensional rarefied gas discussed in section II.3 the minimizer of the left hand side with the prescribed boundary conditions ρ⁡(0)=ρ0\rho(0)=\rho_{0}, ρ⁡(L)=ρ1\rho(L)=\rho_{1} is

ρ^​(x)=[ρ0​(1−x/L)+ρ1​x/L]2\hat{\rho}(x)=\big[\sqrt{\rho_{0}}(1-x/L)+\sqrt{\rho_{1}}x/L\big]^{2}

while the stationary profile is ρ¯​(x)=ρ0​(1−x/L)+ρ1​x/L\bar{\rho}(x)=\rho_{0}(1-x/L)+\rho_{1}x/L. Observe that, in accordance with the near to equilibrium Prigogine principle [116], ρ¯−ρ^=O⁡([(ρ1−ρ0)/L]2)\bar{\rho}-\hat{\rho}=O([(\rho_{1}-\rho_{0})/L]^{2}).

We remark that if we consider the renormalized work (42), the corresponding renormalized power is

W˙ren=∫Λd​x​[f′​(ρ)​ρ˙+JS​(ρ)⋅χ​(ρ)−1​JS​(ρ)].{\dot{W}}^{\mathrm{ren}}=\int_{\Lambda}\!dx\,\big[f^{\prime}(\rho)\dot{\rho}+J_{\mathrm{S}}(\rho)\cdot\chi(\rho)^{-1}J_{\mathrm{S}}(\rho)\big]. (65)

Then, recalling (24), the stationary density profile minimizes the corresponding renormalized dissipation ∫Λd​x​JS​(ρ)⋅χ​(ρ)−1​JS​(ρ)\int_{\Lambda}\!dx\,J_{\mathrm{S}}(\rho)\cdot\chi(\rho)^{-1}J_{\mathrm{S}}(\rho). Once again, in terms of the renormalized quantities, non–equilibrium stationary states behave as equilibrium states.

III.5 Minimum dissipation principle

Generalizing Onsager [109], we introduce the dissipation function, [13]

Φ⁡(ρ,j)=12​∫Λd​x​(j−JA​(ρ))⋅χ​(ρ)−1​(j−JA​(ρ))\Phi(\rho,j)=\frac{1}{2}\int_{\Lambda}\!dx\big(j-J_{\mathrm{A}}(\rho)\big)\cdot\chi(\rho)^{-1}\big(j-J_{\mathrm{A}}(\rho)\big) (66)

and the functional

Ψ(ρ,j)=−∫Λdxδ​V​(ρ)δ​ρ∇⋅j+Φ(ρ,j).\Psi(\rho,j)=-\int_{\Lambda}\!dx\,\frac{\delta V(\rho)}{\delta\rho}\nabla\cdot j+\Phi(\rho,j). (67)

We can then reformulate the constitutive equation j=J⁡(ρ)j=J(\rho) in variational terms,

Ψ⁡(ρ,j)=minimum,\Psi(\rho,j)=\mathrm{minimum}, (68)

where the minimum is understood with respect to jj with ρ\rho fixed. Indeed, by taking the variation of Ψ\Psi with respect to jj we deduce that the minimum is achieved for j=JS​(ρ)+JA​(ρ)=J⁡(ρ)j=J_{\mathrm{S}}(\rho)+J_{\mathrm{A}}(\rho)=J(\rho).

The difference with respect to the near equilibrium Onsager theory (apart from the sign difference) is the insertion of the antisymmetric current JAJ_{A} in the dissipation function (66) and the replacement of the entropy with the quasi-potential. Accordingly, while in Onsager the minimum value of Ψ\Psi is half of the total dissipation, in our case

minjΨ(ρ,j)=Ψ(ρ,J(ρ))=−12∫ΛdxJS(ρ)⋅χ(ρ)−1JS(ρ)\min_{j}\Psi(\rho,j)=\Psi\big(\rho,J(\rho)\big)=-\frac{1}{2}\int_{\Lambda}\!dx\,J_{\mathrm{S}}(\rho)\cdot\chi(\rho)^{-1}J_{\mathrm{S}}(\rho)

is half the negative of the renormalized dissipation.

III.6 Comments

Within the scheme introduced, we considered only one conservation law (the conservation of the mass) and accordingly we did not distinguish between work and heat. A model where heat is naturally introduced is analyzed in [108].

The splitting of the current (25) appears very interesting conceptually. However the two currents JSJ_{S} and JAJ_{A}, apart some special cases, are not easily accessible experimentally. In fact what is directly measurable is the total current which coincides with JAJ_{A} in a stationary state while JSJ_{S} represents the total current in a relaxation to an equilibrium state. In the general case their computation require the knowledge of the quasi-potential. A measurement of the quasi-potential, via rare fluctuations is hopeless as very large times are involved. It can be either obtained from calculations by solving a variational principle (see section IV.1), or from simulations using algorithms like in [68]. Otherwise it can be approximately estimated from measurements of correlation functions in the stationary state. In fact, as we shall see later, VV is the Legendre transform of the generating functional of density correlations in the stationary state.

These remarks imply that the renormalized work is not immediately accessible. There are other possibilities to define a renormalized work [101], which however have similar drawbacks. On the other hand the approach developed in subsection III.3 allows, as remarked in the introduction, a detailed analysis of quasi–static transformations by relating explicitly, for example, the variation of the free energy and the corrections to an infinitely slow transformation (54). Actually this approach provides an infinity of relationships which should be further investigated.

Another benefit of finite time thermodynamics is related to the possibility of optimizing the protocol of a transformation both in equilibrium and non-equilibrium.

As in [109], the dissipation function (66) provides a variational characterization of the evolution equations. For the usefulness of the dissipation function in identifying the various physical contributions, we refer to [110] on the irreversible processes in electrolytes.

IV Statistics of density and current fluctuations

In this section we derive from the fundamental formula the large deviations statistics separately for the density and the current. We discuss their singularities, that will be interpreted as non-equilibrium phase transitions. The long range correlations of non-equilibrium states will be connected to the non locality of the quasi-potential.

IV.1 Density fluctuations

We start by deriving the probability of the density trajectories. We fix a path ρ=ρ⁡(t,x)\rho=\rho(t,x), (t,x)∈[T0,T1]×Λ(t,x)\in[T_{0},T_{1}]\times\Lambda. There are many possible trajectories j=j⁡(t,x)j=j(t,x), differing by divergence free vector fields, satisfying the continuity equation associated to the given density trajectory ρ\rho. . Optimizing over the possible currents we have

I[T0,T1](ρ)=infj:∇⋅j=−∂tρℐ[T0,T1](ρ,j).I_{[T_{0},T_{1}]}(\rho)=\inf_{\begin{subarray}{c}j\,:\\ \nabla\cdot j=-\partial_{t}\rho\end{subarray}}\mathcal{I}_{[T_{0},T_{1}]}(\rho,j). (69)

Then, the asymptotic probability of a density fluctuation is given by

ℙρ0​(ρε​(t)≈ρ⁡(t),t∈[T0,T1])≍exp⁡{−ε−d​I[T0,T1]​(ρ)}.\begin{split}&{\mathbb{P}}_{\rho_{0}}\big(\rho_{\varepsilon}(t)\approx\rho(t)\,,\,t\in[T_{0},T_{1}]\,\big)\\ &\qquad\asymp\exp\big\{-\varepsilon^{-d}\,I_{[{T_{0}},{T_{1}}]}(\rho)\big\}.\end{split}

Due to the exponential character of such probability estimates, only the minimum of the functional ℐ[T0,T1]​(ρ,j){\mathcal{I}}_{[T_{0},T_{1}]}(\rho,j) over all possible currents jj is in fact relevant.

To find the optimal current in (69) we observe that, given any trajectory (ρ⁡(t),j⁡(t))(\rho(t),j(t)) satisfying the continuity equation, we can introduce an external field FF defined by

j⁡(t)=J⁡(ρ⁡(t))+χ⁡(ρ⁡(t))​Fj(t)=J(\rho(t))+\chi(\rho(t))F (70)

so that

ℐ[T0,T1]​(ρ,j)=14​∫T0T1d​t​∫Λd​x​F⋅χ⁡(ρ)​F.{\mathcal{I}}_{[T_{0},T_{1}]}(\rho,j)\,=\,\frac{1}{4}\int_{T_{0}}^{T_{1}}dt\int_{\Lambda}dx\,F\cdot\chi(\rho)F. (71)

The problem can be therefore formulated as follows. Among all possible external fields FF, find the one that minimizes the right hand side of (71) with the constraint

∇⋅(J(ρ)+χ(ρ)F)=−∂tρ.\nabla\cdot(J(\rho)+\chi(\rho)F)=-\partial_{t}\rho.

We claim that the optimal FF is F=−∇πF=-\nabla\pi, where π:[T0,T1]×Λ→ℝ\pi:[T_{0},T_{1}]\times\Lambda\to{\mathbb{R}} is the unique solution to the Poisson equation

∇⋅[χ(ρ)∇π]=∂tρ+∇⋅J(t,ρ)\nabla\cdot\big[\chi(\rho)\nabla\pi\big]=\partial_{t}\rho+\nabla\cdot J(t,\rho) (72)

which vanishes at the boundary of Λ\Lambda for any t∈[T0,T1]t\in[T_{0},T_{1}].

Let F=−∇π+F~F=-\nabla\pi+\tilde{F}, so that ∇⋅χ⁡(ρ)​F~=0\nabla\cdot\chi(\rho)\tilde{F}=0. Since π\pi vanishes at the boundary, an integration by parts yields the orthogonality relationship ∫Λdx∇π⋅χ(ρ)F~=0\int_{\Lambda}\!dx\,\nabla\pi\cdot\chi(\rho)\tilde{F}=0. Whence,

∫ΛdxF⋅χ(ρ)F=∫Λdx{∇π⋅χ(ρ)∇π+F~⋅χ(ρ)F~}.\int_{\Lambda}dx\,F\cdot\chi(\rho)F=\int_{\Lambda}dx\,\Big\{\nabla\pi\cdot\chi(\rho)\nabla\pi+\tilde{F}\cdot\chi(\rho)\tilde{F}\Big\}. (73)

By construction, ∇⋅(J(ρ)−χ(ρ)∇π)=−∂tρ\nabla\cdot(J(\rho)-\chi(\rho)\nabla\pi)=-\partial_{t}\rho, so that, by (73), the choice of FF which minimizes (71) is obtained letting F~=0\tilde{F}=0. We deduce

I[T0,T1]​(ρ)=14​∫T0T1d​t​∫Λd​x​[∂tρ+∇⋅J⁡(ρ)]​K​(ρ)−1​[∂tρ+∇⋅J⁡(ρ)],\begin{split}&I_{[T_{0},T_{1}]}(\rho)=\\ &\frac{1}{4}\int_{{T_{0}}}^{{T_{1}}}\!dt\>\int_{\Lambda}dx\,\big[\partial_{t}\rho+\nabla\cdot J(\rho)\big]\,K(\rho)^{-1}\big[\partial_{t}\rho+\nabla\cdot J(\rho)\big],\\ \end{split} (74)

where the positive operator K⁡(ρ)K(\rho) is defined on functions π:Λ→ℝ\pi:\Lambda\to{\mathbb{R}} vanishing at the boundary ∂Λ\partial\Lambda by

K(ρ)π=−∇⋅(χ(ρ)∇π).K(\rho)\pi=-\nabla\cdot\big(\chi(\rho)\nabla\pi\big).

The above argument shows that we can restrict to gradient external fields FF when we are looking for fluctuations only of the density ρ\rho (this corresponds to particular realizations of the noisy part of the current in the fluctuating hydrodynamics picture). On the other hand, if we are looking for fluctuations of the current jj, then the corresponding external field FF is uniquely defined by (70) and will not be, in general, a gradient field.

We now derive a variational formula for the quasi-potential. From equation (19), we deduce that

V⁡(ρ⁡(T0))+I[T0,T1]​(ρ)=V⁡(ρ⁡(T1))+I[−T1,−T0]∗​(θ​ρ),V(\rho(T_{0}))+I_{[T_{0},T_{1}]}(\rho)=V(\rho(T_{1}))+I_{[-T_{1},-T_{0}]}^{*}(\theta\rho)\;, (75)

where I[−T1,−T0]∗I_{[-T_{1},-T_{0}]}^{*} is the rate function of the adjoint process. Let us consider the time interval taking T1=0T_{1}=0, T0=−TT_{0}=-T. Denoting by ρ^\hat{\rho} a generic path satisfying ρ^​(−T)=ρ¯\hat{\rho}(-T)=\bar{\rho}, which implies V​(ρ^​(−T))=0V(\hat{\rho}(-T))=0, and ρ^​(0)=ρ\hat{\rho}(0)=\rho, we obtain that

I[−T,0]​(ρ^)=V⁡(ρ)+I[0,T]∗​(θ​ρ^).I_{[-T,0]}(\hat{\rho})=V(\rho)+I_{[0,T]}^{*}(\theta\hat{\rho}).

Observing that I[0,T]∗​(θ​ρ^)≥0I_{[0,T]}^{*}(\theta\hat{\rho})\geq 0 and that it is equal to zero when θ​ρ^\theta\hat{\rho} solves the adjoint hydrodynamics, we obtain that

V(ρ)=infρ^I(−∞,0](ρ^),V(\rho)=\inf_{\hat{\rho}}I_{{(-\infty,0]}}(\hat{\rho})\;, (76)

where the infimum is carried over all trajectories ρ^\hat{\rho} such that ρ^​(−∞)=ρ¯\hat{\rho}({-\infty})=\bar{\rho}, ρ^​(0)=ρ\hat{\rho}(0)=\rho. The optimal trajectory ρ^\hat{\rho} satisfies

I[0,∞)∗​(θ​ρ^)=0.I_{[0,\infty)}^{*}(\theta\hat{\rho})=0. (77)

Compare with [62] for the finite dimensional case.

Optimal trajectories for non–reversible finite dimensional systems have been seen in numerical simulations [54] and actually experimentally observed in analogue electrical circuits with noise modeling a two-dimensional diffusion process [99]. We refer to the bibliography in those articles for previous literature on the topic.

We can summarize the previous analysis as follows. While for equilibrium states the path leading to a fluctuation is the time reversal of the relaxation path [111], for non-equilibrium states the spontaneous emergence of a density fluctuation takes place most likely following a trajectory which is the time reversal of the relaxation path along the adjoint hydrodynamics. The optimal field to create the fluctuation is 2∇δ​Vδ​ρ2\nabla\frac{\delta V}{\delta\rho}, that is minus twice the dissipative thermodynamic force. To understand the factor 22 think of an electric circuit. To invert the current one has to add minus twice the original electric field.

From the identity (76) we deduce that for profiles ρ\rho satisfying the boundary condition (9) δ​V/δ​ρ\delta V/\delta\rho vanishes at the boundary of Λ\Lambda. It is in fact enough to take the derivative of (76) and notice that the optimal path ρ^\hat{\rho} has prescribed boundary values.
