The quasi-potential VV (76) is a Lyapunov functional for the hydrodynamic equations (H-theorem). In fact, we can compute the rate of decrease of V⁡(ρ⁡(t))V(\rho(t)) along the hydrodynamic equations. In both cases, using equation (27), we have

dd​t​V​(ρ⁡(t))=∫Λd​x​δ​Vδ​ρ​(ρ⁡(t))​∂tρ⁡(t)=−∫Λdx∇δ​Vδ​ρ(ρ(t))⋅χ(ρ(t))∇δ​Vδ​ρ(ρ(t)).\begin{split}&\frac{d}{dt}V(\rho(t))=\int_{\Lambda}dx\,\frac{\delta V}{\delta\rho}(\rho(t))\,\partial_{t}\rho(t)\\ &\qquad=-\int_{\Lambda}dx\,\nabla\frac{\delta V}{\delta\rho}(\rho(t))\cdot\chi(\rho(t))\nabla\frac{\delta V}{\delta\rho}(\rho(t))\;.\end{split} (78)

Recalling (23) and (65), we see that the rate of decrease of VV is the renormalized dissipation. In particular, we have that dd​t​V​(ρ⁡(t))=0\frac{d}{dt}V(\rho(t))=0 if and only if δ​Vδ​ρ​(ρ​(t))=0\frac{\delta V}{\delta\rho}(\rho(t))=0. Since we assumed that there exists a unique stationary profile ρ¯\bar{\rho}, (78) implies that ρ¯\bar{\rho} is globally attractive.

IV.2 Hamiltonian structure

We regard the functional (74) as an action function on the set of density paths. The corresponding Lagrangian is

ℒ⁡(ρ,∂tρ)=14​∫Λd​x​[∂tρ+∇⋅J⁡(ρ)]​K​(ρ)−1​[∂tρ+∇⋅J⁡(ρ)].{\mathcal{L}}(\rho,\partial_{t}\rho)=\frac{1}{4}\int_{\Lambda}dx\,\big[\partial_{t}\rho+\nabla\cdot J(\rho)\big]\,K(\rho)^{-1}\big[\partial_{t}\rho+\nabla\cdot J(\rho)\big].

The associated Hamiltonian ℋ⁡(ρ,π)\mathcal{H}(\rho,\pi) is obtained by the Legendre transform of ℒ⁡(ρ,∂tρ)\mathcal{L}(\rho,\partial_{t}\rho):

ℋ⁡(ρ,π)=supξ{∫Λd​x​ξ​π−ℒ⁡(ρ,ξ)}=∫Λdx{∇π⋅χ(ρ)∇π−π∇⋅J(ρ)}.\begin{split}&\mathcal{H}(\rho,\pi)=\sup_{\xi}\Big\{\int_{\Lambda}dx\,\xi\,\pi-\mathcal{L}(\rho,\xi)\Big\}\\ &=\;\int_{\Lambda}dx\,\Big\{\nabla\pi\cdot\chi(\rho)\nabla\pi-\pi\,\nabla\cdot J(\rho)\ \Big\}.\end{split} (79)

The canonical equations associated to the Hamiltonian ℋ{\mathcal{H}} are

{∂tρ=∇⋅(D(ρ)∇ρ)−∇⋅χ(ρ)(E+2∇π)∂tπ=−∇π⋅χ′(ρ)(E+∇π)−Tr{D(ρ)Hess(π)}\left\{\begin{array}[]{lll}\vphantom{\Big\{}\partial_{t}\rho&=&{\displaystyle\nabla\cdot\left(D(\rho)\nabla\rho\right)-\nabla\cdot\chi(\rho)(E+2\nabla\pi)}\\ \vphantom{\Big\{}\partial_{t}\pi&=&{\displaystyle-\nabla\pi\cdot\chi^{\prime}(\rho)(E+\nabla\pi)-\text{\rm Tr}\{D(\rho)\,\text{\rm Hess}(\pi)\}}\end{array}\right. (80)

where π\pi vanishes at the boundary of Λ\Lambda, and ρ\rho satisfies (9). In this formula Hess(π)(\pi) represents the Hessian of π\pi, TrAA the trace of a matrix AA and χ′\chi^{\prime} the matrix with entries χi,j′​(ρ)\chi^{\prime}_{i,j}(\rho).

Observe that (ρ⁡(t),0)(\rho(t),0) is a solution of the canonical equations if ρ⁡(t)\rho(t) solves the hydrodynamic equation (5)-(9). In particular, (ρ¯,0)(\bar{\rho},0) is an equilibrium point of the canonical equations.

Within the Hamiltonian formalism, the variational problem (76) becomes a minimal action problem. Classical arguments in analytic mechanics [4] imply that the quasi-potential VV introduced in (76) solves the stationary Hamilton-Jacobi equation

ℋ⁡(ρ,δ​Vδ​ρ)=ℋ⁡(ρ¯,0)=0.\mathcal{H}\Big(\rho,\frac{\delta V}{\delta\rho}\Big)=\mathcal{H}\big(\bar{\rho},0\big)=0. (81)

This is exactly the equation derived in (27) by the time reversal argument.

We next discuss the time reversal within the Hamiltonian formalism. Letting ℒ∗​(ρ,∂tρ)\mathcal{L}^{*}(\rho,\partial_{t}\rho) be the Lagrangian associated to the action function I∗I^{*}, the time reversal relationship (75) implies the following relation between Lagrangians:

ℒ(ρ,∂tρ)=ℒ∗(ρ,−∂tρ)+∫Λdxδ​Vδ​ρ∂tρ.\mathcal{L}(\rho,\partial_{t}\rho)=\mathcal{L}^{*}(\rho,-\partial_{t}\rho)+\int_{\Lambda}dx\,\frac{\delta V}{\delta\rho}\,\partial_{t}\rho. (82)

As a consequence, denoting by ℋ∗{\mathcal{H}}^{*} the Hamiltonian associated to ℒ∗{\mathcal{L}}^{*},

ℋ⁡(ρ,π)=ℋ∗​(ρ,δ​Vδ​ρ−π).\mathcal{H}(\rho,\pi)=\mathcal{H}^{*}\Big(\rho,\,\frac{\delta V}{\delta\rho}-\pi\Big). (83)

Let us introduce the involution Θ\Theta on the phase space (ρ,π)(\rho,\pi) defined by

Θ⁡(ρ,π)=(ρ,δ​Vδ​ρ​(ρ)−π).\Theta(\rho,\pi)=\big(\rho,\,\frac{\delta V}{\delta\rho}(\rho)-\pi\big).

Denoting by 𝒯t{\mathcal{T}}_{t}, 𝒯t∗{\mathcal{T}}_{t}^{*} the Hamiltonian flow of ℋ\mathcal{H}, ℋ∗\mathcal{H}^{*}, respectively, (83) yields that Θ\Theta acts as the time reversal in the sense that

Θ∘𝒯t=𝒯−t∗∘Θ.\Theta\circ{\mathcal{T}}_{t}={\mathcal{T}}^{*}_{-t}\circ\Theta. (84)

The relationship (84) is non trivial also for reversible processes, i.e. when ℋ=ℋ∗\mathcal{H}=\mathcal{H}^{*}, in such a case it tells us how to change the momentum under time reversal. This definition of time reversal in a Hamiltonian context agrees with the one given in [107].

IV.3 Path integral derivation of the Hamiltonian

In alternative to the previous argument, we provide here, following e.g., [47], a derivation of the Hamiltonian (79) from the fundamental formula (11) via a path integral calculation.

When we are interested only in the fluctuations of the density, we can use formally the fundamental formula as a probability distribution in a path integral,

ℙ((ρε,jε):ρε∈A)≍∫A𝒟ρ∫𝒟jδ(∂tρ+∇⋅j)exp{−ε−d4∫T0T1dt∫Λdx[j−J(ρ)]⋅χ(ρ)−1[j−J(ρ)]}.\begin{split}&{\mathbb{P}}\big((\rho_{\varepsilon},j_{\varepsilon}):\,\rho_{\varepsilon}\in A\big)\asymp\int_{A}\!{\mathcal{D}}\rho\!\int\!{\mathcal{D}}j\;\delta\big(\partial_{t}\rho+\nabla\cdot j\big)\\ &\exp\Big\{-\frac{\varepsilon^{-d}}{4}\int_{T_{0}}^{T_{1}}\!dt\!\int_{\Lambda}\!dx\,[j-J(\rho)]\cdot\chi(\rho)^{-1}[j-J(\rho)]\Big\}.\end{split}

We can take into account the constraint of the δ\delta function by introducing an auxiliary field π\pi. By Laplace asymptotics,

ℙ((ρε,jε):ρε∈A)≍∫A𝒟ρ∫𝒟j∫𝒟πexp{−ε−d∫T0T1dt∫Λdx(∂tρ+∇⋅j)π}⋅exp{−ε−d4∫T0T1dt∫Λdx[j−J(ρ)]⋅χ(ρ)−1[j−J(ρ)]}.\begin{split}&{\mathbb{P}}\big((\rho_{\varepsilon},j_{\varepsilon}):\,\rho_{\varepsilon}\in A\big)\asymp\int_{A}\!{\mathcal{D}}\rho\int\!{\mathcal{D}}j\int\!{\mathcal{D}}\pi\>\\ &\exp\Big\{-\varepsilon^{-d}\int_{T_{0}}^{T_{1}}\!dt\!\int_{\Lambda}\!dx\,\big(\partial_{t}\rho+\nabla\cdot j\big)\pi\Big\}\\ &\cdot\exp\Big\{-\frac{\varepsilon^{-d}}{4}\int_{T_{0}}^{T_{1}}\!dt\!\int_{\Lambda}\!dx\,[j-J(\rho)]\cdot\chi(\rho)^{-1}[j-J(\rho)]\Big\}.\end{split}

Integrating by parts the term (∇⋅j)​π(\nabla\cdot j)\pi and computing the Gaussian integral over jj we get

ℙ((ρε,jε):ρε∈A)≍∫A𝒟ρ∫𝒟πexp{−ε−d∫T0T1dt[∫Λdxπ∂tρ−ℋ(ρ,π)]}\begin{split}&{\mathbb{P}}\big((\rho_{\varepsilon},j_{\varepsilon}):\,\rho_{\varepsilon}\in A\big)\asymp\int_{A}\!{\mathcal{D}}\rho\!\int\!{\mathcal{D}}\pi\\ &\quad\exp\Big\{-{\varepsilon^{-d}}\int_{T_{0}}^{T_{1}}\!dt\,\Big[\int_{\Lambda}\!dx\,\pi\,\partial_{t}\rho-{\mathcal{H}}(\rho,\pi)\Big]\Big\}\end{split}

where ℋ{\mathcal{H}} is the Hamiltonian (79). The exponential in the previous equation is the action corresponding to the Hamiltonian ℋ{\mathcal{H}}. In the limit ε→0\varepsilon\to 0 the dominating contributions are thus in a neighborhood of solutions of the canonical equations (80).

IV.4 Non differentiability of the quasi-potential: Lagrangian phase transitions

The quasi-potential may exhibit singularities which can be interpreted as non-equilibrium phase transitions. In a finite-dimensional setting, an analogous phenomenon is discussed in [71] where it is shown that the quasi-potential generically exhibits points of non differentiability. An interesting example of this kind has been discussed in [82]. We refer to [55] for further developments and examples.

We discuss this phenomenon in the infinite dimensional context of the MFT [18]. For equilibrium states, the quasi-potential VV is always convex and the occurrence of first order phase transitions corresponds to the presence of a flat part in the graph of VV. In non-equilibrium states VV is not necessarily convex and phase transitions without an equilibrium analogue can occur. These phase transitions have a natural geometric interpretation in the Hamiltonian formalism that we next illustrate.

Recall that the Hamiltonian dynamics admits the equilibrium point (ρ¯,0)(\bar{\rho},0). The corresponding energy vanishes, ℋ⁡(ρ¯,0)=0{\mathcal{H}}(\bar{\rho},0)=0. Consider the solution of the canonical equations (80) with initial condition (ρ,0)(\rho,0). As ρ¯\bar{\rho} is globally attractive for the hydrodynamics, such a solution of the canonical equations converges to the equilibrium point (ρ¯,0)(\bar{\rho},0) as t→+∞t\to+\infty. The set {(ρ,π):π=0}\{(\rho,\pi)\,:\,\pi=0\} is therefore the stable manifold ℳs{\mathcal{M}}_{\mathrm{s}} associated to the equilibrium point (ρ¯,0)(\bar{\rho},0). The unstable manifold ℳu{\mathcal{M}}_{\mathrm{u}} is defined as the set of points (ρ,π)(\rho,\pi) such that the solution of the canonical equations starting from (ρ,π)(\rho,\pi) converges to (ρ¯,0)(\bar{\rho},0) as t→−∞t\to-\infty. By the conservation of the energy, ℳu{\mathcal{M}}_{\mathrm{u}} is a subset of the manifold {(ρ,π):ℋ⁡(ρ,π)=ℋ⁡(ρ¯,0)=0}\{(\rho,\pi)\,:\>\mathcal{H}(\rho,\pi)=\mathcal{H}(\bar{\rho},0)=0\}.

In the sequel we need the following result in Hamiltonian dynamics, e.g., [4]. Given a closed curve γ\gamma parametrized as γ⁡(α)=(ρ⁡(α),π⁡(α))\gamma(\alpha)=(\rho(\alpha),\pi(\alpha)), α∈[0,1]\alpha\in[0,1], the integral ∮γπ​𝑑ρ=∫01d​α​∫Λd​x​π​(α,x)​∂αρ⁡(α,x)\oint_{\gamma}\pi\,d\rho=\int_{0}^{1}\!d\alpha\int_{\Lambda}\!dx\,\pi(\alpha,x)\,\partial_{\alpha}\rho(\alpha,x) is invariant under the Hamiltonian evolution. This means that, by denoting with γt\gamma_{t} the evolution of γ\gamma under the Hamiltonian flow, ∮γtπ​𝑑ρ=∮γπ​𝑑ρ\oint_{\gamma_{t}}\pi\,d\rho=\oint_{\gamma}\pi\,d\rho. In view of this result, if γ\gamma is a closed curve contained in the unstable manifold ℳu{\mathcal{M}}_{\mathrm{u}} then ∮γπ​𝑑ρ=limt→−∞∮γtπ​𝑑ρ=0\oint_{\gamma}\pi\,d\rho=\lim_{t\to-\infty}\oint_{\gamma_{t}}\pi\,d\rho=0. We can therefore define the pre-potential 𝒱:ℳu→ℝ{\mathcal{V}}:\,{\mathcal{M}}_{\mathrm{u}}\to{\mathbb{R}} by

𝒱⁡(ρ,π)=∫γπ^​𝑑ρ^,{\mathcal{V}}(\rho,\pi)\;=\;\int_{\gamma}\hat{\pi}\,d\hat{\rho}, (85)

where the integral is carried over an arbitrary curve γ⁡(α)\gamma(\alpha), α∈[0,1]\alpha\in[0,1], in ℳu{\mathcal{M}}_{\mathrm{u}} such that γ⁡(0)=(ρ¯,0)\gamma(0)=(\bar{\rho},0) and γ⁡(1)=(ρ,π)\gamma(1)=(\rho,\pi). The possibility of defining such potential is usually referred to by saying that ℳu{\mathcal{M}}_{\mathrm{u}} is a Lagrangian manifold.

We now establish the relationship between the quasi-potential and the pre-potential

V(ρ)=inf{𝒱(ρ,π),π:(ρ,π)∈ℳu}.V(\rho)\;=\;\inf\big\{{\mathcal{V}}(\rho,\pi)\,,\>\pi\,:\>(\rho,\pi)\in{\mathcal{M}}_{\mathrm{u}}\big\}. (86)

Indeed, fix ρ\rho and consider π\pi such that (ρ,π)(\rho,\pi) belongs to ℳu{\mathcal{M}}_{\mathrm{u}}. Let (ρ^​(t),π^​(t))(\hat{\rho}(t),\hat{\pi}(t)) be the solution of the Hamilton equations starting from (ρ,π)(\rho,\pi) at t=0t=0. Since (ρ,π)∈ℳu(\rho,\pi)\in{\mathcal{M}}_{\mathrm{u}}, (ρ^​(t),π^​(t))(\hat{\rho}(t),\hat{\pi}(t)) converges to (ρ¯,0)(\bar{\rho},0) as t→−∞t\to-\infty. Therefore, the path ρ^​(t)\hat{\rho}(t) is a solution of the Euler-Lagrange equations for the action I(−∞,0]I_{(-\infty,0]}, which means that it is a critical path for (76). Since ℒ⁡(ρ^,∂tρ^)=∫Λπ^​∂tρ^−ℋ⁡(ρ^,π^)\mathcal{L}(\hat{\rho},\partial_{t}\hat{\rho})=\int_{\Lambda}\hat{\pi}\,\partial_{t}\hat{\rho}-\mathcal{H}(\hat{\rho},\hat{\pi}) and ℋ​(ρ^​(t),π^​(t))=0\mathcal{H}(\hat{\rho}(t),\hat{\pi}(t))=0, the action of such path ρ^​(t)\hat{\rho}(t) is given by I(−∞,0](ρ^)=𝒱(ρ,π)I_{(-\infty,0]}(\hat{\rho})={\mathcal{V}}(\rho,\pi). Hence the right hand side of (86) selects among all such paths the one with minimal action, and the minimal action is, by definition, the quasi-potential V⁡(ρ)V(\rho).

For equilibrium states, the quasi-potential is given by the expression in (29) and it is simple to check that the unstable manifold is ℳu={(ρ,π):π=f′​(ρ)−f′​(ρ¯)}{\mathcal{M}}_{\mathrm{u}}=\big\{(\rho,\pi)\>:\,\pi=f^{\prime}(\rho)-f^{\prime}(\bar{\rho})\big\}. In particular, ℳu{\mathcal{M}}_{u} is globally a graph which means that for every ρ\rho there exists an unique π\pi so that (ρ,π)∈ℳu(\rho,\pi)\in\mathcal{M}_{u}. On the other hand, for non-equilibrium states the unstable manifold is not necessarily a graph and it may happen, for special ρ\rho, that the variational problem (86) admits more than a single minimizer (Figure 1.a). The set of profiles ρ\rho for which the minimizer is not unique is a caustic. In general, it is a codimension one submanifold of the configuration space. We call the occurrence of this situation a Lagrangian phase transition. In this case, profiles arbitrarily close to each other but lying on opposite sides of the caustic are reached by optimal paths which are not close to each other. This implies that on the caustics the first derivative of the quasi-potential is discontinuous (Figure 1.b).

Recall the discussion in Section IV.1 showing that the optimal field FF in (70) to produce the profile ρ\rho is given by F=2∇δ​Vδ​ρF=2\nabla\frac{\delta V}{\delta\rho}. If ρ\rho is a caustic point then the functional derivative of VV is not defined. However we can take a profile ρ+ρ~\rho+\tilde{\rho} close to caustic, compute the derivative at ρ+ρ~\rho+\tilde{\rho}, and then take the limit as ρ~→0\tilde{\rho}\to 0. However, since VV has a first order discontinuity, we obtain different values for the limiting derivative. In this way, if ρ\rho is a caustic point, we can construct different fields FF in (70) such that the corresponding action (71) is equal to V⁡(ρ)V(\rho). To each field FF there corresponds an optimal trajectory for the variational problem (76).

The previous geometrical considerations make plausible that, for a non-equilibrium state, Lagrangian phase transitions do generically occur. The question whether a specific model, characterized by its transport coefficients, exhibits such transitions is a completely different story. It is remarkable, as we shall see in section V.7, that the weakly asymmetric simple exclusion can be proven analytically to have such phase transitions.

We conclude with some remarks on the possibility of observing Lagrangian phase transitions. Conceptually, they can be directly detected from a detailed statistics of the stationary non-equilibrium ensemble; Lagrangian phase transitions correspond to the presence of corners in the graph of the probability distribution function in logarithmic scale. Alternatively, one could exploit the instability of the exit path. As mentioned, optimal exit paths have been experimentally observed in noisy electronic devices with a finite number of degrees of freedom [99, 37]. On the other hand, in thermodynamic systems the thermal fluctuations are very small and the direct observation of Lagrangian phase transitions appears quite difficult, as it requires an extremely long time. The problem of large fluctuations admits an interpretation as a control problem [13]. This means that rather than considering the optimal path, we look for the field driving the system from the stationary state to a chosen profile with the minimal energetic cost. The Lagrangian phase transition then corresponds to the existence of two different optimal fields dissipating the same energy. In principle, these two fields can be theoretically calculated and an experiment can be designed to check the predictions.

IV.5 Non locality of the quasi-potential and long range correlations

Long range correlations are a generic property of stationary non equilibrium states which have been experimentally measured, see [53] for a review. At the theoretical level, several approaches have been developed around late 70’s - early 80’s, e.g. [90, 117, 123]. In the MFT, long range correlations are a direct consequence of the non locality of the quasi-potential. By perturbatively solving the Hamilton-Jacobi equation, the equations for correlations of arbitrary order have been obtained [17].

We introduce the pressure functional as the Legendre transform of the quasi-potential VV,

V♯​(h)=supρ{∫Λd​x​h​ρ−V⁡(ρ)}.V^{\sharp}(h)=\sup_{\rho}\Big\{\int_{\Lambda}\!dx\,h\rho-V(\rho)\Big\}.

The large deviations asymptotics (13) implies

limε→0εd​log⁡EP​(exp⁡{ε−d​∫Λd​x​ρε​h})=V♯​(h),\lim_{\varepsilon\to 0}{\varepsilon^{d}}\log E_{P}\left(\exp\Big\{\varepsilon^{-d}\int_{\Lambda}\!dx\,\rho_{\varepsilon}\,h\Big\}\right)=V^{\sharp}(h), (87)

where we recall that ρε\rho_{\varepsilon} denotes the empirical density and PP is the stationary ensemble. We point out that the above asymptotics does not imply in general (13). Indeed, while the functional V♯V^{\sharp} is always convex, the functional VV can be recovered as the Legendre transform of V♯V^{\sharp} only when it is convex. For example, for the KMP model, VV turns out to be not convex, [23]. On the other hand, (87) does suffice to recover VV in a small neighborhood of the stationary profile ρ¯\bar{\rho}.

By taking derivatives, (87) yields the asymptotics of truncated correlations of the empirical density,

limε→0(ε−d)n−1​EP​(ρε​(x1),⋯,ρε​(xn))=Cn​(x1,…,xn)\lim_{\varepsilon\to 0}\big(\varepsilon^{-d}\big)^{n-1}E_{P}\big(\rho_{\varepsilon}(x_{1});\,\cdots\,;\rho_{\varepsilon}(x_{n})\big)=C_{n}(x_{1},\dots,x_{n}) (88)

where

Cn​(x1,…,xn)=δn​V♯δh(x1)⋯δh(xn)|h=0.C_{n}(x_{1},\dots,x_{n})=\frac{\delta^{n}V^{\sharp}}{\delta h(x_{1})\cdots\delta h(x_{n})}\,\Big|_{h=0}. (89)

By Legendre duality we have the change of variable formula h=δ​Vδ​ρ,ρ=δ​V♯δ​hh=\frac{\delta V}{\delta\rho},\,\rho=\frac{\delta V^{\sharp}}{\delta h}, so that the Hamilton-Jacobi equation (27) can then be rewritten in terms of V♯V^{\sharp} as

∫Λdx∇h⋅χ(δ​V♯δ​h)∇h+∫Λdx∇h⋅J(δ​V♯δ​h)=0\int_{\Lambda}\!dx\,\nabla h\cdot\chi\Big(\frac{\delta V^{\sharp}}{\delta h}\Big)\nabla h+\int_{\Lambda}\!dx\,\nabla h\cdot J\Big(\frac{\delta V^{\sharp}}{\delta h}\Big)=0 (90)

where hh vanishes at the boundary of Λ\Lambda. This an equation for the generating function V♯V^{\sharp}, which by Taylor expansion yields a recursive relationship for the macroscopic correlations CnC_{n}.

Write the two-point correlation function in the form

C2​(x,y)=Ceq​(x)​δ​(x−y)+B⁡(x,y)C_{2}(x,y)=C_{\mathrm{eq}}(x)\delta(x-y)+B(x,y)

where

Ceq​(x)=D−1​(ρ¯​(x))​χ​(ρ¯​(x)).C_{\mathrm{eq}}(x)=D^{-1}(\bar{\rho}(x))\chi(\bar{\rho}(x)).

By expanding (90) around the stationary profile ρ¯\bar{\rho} we obtain the following equation for BB

ℒ†​B​(x,y)=α⁡(x)​δ​(x−y).\mathcal{L}^{\dagger}B(x,y)=\alpha(x)\delta(x-y). (91)

The operator ℒ†\mathcal{L}^{\dagger} is the formal adjoint of the differential operator ℒ=Lx+Ly\mathcal{L}=L_{x}+L_{y}, where

Lx=Di​j(ρ¯(x))∂xi∂xj+χi​j′(ρ¯(x))Ej(x)∂xiL_{x}=D_{ij}(\bar{\rho}(x))\partial_{x_{i}}\partial_{x_{j}}+\chi^{\prime}_{ij}(\bar{\rho}(x))E_{j}(x)\partial_{x_{i}} (92)

and,

α⁡(x)=∂xi[χi​j′​(ρ¯​(x))​Dj​k−1​(ρ¯​(x))​Jk​(ρ¯​(x))].\alpha(x)=\partial_{x_{i}}\big[\chi^{\prime}_{ij}\big(\bar{\rho}(x)\big)\,D^{-1}_{jk}\big(\bar{\rho}(x)\big)J_{k}(\bar{\rho}(x))\big].

We are using the convention that repeated indices are summed. When α⁡(x)=0\alpha(x)=0, due to the boundary conditions, the unique solution to (91) is B=0B=0 and there are no long range correlations. In the case of equilibrium states α⁡(x)=0\alpha(x)=0 since the current vanishes. There are cases in which α⁡(x)=0\alpha(x)=0 even if J​(ρ¯​(x))≠0J(\bar{\rho}(x))\neq 0. This happens in the Ginzburg–Landau model [73] where χ\chi does not depend on ρ\rho. Another case is the zero range model discussed in Section V.2. If α⁡(x)\alpha(x) is non-vanishing the inhomogeneous equation (91) has a non-trivial solution and long range correlations are present.

Since ℒ\mathcal{L} is an elliptic operator (i.e. it has a negative kernel), the sign of BB is determined by the sign of α\alpha: if α⁡(x)≥0\alpha(x)\geq 0, then B⁡(x,y)≤0B(x,y)\leq 0, while if α⁡(x)≤0\alpha(x)\leq 0, then B⁡(x,y)≥0B(x,y)\geq 0. For example, consider the following special case. The system is one-dimensional, the diffusion coefficient is constant, D⁡(ρ)=D0D(\rho)=D_{0}, the mobility χ⁡(ρ)\chi(\rho) is a quadratic function of ρ\rho, and there is no external field, E=0E=0. Then

B⁡(x,y)=−12​D0​χ′′​(∇ρ¯)2​Δ−1​(x,y),B(x,y)=-\frac{1}{2D_{0}}\chi^{\prime\prime}(\nabla\bar{\rho})^{2}\Delta^{-1}(x,y), (93)

where Δ−1​(x,y)\Delta^{-1}(x,y) is the Green function of the Dirichlet Laplacian. Two well studied models, the symmetric exclusion process, where χ⁡(ρ)=ρ⁡(1−ρ)\chi(\rho)=\rho(1-\rho), and the KMP process, where χ⁡(ρ)=ρ2\chi(\rho)=\rho^{2}, meet the above conditions. Then (93) shows that their correlations have opposite signs.

By developing the arguments presented above, it is possible to deduce recursive equations for the nn-point correlations CnC_{n}; we refer to [17] for the details of this analysis.

The existence of long range correlations in stochastic lattice gases and in particular in the symmetric simple exclusion process was first established, using fluctuating hydrodynamics and a direct computation, in [123]. We refer to [69] for more recent microscopic results. Our derivation shows that long range correlations in diffusive systems with a conservation law are a generic consequence of inhomogeneous chemical potentials and external fields. In real systems couplings between different fluctuating quantities generate non-equilibrium long range correlations as discussed in [113]. These authors consider the coupling of temperature fluctuations with velocity fluctuations. The velocity fluctuating field formally appears as an external field in the hydrodynamic equation for the temperature fluctuations. For the experimental situation the reader may consult the review [53].

IV.6 Current fluctuations

Both from a theoretical and an experimental point of view, a natural observable in non-equilibrium thermodynamics is the time averaged current. The corresponding fluctuations have been analyzed in [24]. By postulating an additivity principle, which relates the fluctuation of the time averaged current in the whole system to the fluctuations in subsystems, the corresponding asymptotic probability is deduced. However, as pointed out in [14, 15], this approach may underestimate the probability of fluctuations due to the possible occurrence of a dynamical phase transition.

We show that the probability of fluctuations of the time averaged current in the time window [0,T][0,T] can be derived, without additional assumptions, from the macroscopic fluctuation theory. The probability of observing a time averaged fluctuation JJ can be described by a functional Φ⁡(J)\Phi(J) which we characterize in terms of a variational problem for the functional ℐ[0,T]\mathcal{I}_{[0,T]}.

Recall that jεj_{\varepsilon} is the empirical current, described after equation (11). Given a vector field JJ, by the fundamental formula (11),

ℙρ0​(1T​∫0Td​t​jε​(t)≈J)≍exp⁡{−ε−d​T​ΦT​(J)},{\mathbb{P}}_{\rho_{0}}\Big(\frac{1}{T}\int_{0}^{T}\!dt\;j_{\varepsilon}(t)\approx J\Big)\asymp\exp\big\{-\varepsilon^{-d}\,T\,\Phi_{T}(J)\big\}, (94)

where ΦT\Phi_{T} is given by

ΦT​(J)=1T​inf(ρ,j)∈𝒜Tℐ[0,T]​(ρ,j).\Phi_{T}(J)\;=\;\frac{1}{T}\,\inf_{(\rho,j)\in{\mathcal{A}}_{T}}{\mathcal{I}}_{[0,T]}(\rho,j). (95)

In this formula, 𝒜T{\mathcal{A}}_{T} is the set of paths (ρ,j)(\rho,j) whose average current is JJ and initial density is ρ0\rho_{0},

𝒜T={(ρ,j):1T∫0Tdtj(t)=J,∂tρ=−∇⋅j,ρ(0)=ρ0}.\begin{split}&{\mathcal{A}}_{T}=\Big\{(\rho,j):\,\frac{1}{T}\int_{0}^{T}\!\!{dt}\,j(t)=J\,,\\ &\qquad\qquad\partial_{t}\rho=-\nabla\cdot j\,,\rho(0)=\rho_{0}\Big\}.\end{split}

By the local conservation of the mass, the asymptotic T→∞T\to\infty of the above probability is relevant only for divergence free vector fields. Indeed, the case in which JJ has not zero divergence leads either to negative mass or to a mass condensation.

For a divergence free current JJ the sequence T​ΦT​(J)T\,\Phi_{T}(J) is subadditive in TT,

(T+S)​ΦT+S​(J)≤T​ΦT​(J)+S​ΦS​(J)(T+S)\Phi_{T+S}(J)\leq T\,\Phi_{T}(J)+S\,\Phi_{S}(J) (96)

for TT, S≥0S\geq 0. Indeed, let (ρ1,j1)∈𝒜T(\rho_{1},j_{1})\in{\mathcal{A}}_{T} and (ρ2,j2)∈𝒜S(\rho_{2},j_{2})\in{\mathcal{A}}_{S}. As J=(1/T)​∫0Td​t​j​(t)J=(1/T)\int_{0}^{T}\!dt\>j(t) is divergence free, by the continuity equation ρ1​(0)=ρ1​(T)+∇⋅∫0Td​t​j​(t)=ρ1​(T)=ρ2​(0)\rho_{1}(0)=\rho_{1}(T)+\nabla\cdot\int_{0}^{T}\!dt\>j(t)=\rho_{1}(T)=\rho_{2}(0). We may therefore glue the trajectories (ρ1,j1)(\rho_{1},j_{1}) and (ρ2,j2)(\rho_{2},j_{2}), obtaining a trajectory (ρ,j)(\rho,j) in 𝒜T+S{\mathcal{A}}_{T+S} which satisfies

ℐ[0,T+S]​(ρ,j)=ℐ[0,T]​(ρ1,j1)+ℐ[0,S]​(ρ2,j2)\mathcal{I}_{[0,T+S]}(\rho,j)=\mathcal{I}_{[0,T]}(\rho_{1},j_{1})+\mathcal{I}_{[0,S]}(\rho_{2},j_{2}) (97)

Therefore, optimizing over all the trajectories, we obtain (96).

Since for a divergence free current JJ the sequence T​ΦT​(J)T\,\Phi_{T}(J) is subadditive in TT, ΦT​(J)\Phi_{T}(J) converges to a limit denoted by Φ⁡(J)\Phi(J), given by

Φ⁡(J)=limT→∞inf(ρ,j)∈𝒜T1T​ℐ[0,T]​(ρ,j)=infT>0inf(ρ,j)∈𝒜T1T​ℐ[0,T]​(ρ,j).\begin{split}\Phi(J)\;&=\;\lim_{T\to\infty}\;\inf_{(\rho,j)\in{\mathcal{A}}_{T}}\frac{1}{T}\;{\mathcal{I}}_{[0,T]}(\rho,j)\\ \;&=\;\inf_{T>0}\;\inf_{(\rho,j)\in{\mathcal{A}}_{T}}\frac{1}{T}\;{\mathcal{I}}_{[0,T]}(\rho,j)\;.\end{split} (98)

The limit Φ⁡(J)\Phi(J) does not depend on the initial condition ρ0\rho_{0}. Indeed given two different initial conditions they can be connected by a transient in a finite time that will be irrelevant for the limit.

We now prove that Φ\Phi is a convex functional. Let 0<p<10<p<1 and J=p​J1+(1−p)​J2J=pJ_{1}+(1-p)J_{2}, we want to show that Φ⁡(J)≤p​Φ​(J1)+(1−p)​Φ​(J2)\Phi(J)\leq p\Phi(J_{1})+(1-p)\Phi(J_{2}). Fix T>0T>0 and an initial density profile ρ0\rho_{0}. Let (ρ1,j1)∈𝒜p​T(\rho_{1},j_{1})\in{\mathcal{A}}_{pT}, and (ρ2,j2)∈𝒜(1−p)​T(\rho_{2},j_{2})\in{\mathcal{A}}_{(1-p)T} be the optimal paths for the variational problem (95) associated to the currents J1J_{1}, J2J_{2}, respectively. Therefore

Φp​T​(J1)=1p​T​ℐ[0,p​T]​(ρ1,j1),Φ(1−p)​T​(J2)=1(1−p)​T​ℐ[0,(1−p)​T]​(ρ2,j2).\begin{split}&\Phi_{pT}(J_{1})=\frac{1}{pT}\ {\mathcal{I}}_{[0,pT]}(\rho_{1},j_{1})\;,\\ &\quad\Phi_{(1-p)T}(J_{2})=\frac{1}{(1-p)T}\,{\mathcal{I}}_{[0,(1-p)T]}(\rho_{2},j_{2})\;.\end{split}

By the same arguments used in (97), the path obtained by gluing j1j_{1} with j2j_{2}, denoted by jj, is in the set 𝒜T{\mathcal{A}}_{T}. Therefore,

ΦT​(J)≤1T​ℐ[0,T]​(ρ,j)=p​Φp​T​(J1)+(1−p)​Φ(1−p)​T​(J2).\Phi_{T}(J)\leq\frac{1}{T}\>{\mathcal{I}}_{[0,T]}(\rho,j)=p\,\Phi_{pT}(J_{1})+(1-p)\,\Phi_{(1-p)T}(J_{2}).

By taking the limit T→∞T\to\infty and since the limiting function does not depend on the initial condition, we conclude that Φ\Phi is convex. These arguments are standard in proving the existence and the convexity of thermodynamic functions in equilibrium statistical mechanics.

We introduce the functional 𝒰{\mathcal{U}} on the set of time independent profiles ρ=ρ⁡(x)\rho=\rho(x) and j=j⁡(x)j=j(x)

𝒰⁡(ρ,j)=14​∫Λd​x​[j−J⁡(ρ)]⋅χ​(ρ)−1​[j−J⁡(ρ)].{\mathcal{U}}(\rho,j)=\frac{1}{4}\int_{\Lambda}dx\,[j-J(\rho)]\cdot\chi(\rho)^{-1}[j-J(\rho)]. (99)

We then define UU on divergence free currents by

U⁡(J)=infρ𝒰⁡(ρ,J),U(J)=\inf_{\rho}\,{\mathcal{U}}(\rho,J), (100)

where the minimum is carried over all profiles ρ\rho satisfying the boundary condition (9). We show that

Φ⁡(J)≤U⁡(J).\Phi(J)\leq U(J)\;. (101)

To see this, since Φ⁡(J)\Phi(J) does not depend on the initial condition, choose as initial condition the density profile ρ0\rho_{0} which minimizes (100). Since JJ is divergence free, the constant path (ρ0,J)(\rho_{0},J) lies in 𝒜T{\mathcal{A}}_{T}. Hence, ΦT​(J)≤1T​ℐ[0,T]​(ρ0,J)=U⁡(J)\Phi_{T}(J)\leq\frac{1}{T}{\mathcal{I}}_{[0,T]}(\rho_{0},J)=U(J). The functional UU is in general non convex.

In one space dimension, the functional UU is the one introduced in [24]. Therefore, the additivity principle postulated there provides the correct asymptotics when equality holds in (101). This is the case for some models and corresponds to the situation in which the optimal path in (98) does not depend on time. On the other hand, as we shall see in Section VI.1, for other models the inequality in (101) is strict and this corresponds to a spontaneous symmetry breaking of time translation invariance.

We now argue that for small deviations of the current, i.e. in a neighborhood of the stationary current J⁡(ρ¯)J(\bar{\rho}), dynamical phase transitions do not occur, i.e. Φ=U\Phi=U. Observe that for J⁡(ρ¯)J(\bar{\rho}) we have Φ⁡(J⁡(ρ¯))=U⁡(J⁡(ρ¯))=0\Phi(J(\bar{\rho}))=U(J(\bar{\rho}))=0 and this is uniquely realized by choosing on the right hand side of (98) the time independent path (ρ¯,J⁡(ρ¯))(\bar{\rho},J(\bar{\rho})). For JJ close to J⁡(ρ¯)J(\bar{\rho}) the optimal path for the right hand side of (98), possibly time-dependent, will be close to (ρ¯,J⁡(ρ¯))(\bar{\rho},J(\bar{\rho})). Since the path (ρ∗,J)(\rho^{*},J) where ρ∗\rho^{*} is the optimal profile in (100) is a stationary point for the right hand side of (98), by continuity it also will be the global minimizer.

The asymptotics (94) can be formulated in terms of the moment generating function of the empirical current. For each time independent, divergence-free vector field v=v⁡(x)v=v(x) we have

limT→∞limε→0εdT​log⁡𝔼ρ0​[eε−d​∫0Td​t​∫Λd​x​jε​(t)⋅v]=Φ♯​(v)\lim_{T\to\infty}\lim_{\varepsilon\to 0}\frac{\varepsilon^{d}}{T}\log{\mathbb{E}}_{\rho_{0}}\Big[e^{\varepsilon^{-d}\,\int_{0}^{T}dt\int_{\Lambda}dx\,j_{\varepsilon}(t)\cdot v}\Big]=\Phi^{\sharp}(v) (102)

where 𝔼ρ0{\mathbb{E}}_{\rho_{0}} denotes the expectation with respect to the probability distribution ℙρ0{\mathbb{P}}_{\rho_{0}}, and Φ♯​(v)\Phi^{\sharp}(v) is the Legendre transform of Φ⁡(J)\Phi(J),

Φ♯​(v)=supJ{∫Λd​x​v⋅J−Φ⁡(J)}.\Phi^{\sharp}(v)=\sup_{J}\Big\{\int_{\Lambda}dx\,v\cdot J-\Phi(J)\Big\}. (103)

The supremum is carried over all the divergence free vector fields JJ.

In connection with the functional Φ\Phi, Varadhan suggested [128] the possibility of the alternative variational representation

Φ⁡(J)=inf⟨𝒰⁡(ρ⁡(t),j⁡(t))⟩.\Phi(J)\;=\;\inf\big\langle\,{\mathcal{U}}(\rho(t),j(t))\,\big\rangle. (104)

In this formula ⟨⋅⟩\langle\cdot\rangle represents the expectation with respect to a stationary process (ρ,j)(\rho,j), and the infimum is carried over all such stationary processes satisfying the continuity equation ∂tρ+∇⋅j=0\partial_{t}\rho+\nabla\cdot j=0 and the constraint ⟨j⁡(t)⟩=J\langle j(t)\rangle=J. Note that ⟨𝒰⁡(ρ⁡(t),j⁡(t))⟩\big\langle\,{\mathcal{U}}(\rho(t),j(t))\,\big\rangle does not depend on tt by stationarity. The representation (104) is not used in this paper.

The fundamental formula (11)–(12) can be used to analyze the fluctuation of the current flux across a surface. As shown in [27], for models in two dimension the asymptotics for closed or open curves are different due to the possible occurrence of vortexes around the endpoints.

IV.7 Gallavotti–Cohen symmetry

Denote by Φ∗\Phi^{*} the functional defined by the variational problem (98) with ℐ∗\mathcal{I}^{*} in place of ℐ\mathcal{I}. By (19) and since θ​j​(t)=−j⁡(−t)\theta j(t)=-j(-t),

Φ⁡(J)=Φ∗​(−J).\Phi(J)=\Phi^{*}(-J)\;.

For equilibrium states this symmetry states that the functional Φ\Phi is even.

Let us consider a path j⁡(t)j(t), t∈[−T,T]t\in[-T,T] such that (2​T)−1​∫−TTd​t​j​(t)=J(2T)^{-1}\int_{-T}^{T}\!dt\>j(t)=J for some divergence free vector field JJ. Recalling the Einstein relation D⁡(ρ)​χ​(ρ)−1=f′′​(ρ)D(\rho)\chi(\rho)^{-1}=f^{\prime\prime}(\rho) we have that

χ​(ρ)−1​J​(ρ)=−∇f′​(ρ)+E\chi(\rho)^{-1}J(\rho)=-\nabla f^{\prime}(\rho)+E

Recall (12) and (15). Since f′​(ρ⁡(x))=λ⁡(x)f^{\prime}(\rho(x))=\lambda(x), x∈∂Λx\in\partial\Lambda, an integration by parts yields

12​T​ℛ[−T,T]​(ρ,j)=12​T​ℛ[−T,T]​(θ​ρ,θ​j)−∫ΛdxJ⋅E+∫∂ΛdσλJ⋅n^\begin{split}\frac{1}{2T}{\mathcal{R}}_{[-T,T]}(\rho,j)&=\frac{1}{2T}{\mathcal{R}}_{[-T,T]}(\theta\rho,\theta j)\\ &-\int_{\Lambda}dx\,J\cdot E+\int_{\partial\Lambda}\!d\sigma\>\lambda\,J\cdot\hat{n}\end{split} (105)

where d​σd\sigma is the surface measure on ∂Λ\partial\Lambda and n^\hat{n} is the outward normal to Λ\Lambda. In particular this relation implies that if (ρ^,ȷ^)(\hat{\rho},\hat{\jmath}) is an optimal path for the variational problem defining Φ⁡(J)\Phi(J) then (θ​ρ^,θ​ȷ^)(\theta\hat{\rho},\theta\hat{\jmath}) is an optimal path for the variational problem defining Φ⁡(−J)\Phi(-J).

By taking the limit T→∞T\to\infty in (105) we get

Φ(J)−Φ(−J)=−∫ΛdxJ⋅E+∫∂ΛdσλJ⋅n^,\Phi(J)-\Phi(-J)=-\int_{\Lambda}dx\,J\cdot E+\int_{\partial\Lambda}\!d\sigma\>\lambda\,J\cdot\hat{n}\;, (106)

which is a Gallavotti–Cohen type symmetry in our space time dependent setup for macroscopic observables. Note that the right hand side of (106) is minus the energy given to the system by the external field and the boundary reservoirs per unit time (36).

When Φ=U\Phi=U the symmetry (106) can be generalized as follows [80]. Consider JJ and J′J^{\prime} two divergence free currents such that |J⁡(x)|2=|J′​(x)|2|J(x)|^{2}=|J^{\prime}(x)|^{2} then it is immediately seen that

U⁡(J)−U⁡(J′)=12​∫∂Λd​σ​λ​(J−J′)⋅n^−12∫Λdx(J−J′)⋅E.\begin{split}U(J)-U(J^{\prime})&=\frac{1}{2}\int_{\partial\Lambda}\!d\sigma\>\lambda\,\left(J-J^{\prime}\right)\cdot\hat{n}\\ &-\frac{1}{2}\int_{\Lambda}dx\,\left(J-J^{\prime}\right)\cdot E\,.\end{split} (107)

If Φ=U\Phi=U, by taking J′=−JJ^{\prime}=-J we recover (106).

IV.8 Extended Hamiltonian structure

In section IV.2 we discussed the Hamiltonian structure related to the density fluctuations. Here we show that there is an underlying (richer) Hamiltonian structure for the joint fluctuations of density and current.

To this end we write (12) as an action associated to a Lagrangian. This is possible using some simple changes of variables. We consider the time interval [0,T][0,T] and assume that the external drivings do not depend on time. Let A0​(x)A_{0}(x) be a vector field related to the initial condition by ∇⋅A0​(x)=ρ⁡(x,0)\nabla\cdot A_{0}(x)=\rho(x,0). For example we can fix A0=−∇hA_{0}=-\nabla h where hh solves Δ​h​(x)=−ρ⁡(x,0)\Delta h(x)=-\rho(x,0). We then define the vector field

A⁡(t,x)=A0​(x)−∫0tj⁡(s,x)​𝑑s,A(t,x)=A_{0}(x)-\int_{0}^{t}j(s,x)\,ds\,, (108)

that, apart from the initial condition and a minus sign, is the time integrated current. Since ρ\rho and jj are related by the continuity equation we have j=−∂tAj=-\partial_{t}A and ρ=∇⋅A\rho=\nabla\cdot A.

We can then write the rate functional (12) in terms of the vector field AA

ℐ[0,T]​(A)=14​∫0Td​t​∫Λd​x​(∂tA+J⁡(∇⋅A))⋅χ−1​(∇⋅A)​(∂tA+J⁡(∇⋅A)).\begin{split}{\mathcal{I}}_{[0,T]}(A)&=\frac{1}{4}\int_{0}^{T}dt\int_{\Lambda}dx\,\Big(\partial_{t}A+J(\nabla\cdot A)\Big)\\ &\quad\cdot\chi^{-1}(\nabla\cdot A)\Big(\partial_{t}A+J(\nabla\cdot A)\Big)\,.\end{split} (109)

Observe that, in this form, the constraint of the continuity equation is automatically satisfied. Formula (109) has the form of an action for the Lagrangian

𝕃⁡(A,∂tA)=14​∫Λd​x​(∂tA+J⁡(∇⋅A))⋅χ−1​(∇⋅A)​(∂tA+J⁡(∇⋅A)).\begin{split}&\mathbb{L}\left(A,\partial_{t}A\right)=\\ &\frac{1}{4}\int_{\Lambda}\!dx\Big(\partial_{t}A+J(\nabla\cdot A)\Big)\cdot\chi^{-1}(\nabla\cdot A)\Big(\partial_{t}A+J(\nabla\cdot A)\Big)\,.\end{split} (110)

The corresponding Hamiltonian is

ℍ⁡(A,B)=supξ{∫Λd​x​B​(x)⋅ξ⁡(x)−𝕃⁡(A,ξ)}=∫Λd​x​[B⋅χ⁡(∇⋅A)​B−B⋅J⁡(∇⋅A)]\begin{split}\mathbb{H}(A,B)=&\sup_{\xi}\left\{\int_{\Lambda}\!dx\,B(x)\cdot\xi(x)-\mathbb{L}\left(A,\xi\right)\right\}\\ =&\int_{\Lambda}dx\,\Big[B\cdot\chi(\nabla\cdot A)B-B\cdot J(\nabla\cdot A)\Big]\end{split} (111)

and the canonical equations are

{∂tA=2​χ​(∇⋅A)​B−J⁡(∇⋅A),∂tB=−∇[Tr(D(∇⋅A)∇TB)+B⋅χ′(∇⋅A)(E−B)],\left\{\begin{array}[]{ll}\partial_{t}A=&2\chi(\nabla\cdot A)B-J(\nabla\cdot A)\,,\\ \\ \partial_{t}B=&-\nabla\Big[\textrm{Tr}\big(D(\nabla\cdot A)\nabla^{T}B\big)\\ &+B\cdot\chi^{\prime}(\nabla\cdot A)\left(E-B\right)\Big]\,,\end{array}\right. (112)

where we denoted by ∇TB\nabla^{T}B the matrix having entries (∇TB)i,j=∂xiBj\left(\nabla^{T}B\right)_{i,j}=\partial_{x_{i}}B_{j} and recall that Tr​(⋅)\textrm{Tr}(\cdot) denotes the trace.

Given a solution (ρ,π)(\rho,\pi) of the canonical equations (80) there corresponds a solution of (112) given by

{A⁡(t)=A0−∫0tds[J(ρ(s))+2χ(ρ(s))∇π(s)],B⁡(t)=−∇π​(t),\left\{\begin{split}A(t)=&A_{0}-\int_{0}^{t}\!ds\left[J(\rho(s))+2\chi(\rho(s))\nabla\pi(s)\right]\,,\\ B(t)=&-\nabla\pi(t)\,,\end{split}\right. (113)

where A0A_{0} satisfies the condition ∇⋅A0=ρ⁡(0)\nabla\cdot A_{0}=\rho(0).

The momentum BB plays the role of the external field FF in (70). When we look only at fluctuations of the density then BB is a gradient vector field with potential π\pi as in (113). On the other hand when we study fluctuations of the current we need a general vector field BB. Correspondingly not all the solutions of (112) are of the form (113).

V Macroscopic models

To illustrate the scope of the general theory developed so far, we begin by discussing some cases where calculations can be made explicitly. From the point of view of the MFT, a system is defined by the transport coefficient DD and χ\chi. In this connection we emphasize that many microscopic models can give rise to the same macroscopic behavior encoded in such coefficients. Only in special cases the microscopic models can be solved. Specific choices of the transport coefficients are named after the underlying microscopic models. In Section VIII we discuss how these coefficients can be obtained from the microscopic dynamics.

V.1 Equilibrium

We briefly look upon equilibrium states from the standpoint of non-equilibrium. Recall that we defined a system in the domain Λ\Lambda to be in an equilibrium state when the current in the stationary profile ρ¯\bar{\rho} vanishes, i.e. J⁡(ρ¯)=0J(\bar{\rho})=0. A particular case is that of a homogeneous equilibrium state, obtained by setting the external field E=0E=0 and choosing a constant chemical potential at the boundary, i.e., λ⁡(x)=λ¯\lambda(x)=\bar{\lambda}.

For equilibrium states the quasi-potential, defined by the variational formula (76), coincides with the functional VV in (29), that is

V⁡(ρ)=∫Λd​x​{f⁡(ρ)−f⁡(ρ¯)−f′​(ρ¯)​(ρ−ρ¯)}.V(\rho)=\int_{\Lambda}\!dx\>\big\{f(\rho)-f(\bar{\rho})-f^{\prime}(\bar{\rho})\big(\rho-\bar{\rho}\big)\big\}. (114)

We show that VV solves the Hamilton-Jacobi equation (27). Its derivative is

δ​Vδ​ρ​(x)=f′​(ρ⁡(x))−f′​(ρ¯​(x))\frac{\delta V}{\delta\rho(x)}=f^{\prime}(\rho(x))-f^{\prime}(\bar{\rho}(x)) (115)

so that, by an integration by parts,

ℋ⁡(ρ,δ​Vδ​ρ)=∫Λdx∇[f′(ρ)−f′(ρ¯)]⋅χ(ρ)∇[f′(ρ)−f′(ρ¯)]+∫Λdx[f′(ρ)−f′(ρ¯)]∇⋅[D(ρ)∇ρ−χ(ρ)E]=∫Λdx∇[f′(ρ)−f′(ρ¯)]⋅χ(ρ)[∇f′(ρ¯)−E]=0\begin{split}&{\mathcal{H}}\big(\rho,\tfrac{\delta V}{\delta\rho}\big)\\ &=\int_{\Lambda}\!dx\,\nabla\big[f^{\prime}(\rho)-f^{\prime}(\bar{\rho})\big]\cdot\chi(\rho)\nabla\big[f^{\prime}(\rho)-f^{\prime}(\bar{\rho})\big]\\ &\quad+\int_{\Lambda}\!dx\,\big[f^{\prime}(\rho)-f^{\prime}(\bar{\rho})\big]\nabla\cdot\Big[D(\rho)\nabla\rho-\chi(\rho)E\Big]\\ &=\int_{\Lambda}\!dx\,\nabla\big[f^{\prime}(\rho)-f^{\prime}(\bar{\rho})\big]\cdot\chi(\rho)\Big[\nabla f^{\prime}(\bar{\rho})-E\Big]=0\end{split} (116)

where we used (8) and ∇f′​(ρ¯)−E=−χ​(ρ¯)−1​J​(ρ¯)=0\nabla f^{\prime}(\bar{\rho})-E=-\chi(\bar{\rho})^{-1}J(\bar{\rho})=0.

This statement is not sufficient to conclude that the functional in (114) is the quasi-potential, observe for instance that V=0V=0 always solves the Hamilton-Jacobi equation. In order to identify VV with the quasi-potential we need to verify that VV is the maximal solution satisfying V⁡(ρ¯)=0V(\bar{\rho})=0. Clearly, VV is positive and zero on ρ¯\bar{\rho}. For checking that it is a maximal solution we refer to [17].

We next show that the condition J⁡(ρ¯)=0J(\bar{\rho})=0 is equivalent to either one of the following conditions.

  • –

    There exists a function λ~:Λ→ℝ\tilde{\lambda}:\Lambda\to{\mathbb{R}} such that

    E⁡(x)=∇λ~​(x),x∈Λλ~​(x)=λ⁡(x),x∈∂Λ,E(x)=\nabla\tilde{\lambda}(x)\,,\quad x\in\Lambda\qquad\quad\tilde{\lambda}(x)=\lambda(x)\,,\quad x\in\partial\Lambda\,, (117)
  • –

    The system is macroscopically time reversal invariant in the sense that for each profile ρ\rho we have J∗​(ρ)=J​(ρ)J^{*}(\rho)=J(\rho).

We emphasize that the notion of macroscopic time reversal invariance does not imply that an underlying microscopic model satisfies the detailed balance condition. Indeed, as it has been shown by explicit examples [64, 63], there are microscopic models not time reversal invariant for which J∗​(ρ)=J​(ρ)J^{*}(\rho)=J(\rho).

We start by showing that J⁡(ρ¯)=0J(\bar{\rho})=0 if and only if (117) holds. From the local Einstein relation (8) and J⁡(ρ¯)=0J(\bar{\rho})=0 we deduce

E(x)=f′′(ρ¯(x))∇ρ¯(x)=∇f′(ρ¯(x))E(x)=f^{\prime\prime}\big(\bar{\rho}(x)\big)\nabla\bar{\rho}(x)=\nabla f^{\prime}(\bar{\rho}(x))

hence (117). Conversely, let the external field EE be such that (117) holds. Since f′′f^{\prime\prime} is positive the function f′f^{\prime} is invertible and we can define ρ¯​(x)=(f′)−1​(λ~​(x))\bar{\rho}(x)=(f^{\prime})^{-1}\big(\tilde{\lambda}(x)\big). The profile ρ¯\bar{\rho} satisfies (9) as well as J⁡(ρ¯)=0J(\bar{\rho})=0.

We next show that J⁡(ρ¯)=0J(\bar{\rho})=0 if and only if J​(ρ)=J∗​(ρ)J(\rho)=J^{*}(\rho). Suppose first that J​(ρ)=J∗​(ρ)J(\rho)=J^{*}(\rho). By evaluating the Hamilton-Jacobi equation for ρ=ρ¯\rho=\bar{\rho} we deduce ∇[δ​V​(ρ¯)/δ​ρ]=0\nabla\big[\delta V(\bar{\rho})/\delta\rho\big]=0. From the first equation in (22) we then get J⁡(ρ¯)=0J(\bar{\rho})=0. To show the converse implication, note that if J⁡(ρ¯)=0J(\bar{\rho})=0 then VV is given by (114). We deduce that

χ(ρ)∇δ​Vδ​ρ=D(ρ)∇ρ−χ(ρ)E=−J(ρ)\chi(\rho)\nabla\frac{\delta V}{\delta\rho}=D(\rho)\nabla\rho-\chi(\rho)E=-J(\rho)

where we used (6). Recalling the first equation in (22) we get J​(ρ)=J∗​(ρ)J(\rho)=J^{*}(\rho).

So far we have assumed the local Einstein relation and we have shown that for equilibrium systems it implies (114). Conversely, we now show that macroscopic reversibility and (114) imply the local Einstein relation (8). If J​(ρ)=J∗​(ρ)J(\rho)=J^{*}(\rho) then (30) holds, which reads, in view of (114),

[χ(ρ)f′′(ρ)−D(ρ)]∇ρ=χ(ρ)[f′′(ρ¯)−χ−1(ρ¯)D(ρ¯)]∇ρ¯\big[\chi(\rho)f^{\prime\prime}(\rho)-D(\rho)\big]\nabla\rho=\chi(\rho)\big[f^{\prime\prime}(\bar{\rho})-\chi^{-1}(\bar{\rho})D(\bar{\rho})\big]\nabla\bar{\rho} (118)

where we used J⁡(ρ¯)=0J(\bar{\rho})=0 to eliminate EE. Note that J⁡(ρ¯)=0J(\bar{\rho})=0 follows from the first equation in (22) and J​(ρ)=J∗​(ρ)J(\rho)=J^{*}(\rho) without further assumptions. Since ρ\rho and ∇ρ\nabla\rho are arbitrary the local Einstein relation D=χ​f′′D=\chi\,f^{\prime\prime} follows from (118).

A peculiar feature of equilibrium states that allowed the explicit derivation of the quasi-potential is that the optimal path for the variational problem (76) is the time reversal of the hydrodynamic trajectory. We emphasize that this can happen also if the identity J​(ρ)=J∗​(ρ)J(\rho)=J^{*}(\rho) is violated but ∇⋅J⁡(ρ)=∇⋅J∗​(ρ)\nabla\cdot J(\rho)=\nabla\cdot J^{*}(\rho) is satisfied. Indeed, we next give an example of a system not invariant under time reversal, i.e., with J⁡(ρ¯)≠0J(\bar{\rho})\neq 0, such that the optimal trajectory for the variational problem (76) is the time reversal of the solution to the relaxation trajectory.

Let Λ=[0,1]\Lambda=[0,1], D⁡(ρ)=χ⁡(ρ)=1D(\rho)=\chi(\rho)=1, λ⁡(0)=λ⁡(1)=λ¯\lambda(0)=\lambda(1)=\bar{\lambda}, and a constant external field E≠0E\neq 0. In this case the hydrodynamic evolution of the density is given by the heat equation independently of the field EE. The stationary profile is ρ¯=λ¯\bar{\rho}=\bar{\lambda}, the associated current is J⁡(ρ¯)=E≠0J(\bar{\rho})=E\neq 0. By a computation analogous to the one leading to (114), we easily get that

V⁡(ρ)=12​∫01d​x​[ρ⁡(x)−ρ¯]2V(\rho)=\frac{1}{2}\int_{0}^{1}\!dx\>\big[\rho(x)-\bar{\rho}\big]^{2}

and the optimal trajectory for the variational problem (76) is the time reversal of the solution to the heat equation. On the other hand J⁡(ρ)=−∇ρ+EJ(\rho)=-\nabla\rho+E while J∗​(ρ)=−∇ρ−EJ^{*}(\rho)=-\nabla\rho-E

We remark that, even if VV is non local, the equality J​(ρ)=J∗​(ρ)J(\rho)=J^{*}(\rho) implies that the thermodynamic force −∇(δ​V/δ​ρ)-\nabla\left(\delta V/\delta\rho\right) is local. Moreover, the first equation in (22) reduces to the statement

J(ρ)=−χ(ρ)∇δ​Vδ​ρ(ρ)J(\rho)=-\chi(\rho)\nabla\frac{\delta V}{\delta\rho}(\rho) (119)

so that VV can be obtained by integrating the above equation. The identity (119) represents the general form, for equilibrium states, of the relationship between currents and thermodynamic forces. It holds both when the free energy is local and non local. When (119) holds, the quasi-potential can be computed by an integration. An example of such a situation with a non local free energy is provided by the ABC model on a ring with equal densities [59].

V.2 Zero range

At the macroscopic level this model is specified by the choice χ⁡(ρ)=φ⁡(ρ)\chi(\rho)=\varphi(\rho) and D​(ρ)=φ′​(ρ)D(\rho)=\varphi^{\prime}(\rho), where φ\varphi is an increasing function on ℝ+{\mathbb{R}}_{+}. In particular, the local Einstein relation (8) holds with f′=φ′/φf^{\prime}=\varphi^{\prime}/\varphi.

This is a very special model in which the quasi-potential is a local functional of the density that can be explicitly computed. It is given similarly to the equilibrium case

V⁡(ρ)=∫Λd​x​{f⁡(ρ)−f⁡(ρ¯)−f′​(ρ¯)​(ρ−ρ¯)},V(\rho)\;=\;\int_{\Lambda}dx\,\big\{f(\rho)-f(\bar{\rho})-f^{\prime}(\bar{\rho})(\rho-\bar{\rho})\big\}, (120)

where ρ¯\bar{\rho} is the unique stationary solution of (10), which in the present case takes the form

{Δφ(ρ)=∇⋅φ(ρ)E,x∈Λ,φ(ρ(x))=eλ⁡(x),x∈∂Λ.\left\{\begin{split}&\Delta\varphi(\rho)=\nabla\cdot\varphi(\rho)E\;,\quad x\in\Lambda\;,\\ &\varphi(\rho(x))=e^{\lambda(x)}\;,\quad x\in\partial\Lambda\;.\end{split}\right.

The proof that the local functional (120) solves the Hamilton-Jacobi equation (27) will be given in Section V.3.

Assume that d=1d=1, that the external field EE is constant, and that Λ=(0,1)\Lambda=(0,1). We denote by λ0\lambda_{0}, λ1\lambda_{1} the values of the chemical potential at the endpoints. In this context one can compute the functional Φ\Phi introduced in (98). As we will show in section VI.1 for this model there are no dynamic phase transitions and Φ=U\Phi=U where UU is the functional introduced in (100). Note that in one-dimension the only vector fields with vanishing divergence are constant. With the change of variable α⁡(x)=φ⁡(ρ⁡(x))\alpha(x)=\varphi(\rho(x)) the variational problem (100) reduces to

infα14​∫01d​x​(J+∇α​(x)−α⁡(x)​E)2α⁡(x),\inf_{\alpha}\frac{1}{4}\int_{0}^{1}dx\,\frac{\left(J+\nabla\alpha(x)-\alpha(x)E\right)^{2}}{\alpha(x)}, (121)

where α⁡(0)=eλ0=φ0\alpha(0)=e^{\lambda_{0}}=\varphi_{0}, α⁡(1)=eλ1=φ1\alpha(1)=e^{\lambda_{1}}=\varphi_{1}. This implies that Φ\Phi does not depend on the function φ⁡(ρ)\varphi(\rho) and in particular coincides with the one for a model of independent particles, i.e.  φ⁡(ρ)=ρ\varphi(\rho)=\rho.

The optimal profile α\alpha of the variational problem (121) is given by

α⁡(x)=C⁡(eE​x−a)​(e−E​x−b)\alpha(x)=C\Big(e^{Ex}-a\Big)\Big(e^{-Ex}-b\Big)

for suitable values of the constants a,b,Ca,b,C to be determined by the boundary conditions and the current JJ. Using the explicit form of the minimizer we have

U⁡(J)\displaystyle U(J) =\displaystyle= J​log⁡(JE​A+J2E2​A2+4​BA2)\displaystyle J\log\left(\frac{\frac{J}{EA}+\sqrt{\frac{J^{2}}{E^{2}A^{2}}+4\frac{B}{A}}}{2}\right)
−\displaystyle- E⁡(A​J2E2​A2+4​BA−A−B),\displaystyle E\left(A\sqrt{\frac{J^{2}}{E^{2}A^{2}}+4\frac{B}{A}}-A-B\right),

where A=eλ01−e−EA=\frac{e^{\lambda_{0}}}{1-e^{-E}} and B=eλ1eE−1B=\frac{e^{\lambda_{1}}}{e^{E}-1}. Its Legendre transform is

Φ♯​(v)=E⁡{A⁡(ev−1)+B⁡(e−v−1)}.\begin{split}\Phi^{\sharp}(v)\;=\;E\Big\{A(e^{v}-1)+B(e^{-v}-1)\Big\}.\end{split} (122)

Notice that this solution converges, as E→0E\to 0, to the solution with no external field that can be easily obtained by the general formulas in section VI.2. For a microscopic counterpart see [75].

V.3 Conditions for locality of the quasi-potential

It is natural to ask under what conditions the quasi-potential V⁡(ρ)V(\rho) is a local functional of the form (120), where ρ¯=ρ¯λ,E\bar{\rho}=\bar{\rho}_{\lambda,E} is the stationary solution associated to the boundary chemical potential λ⁡(x)\lambda(x) and the external driving field E⁡(x)E(x), and ff is the free energy density of the model, related to the diffusion coefficient D⁡(ρ)D(\rho) and the mobility χ⁡(ρ)\chi(\rho) by the Einstein relation (8).

As a first observation, we show that V⁡(ρ)V(\rho) is local if and only if

χ​(ρ)−1​JA​(ρ)\chi(\rho)^{-1}J_{A}(\rho) (123)

is independent of ρ\rho. Indeed, if V⁡(ρ)V(\rho) is as in (120), then JS(ρ)=−χ(ρ)∇δ​Vδ​ρJ_{S}(\rho)=-\chi(\rho)\nabla\frac{\delta V}{\delta\rho} can be computed explicitly, as well as JA​(ρ)=J⁡(ρ)−JS​(ρ)J_{A}(\rho)=J(\rho)-J_{S}(\rho). The result is

JA(ρ)=χ(ρ)[E−χ(ρ¯)−1D(ρ¯)∇ρ¯]J_{A}(\rho)=\chi(\rho)\big[E-\chi(\bar{\rho})^{-1}D(\bar{\rho})\nabla\bar{\rho}\big]

Hence (123) is independent of ρ\rho. Conversely, if (123) is independent of ρ\rho, then the equation χ​(ρ)−1​JA​(ρ)=χ​(ρ¯)−1​JA​(ρ¯)\chi(\rho)^{-1}J_{A}(\rho)=\chi(\bar{\rho})^{-1}J_{A}(\bar{\rho}), can be rewritten, by (6), (23), and (8), as

∇δ​Vδ​ρ​(ρ)=∇[f′​(ρ)−f′​(ρ¯)]\nabla\frac{\delta V}{\delta\rho}(\rho)=\nabla\big[f^{\prime}(\rho)-f^{\prime}(\bar{\rho})\big]

This equation, together with the condition that V⁡(ρ)V(\rho) has a minimum equal to 00 for ρ=ρ¯\rho=\bar{\rho}, gives (120). For example, in equilibrium JA​(ρ)=0J_{A}(\rho)=0 for all ρ\rho, and for the (out of equilibrium) model of particles circulating on a ring driven by a constant field EE, described in Section II.3, we have χ​(ρ)−1​JA​(ρ)=E\chi(\rho)^{-1}J_{A}(\rho)=E, which is independent of ρ\rho.

Next, we assume that the diffusion coefficient and the mobility are scalar matrices, i.e. D​(ρ)i​j=D⁡(ρ)​δi,jD(\rho)_{ij}=D(\rho)\delta_{i,j} and χ​(ρ)i​j=χ⁡(ρ)​δi,j\chi(\rho)_{ij}=\chi(\rho)\delta_{i,j} (i,j=1,…,di,j=1,\dots,d). We derive, in this case, an equivalent condition for the locality of the quasi-potential V⁡(ρ)V(\rho). Assuming that V⁡(ρ)V(\rho) is local as in (120), we can use the fact that (123) is independent of ρ\rho and the orthogonality relation in (26) to get

∫Λd​x​JS​(ρ)⋅χ​(ρ¯)−1​JA​(ρ¯)=0.\int_{\Lambda}dx\,J_{S}(\rho)\cdot\chi(\bar{\rho})^{-1}J_{A}(\bar{\rho})=0. (124)

We have JA​(ρ¯)=J​(ρ¯)J_{A}(\bar{\rho})=J(\bar{\rho}) and

JS(ρ)=−χ(ρ)∇δ​Vδ​ρ=−χ(ρ)(f′′(ρ)∇ρ−f′′(ρ¯)∇ρ¯)=−∇(d(ρ)−d(ρ¯))+(χ(ρ)χ(ρ¯)−1−1)∇d(ρ¯),\begin{array}[]{l}\displaystyle{\vphantom{\Big(}J_{S}(\rho)=-\chi(\rho)\nabla\frac{\delta V}{\delta\rho}=-\chi(\rho)\big(f^{\prime\prime}(\rho)\nabla\rho-f^{\prime\prime}(\bar{\rho})\nabla\bar{\rho}\big)}\\ \displaystyle{\vphantom{\Big(}=-\nabla\big(d(\rho)-d(\bar{\rho})\big)+\big(\chi(\rho)\chi(\bar{\rho})^{-1}-1\big)\nabla d(\bar{\rho})},\end{array} (125)

where d⁡(ρ)=∫ρd​α​D​(α)d(\rho)=\int^{\rho}d\alpha\,D(\alpha). Using (125), equation (124) can be rewritten as

∫Λd​x​1χ​(ρ¯)2​(−(d⁡(ρ)−d⁡(ρ¯))​χ′​(ρ¯)CLOSEOPEN+(χ⁡(ρ)−χ⁡(ρ¯))​D​(ρ¯))​J​(ρ¯)⋅∇ρ¯=0.\begin{array}[]{l}\displaystyle{\vphantom{\Big(}\int_{\Lambda}dx\,\frac{1}{\chi(\bar{\rho})^{2}}\Big(-\big(d(\rho)-d(\bar{\rho})\big)\chi^{\prime}(\bar{\rho})}\\ \displaystyle{\vphantom{\Big(}+\big(\chi(\rho)-\chi(\bar{\rho})\big)D(\bar{\rho})\Big)J(\bar{\rho})\cdot\nabla\bar{\rho}=0}.\end{array} (126)

For this we used an integration by parts and the stationary equation ∇⋅J⁡(ρ¯)=0\nabla\cdot J(\bar{\rho})=0. Equation (126) is the desired condition on the transport coefficients equivalent to the locality of the quasi-potential V⁡(ρ)V(\rho). Indeed, if V⁡(ρ)V(\rho) is local we just proved that (126) holds. Conversely, if (126) holds, then the same computation shows that the local functional V⁡(ρ)V(\rho) as in (120) solves the Hamilton-Jacobi equation (27). In fact, such V⁡(ρ)V(\rho) is the quasi-potential.

For example, in equilibrium J⁡(ρ¯)=0J(\bar{\rho})=0, so (126) holds trivially. In the model of particles circulating on a ring driven by a constant field EE, described in Section II.1, we have ∇ρ¯=0\nabla\bar{\rho}=0, so (126) still holds. Furthermore, equation (126) holds for arbitrary choices of external field EE and boundary chemical potential λ\lambda provided that D⁡(ρ)D(\rho) and χ⁡(ρ)\chi(\rho) are related by the following equation:

−(d⁡(ρ)−d⁡(ρ¯))​χ′​(ρ¯)+(χ⁡(ρ)−χ⁡(ρ¯))​D​(ρ¯)=0-\big(d(\rho)-d(\bar{\rho})\big)\chi^{\prime}(\bar{\rho})+\big(\chi(\rho)-\chi(\bar{\rho})\big)D(\bar{\rho})=0 (127)

for arbitrary ρ\rho and ρ¯\bar{\rho}. This equation is an integral form of the following condition

D⁡(ρ)​χ′′​(ρ)=D′​(ρ)​χ′​(ρ)D(\rho)\chi^{\prime\prime}(\rho)=D^{\prime}(\rho)\chi^{\prime}(\rho) (128)

It is easily seen that there are only two situations in which condition (128) holds: for arbitrary D⁡(ρ)D(\rho) and χ⁡(ρ)\chi(\rho) constant in ρ\rho, which corresponds to the called Ginzburg Landau model, [124, 73], and for D⁡(ρ)=c​χ′​(ρ)D(\rho)=c\chi^{\prime}(\rho), for a constant cc, which corresponds to a “generalized” zero range model (the zero range model is obtained for c=1c=1). We thus conclude, in particular, that in both these cases the quasi-potential V⁡(ρ)V(\rho) is indeed local for arbitrary choices of external field EE and boundary chemical potential λ\lambda.

Another situation in which (126) is satisfied is when J⁡(ρ¯​(x))⋅∇ρ¯​(x)=0J(\bar{\rho}(x))\cdot\nabla\bar{\rho}(x)=0 for any xx. This happens if Λ\Lambda is the dd-dimensional torus and the external field is of the form −∇U+E~-\nabla U+\tilde{E} with ∇⋅E~=0\nabla\cdot\tilde{E}=0 and ∇U​(x)⋅E~​(x)=0\nabla U(x)\cdot\tilde{E}(x)=0 for any x∈Λx\in\Lambda. This can be verified with a simple calculation.

V.4 Simple exclusion processes

We consider here the boundary driven simple exclusion process in one space dimension without external field. In particular we consider Λ=(−1,1)\Lambda=(-1,1) so that ∂Λ=±1\partial\Lambda=\pm 1. The transport coefficients in this case are D⁡(ρ)=1D(\rho)=1 and χ⁡(ρ)=ρ⁡(1−ρ)\chi(\rho)=\rho(1-\rho) and the specific free energy is f⁡(ρ)=ρ​log⁡ρ+(1−ρ)​log⁡(1−ρ)f(\rho)=\rho\log\rho+(1-\rho)\log(1-\rho). We fix the chemical potentials at left and right boundaries as λ±\lambda_{\pm}, correspondingly the macroscopic density will satisfy the boundary conditions ρ⁡(±1)=ρ±\rho(\pm 1)=\rho_{\pm} as required by (9).

By using a matrix representation of the microscopic invariant state and combinatorial techniques, in [48, 50] it is shown that the quasi-potential VV can be expressed in terms of the solution of a non–linear ordinary differential equation. We show how this result can be deduced using the MFT. Namely, we consider the variational problem (76) for the one-dimensional simple exclusion process and show that the associated Hamilton-Jacobi equation

∫Λ(∇δ​Vδ​ρρ(1−ρ)∇δ​Vδ​ρ+δ​Vδ​ρΔρ)dx=0\int_{\Lambda}\left(\nabla\frac{\delta V}{\delta\rho}\rho(1-\rho)\nabla\frac{\delta V}{\delta\rho}+\frac{\delta V}{\delta\rho}\Delta\rho\right)\,dx=0 (129)

can be reduced to the non-linear ordinary differential equation obtained in [48].

We look for a solution of the Hamilton-Jacobi equation (129) by performing the change of variable

δ​Vδ​ρ​(x)=log⁡ρ⁡(x)1−ρ⁡(x)−φ⁡(x,ρ)\frac{\delta V}{\delta\rho(x)}=\log\frac{\rho(x)}{1-\rho(x)}-\varphi(x;\rho) (130)

for some functional φ⁡(x,ρ)\varphi(x;\rho) to be determined satisfying the boundary conditions φ⁡(±1)=log⁡ρ⁡(±1)/[1−ρ⁡(±1)]\varphi(\pm 1)=\log\rho(\pm 1)/[1-\rho(\pm 1)]. Inserting (130) into (129), we get that

0=∫Λdx∇(logρ1−ρ−φ)ρ(1−ρ)∇φ=∫Λdx[∇ρ∇φ−ρ(1−ρ)(∇φ)2].\begin{split}0&=\int_{\Lambda}\!dx\,\nabla\Big(\log\frac{\rho}{1-\rho}-\varphi\Big)\rho(1-\rho)\nabla\varphi\\ &=\int_{\Lambda}\!dx\,\Big[\nabla\rho\nabla\varphi-\rho(1-\rho)(\nabla\varphi)^{2}\Big].\end{split}

Adding and subtracting eφ/(1+eφ)e^{\varphi}/(1+e^{\varphi}), we may rewrite the previous integral as

∫Λdx∇(ρ−eφ1+eφ)∇φ∫Λd​x​(ρ−eφ1+eφ)​(ρ−11+eφ)​(∇φ)2.\begin{split}&\int_{\Lambda}\!dx\,\nabla\Big(\rho-\frac{e^{\varphi}}{1+e^{\varphi}}\Big)\nabla\varphi\\ &\quad\int_{\Lambda}\!dx\,\Big(\rho-\frac{e^{\varphi}}{1+e^{\varphi}}\Big)\Big(\rho-\frac{1}{1+e^{\varphi}}\Big)(\nabla\varphi)^{2}.\end{split}

Since ρ−eφ/(1+eφ)\rho-e^{\varphi}/{(1+e^{\varphi})} vanishes at the boundary, an integration by parts yields

0=∫Λd​x​(ρ−eφ1+eφ)​(Δ​φ+(∇φ)21+eφ−ρ​(∇φ)2).0=\int_{\Lambda}\!dx\,\Big(\rho-\frac{e^{\varphi}}{1+e^{\varphi}}\Big)\Big(\Delta\varphi+\frac{(\nabla\varphi)^{2}}{1+e^{\varphi}}-\rho(\nabla\varphi)^{2}\Big). (131)

We thus obtain a solution of the Hamilton-Jacobi if we solve the following ordinary differential equation which relates the functional φ⁡(x)=φ⁡(x,ρ)\varphi(x)=\varphi(x;\rho) to ρ\rho

{Δ​φ​(x)[∇φ​(x)]2+11+eφ⁡(x)=ρ⁡(x)x∈(−1,1),φ⁡(±1)=log⁡ρ⁡(±1)/[1−ρ⁡(±1)].\left\{\begin{array}[]{l}{\displaystyle\frac{\Delta\varphi(x)}{[\nabla\varphi(x)]^{2}}+\frac{1}{1+e^{\varphi(x)}}=\rho(x)\quad x\in(-1,1)\,,}\\ \\ \varphi(\pm 1)=\log\rho(\pm 1)/[1-\rho(\pm 1)]\,.\end{array}\right. (132)

As proven in [50] this equation admits a unique monotone solution which is the relevant one for the quasi-potential. Recalling (38), a computation shows that the derivative of the functional

V⁡(ρ)=F⁡(ρ)+∫Λd​x​{(1−ρ)​φ+log⁡[∇φ∇ρ¯​(1+eφ)]}V(\rho)=F(\rho)+\int_{\Lambda}\!dx\,\left\{(1-\rho)\varphi+\log\left[\frac{\nabla\varphi}{\nabla\bar{\rho}\left(1+e^{\varphi}\right)}\right]\right\} (133)

is given by (130) when φ⁡(x,ρ)\varphi(x;\rho) solves (132). To prove that this is the maximal positive solution we refer to [12].

According to the general time reversal argument, see in particular equation (22), the adjoint hydrodynamics can be written as

∂tρ=Δρ−2∇⋅(χ(ρ)∇φ)\partial_{t}\rho=\Delta\rho-2\nabla\cdot\big(\chi(\rho)\nabla\varphi\big) (134)

where we used (130) and φ\varphi has to be expressed in function of ρ\rho by solving (132). As shown in [12], it is remarkable that this non local evolution can be directly related to the heat equation. Let γ=γ⁡(t,x)\gamma=\gamma(t,x) be defined by

γ=eφ1+eφ\gamma=\frac{e^{\varphi}}{1+e^{\varphi}} (135)

where φ=φ⁡(t,x)\varphi=\varphi(t,x) is the solution to (132) when ρ=ρ⁡(t,x)\rho=\rho(t,x) evolves according to (134). Then γ\gamma solves

∂tγ=Δ​γ\partial_{t}\gamma=\Delta\gamma (136)

with the appropriate initial and boundary conditions.

One may be tempted to repeat the same computation in arbitrary dimension; one would obtain a partial differential equation analogous to (132). However, in more than one dimension it does not exist, in general, a functional VV whose derivative is given by (130) with φ\varphi and ρ\rho related by such partial differential equation.

For this model, as proved in [48] for the one-dimensional case and in [12] for higher dimensions, the quasi-potential V⁡(ρ)V(\rho) is larger than the local functional (29) with ρ¯\bar{\rho} the non equilibrium stationary profile. For small fluctuations this follows from formula (93).

An interesting result [125, 126] is that this model and the following Kipnis-Marchioro-Presutti model can be mapped into equilibrium models. This result depends on the Hamiltonian structure and the non local map (132). We briefly outline the argument. Recall the Hamiltonian (79) that for the simple exclusion process reads

ℋ⁡(ρ,π)=∫−11d​x​{ρ⁡(1−ρ)​(∇π)2+π​Δ​ρ}\mathcal{H}(\rho,\pi)=\int_{-1}^{1}dx\,\left\{\rho(1-\rho)\left(\nabla\pi\right)^{2}+\pi\Delta\rho\right\} (137)

with the boundary conditions ρ⁡(±1)=ρ±\rho(\pm 1)=\rho_{\pm} and π⁡(±1)=0\pi(\pm 1)=0. Consider the symplectic transformation (ρ,π)→(φ,ψ)(\rho,\pi)\to(\varphi,\psi) given by

{∇(11−eψ)=eπ−1−ρ⁡(eπ+e−π−2)∇(ρρ+(1−ρ)​eπ)=eψ−1−φ⁡(eψ+e−ψ−2).\left\{\begin{array}[]{l}\nabla\left(\frac{1}{1-e^{\psi}}\right)=e^{\pi}-1-\rho(e^{\pi}+e^{-\pi}-2)\\ \nabla\left(\frac{\rho}{\rho+(1-\rho)e^{\pi}}\right)=e^{\psi}-1-\varphi(e^{\psi}+e^{-\psi}-2)\,.\end{array}\right. (138)

The new Hamiltonian has the same form of (137), that is

ℋ~​(φ,ψ)=∫−11d​x​{φ⁡(1−φ)​(∇ψ)2+ψ​Δ​φ},\tilde{\mathcal{H}}(\varphi,\psi)=\int_{-1}^{1}dx\,\left\{\varphi(1-\varphi)\left(\nabla\psi\right)^{2}+\psi\Delta\varphi\right\}, (139)

but the boundary conditions are ∇φ​(±1)=∇ψ​(±1)=0\nabla\varphi(\pm 1)=\nabla\psi(\pm 1)=0 [125]. Since these boundary conditions corresponds to an isolated exclusion process, (138) realizes a map into an equilibrium system. In particular ℋ~\tilde{\mathcal{H}} satisfies (83) with ℋ~∗=ℋ~\tilde{\mathcal{H}}^{*}=\tilde{\mathcal{H}} and the optimal exit trajectory is simply given by the time reversal of the relaxation one. By mapping back this solution and computing the corresponding action the expression (133) for the quasi–potential is recovered.

From a physical point of view, besides the case of external reservoirs, boundary conditions modeling a battery appear natural. Namely, we can consider the system in a ring with an external field and take the limit in which the field becomes a delta function localized at one point. The application of the MFT to this case is discussed in [28].

V.5 Kipnis-Marchioro-Presutti model

We consider the one dimensional boundary driven Kipnis-Marchioro-Presutti (KMP) model [88]. This is a diffusive system with transport coefficients given by D⁡(ρ)=1D(\rho)=1 and χ⁡(ρ)=ρ2\chi(\rho)=\rho^{2}. It derives from a simple stochastic model of heat conduction in a crystal. Like in the exclusion process the computation of the quasi-potential can be reduced to the solution of a non linear differential equation [23].

The procedure is similar to the one for the simple exclusion process. The Hamilton-Jacobi equation for the quasi-potential VV is

∫Λdx(∇δ​Vδ​ρρ2∇δ​Vδ​ρ+δ​Vδ​ρΔρ)=0.\int_{\Lambda}\!dx\,\left(\nabla\frac{\delta V}{\delta\rho}\rho^{2}\nabla\frac{\delta V}{\delta\rho}+\frac{\delta V}{\delta\rho}\Delta\rho\right)=0. (140)

We assume that Λ=(−1,1)\Lambda=(-1,1). We shall also assume the macroscopic density profile ρ=ρ⁡(x)\rho=\rho(x) satisfies the boundary conditions ρ⁡(±1)=ρ±\rho(\pm 1)=\rho_{\pm}. We emphasize that ρ\rho now represents an energy density.

We look for a solution of the Hamilton-Jacobi equation (140) by performing the change of variable

δ​Vδ​ρ​(x)=1α⁡(x,ρ)−1ρ⁡(x)\frac{\delta V}{\delta\rho(x)}=\frac{1}{\alpha(x;\rho)}-\frac{1}{\rho(x)} (141)

for some functional α⁡(x,ρ)\alpha(x;\rho) to be determined satisfying the boundary conditions α⁡(±1)=ρ⁡(±1)\alpha(\pm 1)=\rho(\pm 1).

With a calculation similar to the one in the previous section we find that the quasi–potential is

V⁡(ρ)=∫Λd​x​(ρα−1−log⁡ρα−log⁡∇α∇ρ¯),V(\rho)=\int_{\Lambda}\!dx\,\Big(\frac{\rho}{\alpha}-1-\log\frac{\rho}{\alpha}-\log\frac{\nabla\alpha}{\nabla\bar{\rho}}\Big), (142)

where α=α⁡(x,ρ)\alpha=\alpha(x;\rho) is the unique monotone solution to

{α2​Δ​α(∇α)2+ρ−α=0α⁡(±1)=ρ±.\left\{\begin{array}[]{l}\alpha^{2}\frac{\Delta\alpha}{\left(\nabla\alpha\right)^{2}}+\rho-\alpha=0\\ \alpha(\pm 1)=\rho_{\pm}.\end{array}\right. (143)

By a direct computation it can be shown that V⁡(ρ)V(\rho) is not convex. For this model, as proved in [23], the quasi-potential V⁡(ρ)V(\rho) is smaller than the local functional (29) with ρ¯\bar{\rho} the stationary profile. For small fluctuations this follows from formula (93).

V.6 Exclusion process with external field

The computation of the quasi-potential for the one-dimensional boundary driven simple exclusion process reviewed in section V.4 can be generalized to the case in which a constant external field is applied to the system. The first result has been obtained, using the matrix approach, in [57] and refers to the case in which the driving due to the external reservoirs and the field are in the same direction. In the same situation an approach based on the macroscopic fluctuation theory is presented in [22]. The case when the field drives in the opposite direction with respect to the boundary sources exhibits Lagrangian phase transitions and will be discussed in the following section.

The weakly asymmetric boundary driven simple exclusion process is defined, in appropriate units, by the following choices. The transport coefficient are D=1D=1 and χ⁡(ρ)=ρ⁡(1−ρ)\chi(\rho)=\rho(1-\rho) so that the specific free energy is f⁡(ρ)=ρ​log⁡ρ+(1−ρ)​log⁡(1−ρ)f(\rho)=\rho\log\rho+(1-\rho)\log(1-\rho). Observe that the hydrodynamic equation is the viscous Burgers equation. We consider it on the space domain Λ=(−1,1)\Lambda=(-1,1) with a constant external field EE and denote by λ±\lambda_{\pm} the chemical potentials of the boundary reservoirs. We let ρ±=eλ±/(1+eλ±)\rho_{\pm}=e^{\lambda_{\pm}}/(1+e^{\lambda_{\pm}}) be the boundary values of the density.

The Hamilton-Jacobi equation for the quasi-potential (27) thus reads

∫Λ(∇δ​Vδ​ρρ(1−ρ)∇δ​Vδ​ρ+δ​Vδ​ρ{Δρ−E∇[ρ(1−ρ)]})dx=0.\begin{split}&\int_{\Lambda}\Big(\nabla\frac{\delta V}{\delta\rho}\rho(1-\rho)\nabla\frac{\delta V}{\delta\rho}\\ &\qquad+\frac{\delta V}{\delta\rho}\big\{\Delta\rho-E\nabla[\rho(1-\rho)]\big\}\Big)\,dx=0.\end{split} (144)

As in the symmetric case we look for a solution VV whose derivative has the form

δ​Vδ​ρ​(x)=f′​(ρ⁡(x))−φ⁡(x,ρ)\frac{\delta V}{\delta\rho(x)}=f^{\prime}(\rho(x))-\varphi(x;\rho) (145)

where, for density profiles ρ\rho satisfying the boundary conditions ρ⁡(±1)=ρ±\rho(\pm 1)=\rho_{\pm}, we have φ⁡(±1,ρ)=λ±\varphi(\pm 1,\rho)=\lambda_{\pm}. Few integrations by parts similar to (131) show that (144) is satisfied provided φ\varphi solves

{Δ​φ​(x)∇φ​(x)​[∇φ​(x)−E]+11+eφ⁡(x)=ρ⁡(x)x∈(−1,1)φ⁡(±1)=λ±.\left\{\begin{array}[]{l}{\displaystyle\frac{\Delta\varphi(x)}{\nabla\varphi(x)[\nabla\varphi(x)-E]}+\frac{1}{1+e^{\varphi(x)}}=\rho(x)\quad x\in(-1,1)}\\ \\ \varphi(\pm 1)=\lambda_{\pm}\,.\end{array}\right. (146)

In order to identify the quasi-potential we need show that φ\varphi is properly defined, namely that (146) has a unique solution, and that there exists a functional VV with derivative given by (145).

Fix ρ−<ρ+\rho_{-}<\rho_{+} and observe that when E=E0≡[λ+−λ−]/2E=E_{0}\equiv[\lambda_{+}-\lambda_{-}]/2 the model describes an inhomogeneous equilibrium state as in Section V.1. We here consider the case in which E<E0E<E_{0} that corresponds to a negative stationary current. Recalling F⁡(ρ)=∫Λd​x​f​(ρ)F(\rho)=\int_{\Lambda}dx\,f(\rho), we introduce the auxiliary functional of two variables

𝒢(ρ,φ)=F(ρ)+∫Λdx{(1−ρ)φ−log(1+eφ)+1E[∇φlog∇φ−(∇φ−E)log(∇φ−E)]},\begin{split}&{\mathcal{G}}(\rho,\varphi)=F(\rho)+\int_{\Lambda}\!dx\,\Big\{(1-\rho)\varphi-\log\big(1+e^{\varphi}\big)\\ &\;\;+\frac{1}{E}\Big[\nabla\varphi\log\nabla\varphi-(\nabla\varphi-E)\log(\nabla\varphi-E)\Big]\Big\},\end{split} (147)

which has the property that (146) is the stationarity condition δ​𝒢/δ​φ=0\delta{\mathcal{G}}/\delta\varphi=0 while δ​𝒢/δ​ρ=f′​(ρ)−φ\delta{\mathcal{G}}/\delta\rho=f^{\prime}(\rho)-\varphi is the right hand side of (145).

The functional 𝒢{\mathcal{G}} is well defined provided φ\varphi is increasing and ∇φ≥E\nabla\varphi\geq E. In [22] is shown that (146) has a unique solution φ\varphi satisfying these requirements. The quasi-potential, up to an additive constant that is fixed by the normalization V⁡(ρ¯)=0V(\bar{\rho})=0, can thus be expressed in terms of the auxiliary functional 𝒢{\mathcal{G}} as

V⁡(ρ)=supφ𝒢⁡(ρ,φ)=𝒢⁡(ρ,φ⁡(ρ))V(\rho)=\sup_{\varphi}{\mathcal{G}}(\rho,\varphi)={\mathcal{G}}\big(\rho,\varphi(\rho)\big)

where φ⁡(ρ)\varphi(\rho) is the solution to (146). Indeed, if φ⁡(ρ)\varphi(\rho) solves (146) then by chain rule

δ​Vδ​ρ​(ρ)=δ​𝒢δ​ρ​(ρ,φ⁡(ρ))+δ​𝒢δ​φ​(ρ,φ⁡(ρ))​δ​φδ​ρ​(ρ)=f′​(ρ)−φ⁡(ρ)\begin{split}\frac{\delta V}{\delta\rho}(\rho)&=\frac{\delta{\mathcal{G}}}{\delta\rho}(\rho,\varphi(\rho))+\frac{\delta{\mathcal{G}}}{\delta\varphi}(\rho,\varphi(\rho))\,\frac{\delta\varphi}{\delta\rho}(\rho)\\ &=f^{\prime}(\rho)-\varphi(\rho)\end{split}

The fact that φ\varphi solving (146) corresponds to a maximum of 𝒢{\mathcal{G}} follows from the concavity with respect to φ\varphi of 𝒢{\mathcal{G}}.

We mention that the computation reducing the (infinite dimensional) Hamilton-Jacobi equation (144) to the (one dimensional) problem (146) can be extended to the models with constant diffusion coefficient, quadratic mobility, and constant external field [23, 47].

V.7 An example of Lagrangian phase transition

As in the previous Section, we consider the one-dimensional boundary driven weakly asymmetric exclusion process on the interval (−1,1)(-1,1) with λ−<λ+\lambda_{-}<\lambda_{+}. We consider here the case in which the driving from the field is in the opposite direction with respect to the one from the boundary reservoirs and the the stationary current J⁡(ρ¯)J(\bar{\rho}) is positive, that is E>E0=[λ+−λ−]/2E>E_{0}=[\lambda_{+}-\lambda_{-}]/2. We shall show that for E≫E0E\gg E_{0} this model provides an example of a Lagrangian phase transition, see Section IV.4. This appears to be the first concrete example where this can be rigorously proven [19].

As a first step, we discuss the change of variable (145) in the framework of the underlying Hamiltonian structure. Recalling that the Hamiltonian is given in (79), we perform the symplectic change of variables

{φ=f′​(ρ)−πψ=ρ\begin{cases}\varphi=f^{\prime}(\rho)-\pi\\ \psi=\rho\end{cases} (148)

where we recall that f⁡(ρ)=ρ​log⁡ρ+(1−ρ)​log⁡(1−ρ)f(\rho)=\rho\log\rho+(1-\rho)\log(1-\rho) is the specific free energy.

In the new variables (φ,ψ)(\varphi,\psi) the Hamiltonian ℋ~​(φ,ψ)=ℋ⁡(ψ,f′​(ψ)−φ){\widetilde{{\mathcal{H}}}}(\varphi,\psi)={\mathcal{H}}(\psi,f^{\prime}(\psi)-\varphi) reads

ℋ~​(φ,ψ)=∫−11dx{ψ(1−ψ)(∇φ)2−[∇ψ+Eψ(1−ψ)]∇φ+E(ρ+−ρ−)}\begin{split}{\widetilde{{\mathcal{H}}}}(\varphi,\psi)=&\int_{-1}^{1}\!dx\,\big\{\psi(1-\psi)\,(\nabla\varphi)^{2}\\ &-[\nabla\psi+E\,\psi(1-\psi)]\,\nabla\varphi+E\,(\rho_{+}-\rho_{-})\big\}\end{split}

where we used that ρ⁡(±1)=ρ±\rho(\pm 1)=\rho_{\pm}. The corresponding canonical equations are

{∂tφ=Δφ−(1−2ψ)∇φ(E−∇φ)∂tψ=−Δψ−E∇[ψ(1−ψ)]+2∇[ψ(1−ψ)∇φ]\left\{\begin{array}[]{l}\partial_{t}\varphi=\Delta\varphi-(1-2\psi)\,\nabla\varphi\,(E-\nabla\varphi)\\ \partial_{t}\psi=-\Delta\psi-E\,\nabla[\psi(1-\psi)]+2\,\nabla\big[\psi(1-\psi)\,\nabla\varphi\big]\end{array}\right. (149)

with the boundary conditions inherited from (148).

In the new variables the equilibrium position (ρ¯,0)(\bar{\rho},0) becomes (f′​(ρ¯),ρ¯)(f^{\prime}(\bar{\rho}),\bar{\rho}). The associated stable manifold is ℳs={(φ,ψ):φ=f′​(ψ)}{\mathcal{M}}_{\mathrm{s}}=\{(\varphi,\psi):\,\varphi=f^{\prime}(\psi)\}. As shown in [18] the unstable manifold is given by

ℳu={(φ,ψ): 0<∇φ<E,ψ=11+eφ−Δ​φ∇φ​(E−∇φ)}.\begin{split}{\mathcal{M}}_{\mathrm{u}}=\Big\{&(\varphi,\psi)\,:\>0<\nabla\varphi<E,\\ &\psi=\frac{1}{1+e^{\varphi}}-\frac{\Delta\varphi}{\nabla\varphi(E-\nabla\varphi)}\Big\}.\end{split} (150)

Note that in the variables (φ,ψ)(\varphi,\psi) the unstable manifold ℳu{\mathcal{M}}_{\mathrm{u}} can be described as the graph of a single-valued function while this is not the case in the original variables (ρ,π)(\rho,\pi), recall Fig. 1 (a) of Section IV.4.

In view of the expression (150) of the unstable manifold, the pre–potential 𝒱{\mathcal{V}} in (85) can be obtained by direct computations using the new variables (φ,ψ)(\varphi,\psi). Let 𝒢{\mathcal{G}} be the functional (compare with (147))

𝒢(ρ,φ)=∫−11dx{f(ρ)+(1−ρ)φ−log(1+eφ)+1E[∇φlog∇φ+(E−∇φ)log(E−∇φ)]}\begin{split}&{\mathcal{G}}(\rho,\varphi)=\int_{-1}^{1}\!dx\,\Big\{f(\rho)+(1-\rho)\varphi-\log\big(1+e^{\varphi}\big)\\ &\;+\frac{1}{E}\Big[\nabla\varphi\log{\nabla\varphi}+(E-\nabla\varphi)\log\big(E-{\nabla\varphi}\big)\Big]\Big\}\end{split} (151)

up to an additive constant fixed by the normalization 𝒢⁡(ρ¯,f′​(ρ¯))=0{\mathcal{G}}(\bar{\rho},f^{\prime}(\bar{\rho}))=0. Then the pre-potential (in the original variables) is

𝒱⁡(ρ,π)=𝒢⁡(ρ,f′​(ρ)−π).{\mathcal{V}}(\rho,\pi)={\mathcal{G}}(\rho,f^{\prime}(\rho)-\pi). (152)

We deduce that the quasi-potential is given, up to an additive constant, by

V(ρ)=inf{𝒢(ρ,φ),φ:(φ,ρ)∈ℳu}.{V}(\rho)=\inf\big\{{\mathcal{G}}(\rho,\varphi)\,,\>\varphi\,:\>(\varphi,\rho)\in{\mathcal{M}}_{\mathrm{u}}\big\}. (153)

According to the general arguments in Section IV.4 the pre-potential is defined on the unstable manifold ℳu{\mathcal{M}}_{\mathrm{u}}. On the other hand, the right hand side of (151) extends to a function defined for all φ\varphi satisfying 0<∇φ<E0<\nabla\varphi<E. By denoting still with 𝒢{\mathcal{G}} this extension we realize that the condition (φ,ρ)∈ℳu(\varphi,\rho)\in{\mathcal{M}}_{\mathrm{u}} is equivalent to δ​𝒢​(ρ,φ)/δ​φ=0\delta{\mathcal{G}}(\rho,\varphi)/\delta\varphi=0. We conclude that (153) still holds if the constraint between ρ\rho and φ\varphi is dropped.

When the external field EE is large enough, the weakly asymmetric exclusion process exhibits Lagrangian phase transitions. Namely the variational problem in (153) admits more than a single critical point or equivalently the equation on the second line of (150) has multiple solutions. We argue as follows. Consider first the limiting case E=∞E=\infty in which the hydrodynamic equation becomes the inviscid Burgers equation and corresponds to the asymmetric simple exclusion process examined in [51]. The functional 𝒢{\mathcal{G}} becomes

𝒢∞​(ρ,φ)=∫−11d​x​[f⁡(ρ)+(1−ρ)​φ−log⁡(1+eφ)].{\mathcal{G}}_{\infty}(\rho,\varphi)=\int_{-1}^{1}\!dx\,\Big[f(\rho)+(1-\rho)\varphi-\log\big(1+e^{\varphi}\big)\Big]. (154)

In this limit the variational problem (153) becomes a one-dimensional problem and it is possible to exhibit explicitly density profiles such that uniqueness fails. For instance this is the case if ρ\rho is of the form drawn in Fig. 2. By a continuity (topological) argument one shows that this phase transition persists also for EE finite and large.

Comparing the formula (147) of the previous section with (151) we obtain easily, by inserting the absolute value inside the argument of the logarithm, an expression for 𝒢{\mathcal{G}} that covers both cases. On the other hand, if E<E0E<E_{0} the function φ↦𝒢⁡(ρ,φ)\varphi\mapsto{\mathcal{G}}(\rho,\varphi) has a unique critical point which corresponds to a maximum, while for E>E0E>E_{0} it may have more critical points and the quasi-potential is obtained in correspondence to the global minimum.

The analysis of the weakly asymmetric exclusion process has been further developed, by considering density profiles ρ\rho with more critical points, in [2], see also references therein.

V.8 Reaction-diffusion dynamics

In this Section we discuss the case in which the macroscopic dynamic is not a conservation law but there is a reaction term allowing creation/destruction of particles in the bulk. This class of models, with added random forces, has been investigated in the literature, e.g. [127] for a recent reference. Here we just show, in a specific example, how the basic principles of the MFT need to be modified to cover these processes.

The macroscopic evolution has the form

∂tρ=Δ​ρ+b⁡(ρ)−d⁡(ρ)=Δ​ρ+K⁡(ρ),\partial_{t}\rho=\Delta\rho+b(\rho)-d(\rho)=\Delta\rho+K(\rho), (155)

where bb and dd are respectively the creation and destruction rates. For simplicity we restrict to the case Λ=(−1,1)d\Lambda=(-1,1)^{d} with periodic boundary conditions.

This evolution can be derived as the typical behavior of some underlying stochastic microscopic dynamics in which particles can jump on the lattice and be created or destroyed. For instance, as shown in [42], it can be derived from the so-called Glauber+Kawasaki process that we describe in Section VIII.3.

The associated large deviation functional for the density trajectories was first calculated in [84]

I[0,T](ρ)=∫0Tdt∫Λdx{14∇H⋅ρ(1−ρ)∇H\displaystyle I_{[0,T]}(\rho)=\int_{0}^{T}\!dt\int_{\Lambda}\!dx\,\Big\{\frac{1}{4}\nabla H\cdot\rho(1-\rho)\nabla H\quad\quad\quad
+b(ρ)(1−eH+HeH)+d(ρ)(1−e−H−He−H)},\displaystyle+b(\rho)\big(1-e^{H}+He^{H}\big)+d(\rho)\big(1-e^{-H}-He^{-H}\big)\Big\},

where the external potential HH is connected to the fluctuation ρ\rho by

∂tρ=Δρ−∇⋅(ρ(1−ρ)∇H)+b(ρ)eH−d(ρ)e−H.\partial_{t}\rho=\Delta\rho-\nabla\cdot\big(\rho(1-\rho)\nabla H\big)+b(\rho)e^{H}-d(\rho)e^{-H}. (157)

The structure of the functional II reflects the Poissonian nature of the underlying microscopic dynamics. The Hamiltonian associated to the large deviation functional (V.8)–(157) for this model is

ℋ(ρ,π)=∫Λdx{πΔρ+(∇π)2ρ(1−ρ)\displaystyle{\cal H}(\rho,\pi)=\int_{\Lambda}\!dx\,\bigg\{\pi\Delta\rho+(\nabla\pi)^{2}\rho(1-\rho)
−b(ρ)(1−eπ)−d(ρ)(1−e−π)},\displaystyle-b(\rho)\big(1-e^{\pi}\big)-d\big(\rho)(1-e^{-\pi}\big)\bigg\}, (158)

where π\pi is the conjugate momentum. Observe that while II has an implicit expression, since HH has to be expressed in terms of ρ\rho by solving (157), the Hamiltonian ℋ{\mathcal{H}} has a closed form.

As ℋ{\mathcal{H}} is not quadratic, the Hamilton-Jacobi equation

ℋ⁡(ρ,δ​Vδ​ρ)=0{\cal H}\left(\rho,\frac{\delta V}{\delta\rho}\right)=0 (159)

is very complicated but can be solved in some special cases. This happens when b⁡(ρ)=c1​(1−ρ)​h​(ρ)b(\rho)=c_{1}(1-\rho)h(\rho) and d⁡(ρ)=c2​ρ​h​(ρ)d(\rho)=c_{2}\rho h(\rho) where cic_{i} are positive constants and h⁡(ρ)h(\rho) is a positive function. In this case [65]

V⁡(ρ)=∫Λd​x​{ρ​log⁡ρc¯+(1−ρ)​log⁡(1−ρ)(1−c¯)},V(\rho)=\int_{\Lambda}\!dx\,\Big\{\rho\log\frac{\rho}{\bar{c}}+(1-\rho)\log\frac{(1-\rho)}{(1-\bar{c})}\Big\}, (160)

where c¯=c1/(c1+c2)\bar{c}=c_{1}/(c_{1}+c_{2}). This corresponds to the situation that we call macroscopic reversibility of which the validity of microscopic detailed balance (see (212)) is a special case.

In the general case equation (159) can be solved by successive approximations using as an expansion parameter ρ−ρ¯\rho-\bar{\rho} where ρ¯\bar{\rho} is a solution of B⁡(ρ)=D⁡(ρ)B(\rho)=D(\rho) that is a stationary solution of hydrodynamics. More precisely we look for an approximate solution of (159) of the form

V⁡(ρ)=12​∫Λ×Λd​x​𝑑y​[ρ⁡(x)−ρ¯]​k​(x,y)​[ρ⁡(y)−ρ¯]+o​(ρ−ρ¯)2.V(\rho)=\frac{1}{2}\int_{\Lambda\times\Lambda}\!dx\,dy\,[\rho(x)-\bar{\rho}]k(x,y)[\rho(y)-\bar{\rho}]+o(\rho-\bar{\rho})^{2}. (161)

By inserting (161) in (159) one can show that k⁡(x,y)k(x,y) satisfies the following equation

ρ¯​(1−ρ¯)​Δx​k​(x,y)−b0​k​(x,y)−Δx​δ​(x−y)+(d1−b1)​δ​(x−y)=0,\begin{split}&\bar{\rho}(1-\bar{\rho})\Delta_{x}k(x,y)-b_{0}k(x,y)\\ &-\Delta_{x}\delta(x-y)+(d_{1}-b_{1})\delta(x-y)=0,\end{split} (162)

where

b1=b′​(ρ¯),d1=d′​(ρ¯),b0=b⁡(ρ¯)=d⁡(ρ¯).b_{1}=b^{\prime}(\bar{\rho}),\quad d_{1}=d^{\prime}(\bar{\rho}),\qquad b_{0}=b(\bar{\rho})=d(\bar{\rho}).

If VV is a local functional of the density, k⁡(x,y)k(x,y) must be of the form k⁡(x,y)=g⁡(ρ¯)​δ​(x−y)k(x,y)=g(\bar{\rho})\delta(x-y) which inserted in (162) gives

g⁡(ρ¯)=[ρ¯​(1−ρ¯)]−1g(\bar{\rho})=[\bar{\rho}(1-\bar{\rho})]^{-1} (163)

and

b0​[ρ¯​(1−ρ¯)]−1−(d1−b1)=0.b_{0}[\bar{\rho}(1-\bar{\rho})]^{-1}-(d_{1}-b_{1})=0. (164)

Condition (164) is satisfied in the cases when (160) is the quasi-potential. On the other hand if b0,b1,d1b_{0},b_{1},d_{1} do not satisfy the last equation the quasi-potential cannot be a local functional of the density.

For this model it is possible to prove [30] an analogue of the fundamental formula (11),(12). The hydrodynamic equation has a local source term KK and we are interested in the joint fluctuations of ρ\rho, J⁡(ρ)=−∇ρJ(\rho)=-\nabla\rho, K⁡(ρ)=b⁡(ρ)−d⁡(ρ)K(\rho)=b(\rho)-d(\rho). The large deviation functional is

ℐ[0,T]​(ρ,j,k)=∫0Td​t​∫Λd​x​{14​|j−J⁡(ρ)|2ρ⁡(1−ρ)+Ψ⁡(ρ,k)},{\mathcal{I}}_{[0,T]}(\rho,j,k)=\int_{0}^{T}\!dt\int_{\Lambda}\!dx\,\Big\{{\frac{1}{4}}\frac{\big|j-J(\rho)\big|^{2}}{\rho(1-\rho)}+\Psi(\rho,k)\Big\}, (165)

with

Ψ⁡(ρ,k)\displaystyle\Psi(\rho,k) =\displaystyle= b⁡(ρ)+d⁡(ρ)−k2+4​d​(ρ)​b​(ρ)\displaystyle b(\rho)+d(\rho)-\sqrt{k^{2}+4d(\rho)b(\rho)} (166)
+\displaystyle+ k​log⁡(k2+4​d​(ρ)​b​(ρ)+k2​b​(ρ)).\displaystyle k\log\left(\frac{\sqrt{k^{2}+4d(\rho)b(\rho)}+k}{2b(\rho)}\right).

Here ρ\rho, jj and kk are connected by the equation

∂tρ=−∇j+k.\partial_{t}\rho=-\nabla j+k. (167)

The rate function (V.8) can be recovered from (165) by optimizing with respect to jj and kk.

For driven diffusive systems, we have shown that long range correlations of the density are a generic feature of non-equilibrium states. If b⁡(ρ¯)=d⁡(ρ¯)b(\bar{\rho})=d(\bar{\rho}) the reaction diffusion dynamics does not exhibit a macroscopic current and, in this respect, may be regarded as an equilibrium state. On the other hand, the previous discussion implies that long range correlations do appear if (164) is violated.
