From the point of view of the MFT, violation of (164) corresponds to a breaking of macroscopic reversibility. We refer to [7, 16] for more details.

V.9 Mean field models

The macroscopic fluctuation theory can be applied to diffusion processes coupled via a mean field interaction, [32]. A prototype of such systems is the Kuramoto model with noise. This is a system of NN coupled planar rotators described by the phases θi\theta_{i} in a rotating magnetic field with amplitude HH and frequency FF. In the frame comoving with the rotators, the evolution is given by the Langevin equations

θ˙i=F−Hsinθi−JN∑j=1Nsin(θi−θj)+2​κ​Tαi\dot{\theta}_{i}=F-H\sin\theta_{i}-\frac{J}{N}\sum_{j=1}^{N}\sin(\theta_{i}-\theta_{j})+\sqrt{2\kappa T}\alpha_{i}

where JJ is the coupling constant, κ\kappa the Boltzmann constant TT the temperature, and αi\alpha_{i} independent white noises.

If the frequency FF vanishes this is an equilibrium model and the stationary ensemble has a Gibbsian description with a mean field interaction that undergoes a phase transition. On the other hand for F≠0F\neq 0 it is a non-equilibrium model. With the proper definition of the current J⁡(ρ)J(\rho), the fundamental formula of the macroscopic fluctuation theory holds and thus allows an analysis of the asymptotic properties of this model. In particular, the quasi-potential can be computed perturbatively. Moreover, the current fluctuations exhibit rich and interesting phenomena of the type of the dynamical phase transition that will be discussed in Section VI.1.

V.10 Models with several conservation laws

So far we have considered for simplicity conservative models with only one conservation law. The theory however is not limited by this restriction and models with more than one thermodynamic variable have been considered.

We mention in particular the work [8]. It deals with a stochastic heat conduction model for solids. The system is in contact with two heat baths at different temperatures. There are two conserved quantities: the energy and the deformation between atoms. The author establishes the hydrodynamic limit for the two conserved quantities and calculates a large deviation functional analogous to (74) for the joint fluctuations of the energy and the deformation. From this formula he obtains the quasi-potential for temperature fluctuations which is the same as for the KMP model (142).

Another interesting case is the ABC model [59, 38]. In this case there are three conserved quantities but only two are independent. The hydrodynamic equations are not of the standard form (6) but the quasi-potential can be calculated exactly when the total densities of the the three species are equal. It is non local but this is not in contradiction with our previous statements due to the non standard form of the hydrodynamics. It satisfies the Hamilton-Jacobi equation which in this case is equivalent to (119) due to reversibility. If the total densities are not equal the MFT has been used in [29] to compute perturbatively the quasi-potential.

VI Thermodynamics of currents

The study of current fluctuations is one of the most interesting topic that can be developed within the MFT and has received a considerable attention in the literature. In this section we first discuss a striking prediction of the theory on the possibility of dynamical phase transitions in current fluctuations leading to a state of the system spontaneously breaking time translation invariance [14, 15]. We then show that universal properties of the cumulants of the time averaged current can be obtained both in stationary and non stationary states.

VI.1 Examples of dynamical phase transition

Recalling the discussion in Section IV.6, we first show that, under some structural conditions on the transport coefficients, the identity Φ=U\Phi=U holds. In this case the additivity principle in [24] is satisfied and there are no dynamical phase transitions. The computation of Φ\Phi is simpler as we have to solve a time independent variational problem.

We assume that the matrices D⁡(ρ)D(\rho) and χ⁡(ρ)\chi(\rho) are multiples of the identity. In the case with no external field, E=0E=0, if

D⁡(ρ)​χ′′​(ρ)≤D′​(ρ)​χ′​(ρ) for any ​ρD(\rho)\chi^{\prime\prime}(\rho)\leq D^{\prime}(\rho)\chi^{\prime}(\rho)\quad\textrm{ for any }\rho (168)

then Φ=U\Phi=U, which implies also that UU is convex. Moreover if

D⁡(ρ)​χ′′​(ρ)=D′​(ρ)​χ′​(ρ) for any ​ρD(\rho)\chi^{\prime\prime}(\rho)=D^{\prime}(\rho)\chi^{\prime}(\rho)\quad\textrm{ for any }\rho (169)

then Φ=U\Phi=U for any external field EE.

For the proof of these statements we refer to [15] where we also discuss the case with periodic boundary conditions which requires the further restriction that DD is constant. Condition (168) is satisfied e.g., for the symmetric simple exclusion process, where D=1D=1 and χ⁡(ρ)=ρ⁡(1−ρ)\chi(\rho)=\rho(1-\rho), ρ∈[0,1]\rho\in[0,1]. We recall that, as shown in Section V.3, condition (169) implies the locality of the quasi potential and is satisfied by the zero range and the Ginzburg Landau processes.

To exemplify situations in which Φ<U\Phi<U, that is the presence of a dynamical phase transition, consider the fluctuations of the time averaged current in the one dimensional case with periodic boundary conditions. Two models have been discussed so far, the KMP model and the exclusion process with an external field.

In [15] by simple arguments (Jensen inequality and convexity properties of the transport coefficients), we find sufficient conditions on DD, χ\chi, EE and JJ implying that the optimal profile for the variational problem (100) defining the functional UU is the constant one. More precisely we show that if DD is constant and J2/χ⁡(ρ)+E2​χ​(ρ)J^{2}/\chi(\rho)+E^{2}\chi(\rho) is a convex function in ρ\rho then

U⁡(J)=14​(J−E​χ​(ρ¯))2χ⁡(ρ¯).U(J)=\frac{1}{4}\frac{\left(J-E\chi(\bar{\rho})\right)^{2}}{\chi(\bar{\rho})}. (170)

Under suitable conditions, we shall exhibit a time-dependent path for which (1/T)​ℐ[0,T]​(ρ,j)(1/T){\mathcal{I}}_{[0,T]}(\rho,j) is strictly less then UU. This implies the inequality Φ<U\Phi<U. Let Λ=(0,1)\Lambda=(0,1) and (ρ⁡(t),j⁡(t))(\rho(t),j(t)) be a periodic trajectory, with time averaged current JJ, in the form of a traveling wave of velocity vv,

{ρ⁡(t,x)=ρ0​(x−v​t)j⁡(t,x)=J+v⁡[ρ0​(x−v​t)−ρ¯],\left\{\begin{array}[]{l}\rho(t,x)=\rho_{0}(x-vt)\\ j(t,x)=J+v\left[\rho_{0}(x-vt)-\bar{\rho}\right]\,,\end{array}\right. (171)

where ρ0\rho_{0} is an arbitrary periodic function with period one such that ∫01d​x​ρ0​(x)=ρ¯\int_{0}^{1}\!dx\,\rho_{0}(x)=\bar{\rho}. As functions of tt, ρ\rho and jj are periodic with period 1/v1/v. It is easy to verify that the continuity equation holds and that the time average of jj over the time interval v−1v^{-1} is equal to JJ. For this choice we have

Φ⁡(J)≤v​ℐ[0,v−1]​(ρ,j)=v4​∫0v−1d​t​𝒰​(ρ⁡(t),j⁡(t))\displaystyle\Phi(J)\leq v\,\mathcal{I}_{[0,v^{-1}]}(\rho,j)=\frac{v}{4}\int_{0}^{v^{-1}}\!dt\,\mathcal{U}(\rho(t),j(t))
=14​∫01d​x​{J+v⁡[ρ0−ρ¯]−J⁡(ρ0)}2χ⁡(ρ0)\displaystyle=\frac{1}{4}\int_{0}^{1}\!dx\,\frac{\left\{J+v\left[\rho_{0}-\bar{\rho}\right]-J(\rho_{0})\right\}^{2}}{\chi(\rho_{0})} (172)

As shown in [15] under the condition

[1−E2​χ2​(ρ¯)J2]​χ′′​(ρ¯)>0,\left[1-\frac{E^{2}\chi^{2}(\bar{\rho})}{J^{2}}\right]\chi^{\prime\prime}(\bar{\rho})>0, (173)

for JJ large enough it is possible to find ρ0\rho_{0} and vv such that the right hand side of (172) is less then (170).

Consider the KMP model. Since χ′′>0\chi^{\prime\prime}>0 condition (173) is satisfied when EE is small enough, in particular in the case of no external field, that is for an equilibrium state. The above argument thus provides a complete analytic proof of the strict inequality Φ<U\Phi<U. The existence of this dynamical phase transition has been also observed in simulations in [78]. An open problem is whether the phase transition exists in the case of a boundary driven model. At the numerical level so far the answer has been negative [77].

In the case of the exclusion process, since χ′′<0\chi^{\prime\prime}<0, in order to have a dynamical phase transition we need an external field. This case has been discussed in [25]. When EE and JJ are small, Φ=U\Phi=U and the optimal density profile for the variational problem (100) defining UU is constant. These authors perform a linear stability analysis showing, in particular, that the constant profile becomes unstable for sufficiently large external fields and currents and conclude the existence of a dynamical phase transition. By a numerical computation, they also show that the traveling wave path is the optimal one for the variational problem (98) defining Φ\Phi.

VI.2 Cumulants of the current and their universality properties

We define the average total current as

𝒬ε,T=1T​∫0Td​t​∫Λd​x​jε​(t,x),{\mathcal{Q}}_{\varepsilon,T}=\frac{1}{T}\int_{0}^{T}\!dt\int_{\Lambda}\!dx\,j_{\varepsilon}(t,x)\,, (174)

whose relationship with the microscopic dynamics will be detailed in section VIII.6. In the limit ε→0\varepsilon\to 0 and T→∞T\to\infty 𝒬ε,T{\mathcal{Q}}_{\varepsilon,T} converges to ∫Λd​x​J​(ρ¯)\int_{\Lambda}\!dx\,J(\bar{\rho}), where J⁡(ρ¯)J(\bar{\rho}) is the hydrodynamic current corresponding to the stationary density profile ρ¯\bar{\rho}. The MFT allows to describe the asymptotic behavior of the cumulants of 𝒬ε,T{\mathcal{Q}}_{\varepsilon,T}. We present in this section some results obtained in [24, 44, 3, 1].

We assume throughout this section that there is no external field, E=0E=0. We start with the case of a one-dimensional boundary driven system and choose Λ=(0,1)\Lambda=(0,1). Since in one space dimension the only divergence-free vector fields are the constant fields, the analysis of the asymptotic behavior of 𝒬ε,T{\mathcal{Q}}_{\varepsilon,T} is equivalent to (94). Assume that ρ0<ρ1\rho_{0}<\rho_{1} so that the stationary current is negative. The asymptotics of the cumulants of Qε,TQ_{\varepsilon,T} can be deduced from the general formulas (102), (103) by computing the derivatives of Φ♯\Phi^{\sharp} at 00. Note that the behavior of Φ♯\Phi^{\sharp} in a neighborhood of 00 corresponds to the behavior of Φ\Phi in a neighborhood of the stationary current J⁡(ρ¯)J(\bar{\rho}). In view of the continuity argument given in the paragraph before (102), we can compute the cumulants analyzing the time-independent variational problem (100). The same continuity argument implies that, in a neighborhood of J⁡(ρ¯)J(\bar{\rho}), the optimal ρ\rho for (100) is increasing.

As shown in [24], we then obtain

Φ⁡(J)=U⁡(J)=J4​∫ρ0ρ1D⁡(ρ)χ⁡(ρ)​(2−2+A⁡(J)​χ​(ρ)1+A⁡(J)​χ​(ρ))​𝑑ρ\Phi(J)=U(J)=\frac{J}{4}\int_{\rho_{0}}^{\rho_{1}}\frac{D(\rho)}{\chi(\rho)}\,\Big(2\,-\,\frac{2+A(J)\chi(\rho)}{\sqrt{1+A(J)\chi(\rho)}}\Big)\,d\rho (175)

where A⁡(J)A(J) is related to JJ by

J=−∫ρ0ρ1D⁡(ρ)1+A⁡(J)​χ​(ρ)dρ.J=-\,\int_{\rho_{0}}^{\rho_{1}}\frac{D(\rho)}{\sqrt{1+A(J)\chi(\rho)}}\,d\rho. (176)

By taking the Legendre transform (103) we deduce that for θ\theta small

Φ♯​(θ)=−B⁡(θ)4​[∫ρ0ρ1D⁡(ρ)1+B⁡(θ)​χ​(ρ)​𝑑ρ]2,\Phi^{\sharp}(\theta)\,=\,-\,\frac{B(\theta)}{4}\,\Big[\int_{\rho_{0}}^{\rho_{1}}\frac{D(\rho)}{\sqrt{1+B(\theta)\chi(\rho)}}\,d\rho\Big]^{2}, (177)

where BB is a related to θ\theta by

θ=12​∫ρ0ρ1D⁡(ρ)χ⁡(ρ)​(1−11+B⁡(θ)​χ​(ρ))​𝑑ρ.\theta\,=\,\frac{1}{2}\,\int_{\rho_{0}}^{\rho_{1}}\frac{D(\rho)}{\chi(\rho)}\,\Big(1\,-\,\frac{1}{\sqrt{1+B(\theta)\chi(\rho)}}\Big)\,d\rho. (178)

Denote by (Φ♯)(k)(\Phi^{\sharp})^{(k)} the kk-th derivative of Φ♯\Phi^{\sharp} and by CkC_{k} the kk-th cumulant of 𝒬ε,T{\mathcal{Q}}_{\varepsilon,T} From (102) we deduce that

Ck≈(εT)k−1​(Φ♯)(k)​(0),k≥1,C_{k}\approx\Big(\frac{\varepsilon}{T}\Big)^{k-1}(\Phi^{\sharp})^{(k)}(0),\qquad k\geq 1, (179)

where the approximation becomes exact as ε→0\varepsilon\to 0 and T→∞T\to\infty. We point out that the cumulants calculated in [24] are related to a random variable which differs from 𝒬ε,T{\mathcal{Q}}_{\varepsilon,T} by the scaling factor ε/T\varepsilon/T.

By expanding (177) and (178) in powers series we can compute the derivatives of Φ♯\Phi^{\sharp} .The first three are (Φ♯)(1)​(0)=−I1(\Phi^{\sharp})^{(1)}(0)=-I_{1}, (Φ♯)(2)​(0)=I2/I1(\Phi^{\sharp})^{(2)}(0)=I_{2}/I_{1}, (Φ♯)(3)(0)=−3(I3I1−I22)/I13(\Phi^{\sharp})^{(3)}(0)=-3(I_{3}I_{1}-I^{2}_{2})/I^{3}_{1}, where

In=∫ρ0ρ1D(ρ)[2χ(ρ)]n−1dρ,n=1,2,3.I_{n}\;=\;\int_{\rho_{0}}^{\rho_{1}}D(\rho)\,[2\chi(\rho)]^{n-1}d\rho\;,\quad n=1,2,3.

In the case where DD is constant and χ⁡(ρ)=ρ⁡(1−ρ)\chi(\rho)=\rho(1-\rho), which corresponds to the case of the simple exclusion process, condition (168) holds. By the results of section VI.1 we get that Φ⁡(J)=U⁡(J)\Phi(J)=U(J) for all JJ. The optimal solution ρ\rho of the variational problem (100) for UU has been computed in [24]. For any value of θ\theta one then gets the closed form

Φ♯​(θ)=(arcsinh​ω)2.\Phi^{\sharp}(\theta)=\left(\mathrm{arcsinh}\sqrt{\omega}\right)^{2}\,.

where

ω=ρ0​(eθ−1)+ρ1​(e−θ−1)+ρ0​ρ1​(eθ−1)​(e−θ−1).\omega\,=\,\rho_{0}(e^{\theta}-1)\,+\,\rho_{1}(e^{-\theta}-1)\,+\,\rho_{0}\rho_{1}(e^{\theta}-1)(e^{-\theta}-1)\,. (180)

The computation of the Legendre transform has been extended to higher dimensions in [1]. Consider a domain Λ\Lambda in dimension d>1d>1 and assume that there are two external reservoirs, at densities ρA\rho_{A} and ρB\rho_{B}, in the regions A,B⊂ΛA,B\subset\Lambda. For JJ close to the stationary value or globally under the assumption (168) we have that Φ\Phi is equal to UU. The fluctuations of the net flow between AA and BB are analyzed in [1] where it is shown that

Φ♯​(θ)=CapΛ​(A,B)​Φ1♯​(θ)\Phi^{\sharp}(\theta)={\mathrm{Cap}}_{\Lambda}\big(A,B\big)\,\Phi^{\sharp}_{1}(\theta) (181)

where Φ1♯\Phi^{\sharp}_{1} is computed for a one-dimensional system on the interval (0,1)(0,1) with boundary densities ρA\rho_{A}, ρB\rho_{B}, and CapΛ​(A,B){\mathrm{Cap}}_{\Lambda}\big(A,B\big) is the capacity, that depends only on the geometry, of a condenser formed by AA and BB in Λ\Lambda. From (181) it follows in particular that the ratio between any pair of cumulants is the same as in one dimension.

We now turn to the one-dimensional ring. Under the assumption that D⁡(ρ)D(\rho) is constant and that χ⁡(ρ)\chi(\rho) is concave, in [15] it is proven that Φ⁡(J)=U⁡(J)\Phi(J)=U(J). Moreover, if 1/χ⁡(ρ)1/\chi(\rho) is a convex function then U⁡(J)=(1/4)​(J2/χ⁡(ρ¯))U(J)\,=\,(1/4)(J^{2}/\chi(\bar{\rho})). Therefore, under the two previous conditions, the Legendre transform Φ♯\Phi^{\sharp} of Φ\Phi is simply given by

Φ♯​(θ)=θ2​χ​(ρ¯).\Phi^{\sharp}(\theta)\,=\,\theta^{2}\,\chi(\bar{\rho}).

As Φ♯\Phi^{\sharp} is quadratic, in view of (179), the limiting variance of ε−1​T​𝒬ε,T\varepsilon^{-1}T{\mathcal{Q}}_{\varepsilon,T} is equal to 2​χ​(ρ¯)2\chi(\bar{\rho}) while the remaining cumulants vanish as ε→0\varepsilon\to 0 and T→∞T\to\infty. The finite size corrections to this Gaussian behavior are studied in [3]. The relationship between the variable QtQ_{t} used in this reference and (174) is

𝒬ε,T=ε2T​Qε−2​T.{\mathcal{Q}}_{\varepsilon,T}=\frac{\varepsilon^{2}}{T}Q_{\varepsilon^{-2}T}.

In our notation, the finite size correction to the function Φ⁡(J)\Phi(J) is

Φε​(J)=Φ⁡(J)−ε⁡{J24​χ+D​ℱ​(J2​χ′′16​D2​χ)}+o⁡(ε).\Phi_{\varepsilon}(J)\;=\;\ \Phi(J)-\,\varepsilon\Big\{\frac{J^{2}}{4\chi}+D\,{\mathcal{F}}\Big(\frac{J^{2}\chi^{\prime\prime}}{16D^{2}\chi}\Big)\Big\}\,+\,o(\varepsilon).

In this formula, D=D⁡(ρ¯)D=D(\bar{\rho}), χ=χ⁡(ρ¯)\chi=\chi(\bar{\rho}), χ′′=χ′′​(ρ¯)\chi^{\prime\prime}=\chi^{\prime\prime}(\bar{\rho}), and

ℱ⁡(u)=∑k≥2B2​k−2(k−1)!​k!​(−2​u)k,{\mathcal{F}}(u)\,=\,\sum_{k\geq 2}\frac{B_{2k-2}}{(k-1)!k!}(-2u)^{k}\,,

where BnB_{n} are the Bernoulli numbers, the coefficients of the expansion x​(ex−1)−1=∑n≥0Bn​xn/n!x(e^{x}-1)^{-1}=\sum_{n\geq 0}B_{n}x^{n}/n!. Accordingly, the finite size correction to Φ♯\Phi^{\sharp} up to first order in ε\varepsilon is

Φε♯​(θ)=Φ♯​(θ)+ε⁡{χ​θ2+D​ℱ​(χ​χ′′4​D2​θ2)}.\Phi^{\sharp}_{\varepsilon}(\theta)\,=\,\Phi^{\sharp}(\theta)+\varepsilon\Big\{\chi\theta^{2}+D\,{\mathcal{F}}\Big(\frac{\chi\chi^{\prime\prime}}{4D^{2}}\theta^{2}\Big)\Big\}.

From this expansion we derive the asymptotic for the cumulants of the integrated current. More precisely, recalling (174) the variance of 𝒬ε,T{\mathcal{Q}}_{\varepsilon,T} (including the first order correction) is

C2≈εT​(1+ε)​ 2​χ,C_{2}\approx\frac{\varepsilon}{T}(1+\varepsilon)\,2\chi,

while the cumulant of order 2​k2k, k≥2k\geq 2, is

C2​k≈ε2​kT2​k−1​B2​k−2​(2​k)!(k−1)!​k!​D​(−χ​χ′′2​D2)k.C_{2k}\approx\frac{\varepsilon^{2k}}{T^{2k-1}}\,B_{2k-2}\,\frac{(2k)!}{(k-1)!k!}D\,\Big(\frac{-\chi\chi^{\prime\prime}}{2D^{2}}\Big)^{k}.

VI.3 Current fluctuations for non stationary infinite systems

The MFT has been applied also to study current fluctuations for diffusive infinite systems in non stationary states. More precisely, in [47] the authors consider a diffusive stochastic lattice gas on the infinite lattice with step initial condition. This means that at the initial time the particles are distributed in a non steady state having density ρa\rho_{a} at the left of the origin and density ρb\rho_{b} at the right. Let QτQ_{\tau} be the net flow of particles across the origin up to time τ\tau and let

Φ♯​(θ)=limτ→+∞1τ​log⁡𝔼⁡(eθ​Qτ)\Phi^{\sharp}(\theta)=\lim_{\tau\to+\infty}\frac{1}{\sqrt{\tau}}\log\mathbb{E}\left(e^{\theta Q_{\tau}}\right) (182)

be the corresponding generating function of the cumulants. The appearance of the τ\sqrt{\tau} in this formula is due to the fact that a law of large numbers holds for Qτ/τQ_{\tau}/\sqrt{\tau} for large τ\tau. In (182) the expected value can be interpreted in two different ways depending on whether we consider fluctuations of the initial condition (annealed case) or not (quenched case). In the annealed case Φ♯​(θ)\Phi^{\sharp}(\theta) satisfies a relationship reminiscent of the Gallavotti-Cohen symmetry. In [47] the authors argue that Φ♯​(θ)\Phi^{\sharp}(\theta) in (182) can be computed using MFT. The correct asymptotic behavior is obtained considering the scaling parameter ε=(τ)−1\varepsilon=\left(\sqrt{\tau}\right)^{-1} and letting the macroscopic time TT vary on the finite window [0,1][0,1]. Since there is conservation of the mass and the system is one dimensional the net flow QτQ_{\tau} in this approximation will coincide with

τ​∫0+∞(ρε​(x,1)−ρε​(x,0))​𝑑x.\sqrt{\tau}\int_{0}^{+\infty}\left(\rho_{\varepsilon}(x,1)-\rho_{\varepsilon}(x,0)\right)\,dx\,. (183)

By (11) and (12), in the annealed regime Φ♯​(θ)\Phi^{\sharp}(\theta) can be obtained as

Φ♯(θ)=inf{−Vin(ρ(0))+θ∫0+∞dx[ρ(x,1)−ρ(x,0)]−∫01dt∫−∞+∞dx[j+D(ρ)∇ρ]2χ⁡(ρ)},\begin{split}&\Phi^{\sharp}(\theta)=\inf\bigg\{-V_{\mathrm{in}}(\rho(0))+\theta\int_{0}^{+\infty}\!dx\,\left[\rho(x,1)-\rho(x,0)\right]\ \\ &\qquad-\int_{0}^{1}\!dt\int_{-\infty}^{+\infty}\!dx\,\frac{\left[j+D(\rho)\nabla\rho\right]^{2}}{\chi(\rho)}\bigg\}\,,\end{split} (184)

where the infimum is carried out over all (ρ,j)(\rho,j) satisfying the continuity equation. The term VinV_{\mathrm{in}} is due to fluctuations of the initial condition. This is a product of Bernoulli distributions of parameter ρa\rho_{a} in the negative axis and ρb\rho_{b} in the positive one. The functional VinV_{\mathrm{in}} coincides with (29) with ρ¯​(x)\bar{\rho}(x) substituted by

ρa​(1−θ⁡(x))+ρb​θ​(x),\rho_{a}\left(1-\theta(x)\right)+\rho_{b}\theta(x)\,, (185)

where θ⁡(x)\theta(x) is the Heaviside function. In the quenched case there is an expression similar to (184) but without the term VinV_{\mathrm{in}} and the minimization has to be done over all the (ρ,j)(\rho,j) such that ρ⁡(x,0)\rho(x,0) coincides with (185). The variational problem (184) and the corresponding one for the quenched case cannot be solved explicitly in general. An exact solution is possible for free particles [47] and in some cases for the symmetric exclusion process [105].

In the annealed case for the symmetric exclusion process it is possible to apply some symmetry argument to (184) showing that the dependence of Φ♯​(θ)\Phi^{\sharp}(\theta) on the parameters ρa\rho_{a}, ρb\rho_{b} and θ\theta is only through their combination ω\omega as in (180) (with ρ0\rho_{0} and ρ1\rho_{1} replaced by ρa\rho_{a} and ρb\rho_{b}). This means that Φ♯​(θ)=F⁡(ω)\Phi^{\sharp}(\theta)=F(\omega) for a suitable function FF whose explicit expression has been obtained in [46] using microscopic combinatorial arguments. An open problem is to recover such an expression using instead (184). Still a symmetry argument for (184) shows that, in the annealed case, from the exact expression for the symmetric simple exclusion it is possible to obtain the expression of Φ♯​(θ)\Phi^{\sharp}(\theta) for other models, like the KMP model, having constant diffusion matrix and quadratic mobility.

Another result that can be deduced from (184) is a non-Gaussian decay of the distribution of the net flow QτQ_{\tau}. This holds under some conditions on the transport coefficients both in the annealed and in the quenched regime. More precisely, under some conditions that hold e.g., for the exclusion process, for large τ\tau and large qq the net flow QτQ_{\tau} has the super-Gaussian statistics

ℙ⁡(Qττ≈q)≍e−α​τ​q3,\mathbb{P}\left(\frac{Q_{\tau}}{\sqrt{\tau}}\approx q\right)\asymp e^{-\alpha\sqrt{\tau}\,q^{3}}\,, (186)

for a suitable positive constant α\alpha. On the other hand, in [104] it is shown that the KMP model in the quenched regime exhibits instead a sub-Gaussian statistics.

VII Hyperbolic conservation laws

The MFT for hyperbolic conservation laws is less developed than the case of driven diffusive systems. In this section we show however how some results can be obtained by taking the formal limit of vanishing viscosity. We restrict the discussion to the one-dimensional inviscid Burgers equation [35], which is a simple model for a compressible fluid. It can be obtained as hydrodynamic limit of the asymmetric exclusion process under Eulerian rescaling of space-time, that is keeping x/tx/t fixed.

VII.1 Hydrodynamics

The hydrodynamic equation is

∂tρ+∇χ​(ρ)=0\partial_{t}\rho+\nabla\chi(\rho)=0 (187)

where χ⁡(ρ)=ρ⁡(1−ρ)\chi(\rho)=\rho(1-\rho) is the mobility of the exclusion process (called flow in the context of hyperbolic conservation laws) and we consider an external field toward the right with unit strength. The standard inviscid Burgers equation, that is usually written in the form ∂tu+∇u2=0\partial_{t}u+\nabla u^{2}=0, can be obtained from (187) by a simple change of variables. According to the interpretation in terms of the exclusion process, we shall however consider 0≤ρ≤10\leq\rho\leq 1.

An important difference between the evolution (187) and the driven diffusive (parabolic) equations considered before is that, even if the initial condition is smooth, the solution to (187) may develop singularities, called shocks, after a finite time. This is easily seen by the method of characteristics. Indeed, in the Lagrangian coordinates, an element of the “fluid” at local density ρ\rho has a velocity vρ=χ′​(ρ)=1−2​ρv_{\rho}=\chi^{\prime}(\rho)=1-2\rho. In particular, low density regions ρ≪1\rho\ll 1 will overtake the regions of intermediate density ρ≈1/2\rho\approx 1/2 resulting in the formation of a singularity.

Let us discuss these shock solutions to (187) in more detail. Consider the function

φ⁡(x)=φρ−,ρ+​(x)={ρ−x<0ρ+x>0\varphi(x)=\varphi_{\rho_{-},\rho_{+}}(x)=\begin{cases}\rho_{-}&x<0\\ \rho_{+}&x>0\end{cases} (188)

describing a shock from ρ−\rho_{-} to ρ+\rho_{+}. If we set

v=vρ−,ρ+=χ⁡(ρ+)−χ⁡(ρ−)ρ+−ρ−=1−(ρ++ρ−)v=v_{\rho_{-},\rho_{+}}=\frac{\chi(\rho_{+})-\chi(\rho_{-})}{\rho_{+}-\rho_{-}}=1-(\rho_{+}+\rho_{-}) (189)

then it is not difficult to check that φ⁡(x−v​t)\varphi(x-vt) solves (187) in the sense of distributions. Observe that as ρ+−ρ−→0\rho_{+}-\rho_{-}\to 0 the shock velocity vρ−,ρ+v_{\rho_{-},\rho_{+}} approaches the velocity of the characteristics. As far as the hydrodynamic equation (187) is concerned, both ρ−<ρ+\rho_{-}<\rho_{+} and ρ−>ρ+\rho_{-}>\rho_{+} are allowed. These cases correspond to quite different situations from a physical point of view. Recalling that we have chosen an external field toward the right, the case ρ−<ρ+\rho_{-}<\rho_{+} corresponds to a low density region at the left blocked by a high density region (a pile of particles in the microscopic picture) at the right and appears a natural feature of the system. On the other hand, the case ρ−>ρ+\rho_{-}>\rho_{+} does not have a natural interpretation and should be regarded as unphysical.

The hyperbolic evolution (187) can be obtained from the driven diffusive equation in the limit of vanishing viscosity. Namely, by considering

∂tρ+∇χ(ρ)=ν∇(D(ρ)∇ρ)\partial_{t}\rho+\nabla\chi(\rho)=\nu\nabla\big(D(\rho)\nabla\rho\big) (190)

and taking the formal limit ν→0\nu\to 0. For the exclusion process DD is constant but for a while we consider arbitrary diffusion coefficient. By setting ν=0\nu=0 we recover the evolution (187), but as we next show there is another condition from (190) that survives in the limit ν→0\nu\to 0 and rules out the unphysical decreasing shocks. Let h⁡(ρ)h(\rho) be a convex function (an entropy in the terminology of hyperbolic conservation laws) and let g⁡(ρ)g(\rho) be the function defined by

h′​(ρ)​χ′​(ρ)=g′​(ρ).h^{\prime}(\rho)\chi^{\prime}(\rho)=g^{\prime}(\rho). (191)

In the terminology of hyperbolic conservation laws gg is called the entropy flow associated to hh. Multiplying (190) by h′​(ρ)h^{\prime}(\rho) we deduce

∂th(ρ)+∇g(ρ)=νh′(ρ)∇(D(ρ)∇ρ)=−νh′′(ρ)D(ρ)(∇ρ)2+ν∇(h′(ρ)D(ρ)∇ρ).\begin{split}&\partial_{t}h(\rho)+\nabla g(\rho)=\nu h^{\prime}(\rho)\nabla\big(D(\rho)\nabla\rho\big)\\ &\quad=-\nu h^{\prime\prime}(\rho)D(\rho)\big(\nabla\rho\big)^{2}+\nu\nabla\big(h^{\prime}(\rho)D(\rho)\nabla\rho\big).\end{split}

Since the last term is a total derivative and h′′​(ρ)≥0h^{\prime\prime}(\rho)\geq 0, by taking the limit ν→0\nu\to 0, we deduce the inequality ∂th⁡(ρ)+∇g​(ρ)≤0\partial_{t}h(\rho)+\nabla g(\rho)\leq 0. We conclude that the appropriate formulation of (190) in the vanishing viscosity limit is

{∂tρ+∇χ​(ρ)=0∂th⁡(ρ)+∇g​(ρ)≤0\begin{cases}\partial_{t}\rho+\nabla\chi(\rho)=0\\ \partial_{t}h(\rho)+\nabla g(\rho)\leq 0\end{cases} (192)

where hh is an arbitrary convex function and gg is defined by (191). In view of the specific form of the flow χ⁡(ρ)\chi(\rho) (more precisely in view of its concavity), it is simple to check that increasing shocks, i.e. φρ−,ρ+​(x−vρ−,ρ+​t)\varphi_{\rho_{-},\rho_{+}}(x-v_{\rho_{-},\rho_{+}}t) with ρ−<ρ+\rho_{-}<\rho_{+} solve (192) while decreasing shocks do not.

Observe that while (187) in invariant under time and space reflection the entropy condition in (192) is not and implies a time arrow. The initial value problem corresponding to (192) on the whole line is well posed [122], while uniqueness fails for (187).

As we would like to include boundary reservoirs in the model, we need to discuss the role of boundary conditions when the hyperbolic evolution (192) is considered on the interval Λ=(0,1)\Lambda=(0,1). More precisely, we consider boundary reservoirs with chemical potentials λ0,λ1\lambda_{0},\lambda_{1} at the endpoints of Λ\Lambda and denote by ρ0\rho_{0}, ρ1\rho_{1} the corresponding values of the density, i.e., λi=f′​(ρi)\lambda_{i}=f^{\prime}(\rho_{i}). While for driven diffusive systems the effect of the boundary reservoirs is to fix the value of the density, for hyperbolic conservation laws the situation is more subtle. As we have discussed above, the hyperbolic evolution develops shocks which may occur also at the boundary. In this case the value of the density at the boundary will not be fixed by the reservoirs but rather constrained by the admissibility of the shock. The boundary conditions will thus be given in terms of inequalities and not of identities.

Referring to [122] for the general theory of boundary conditions for hyperbolic conservation laws, we only discuss the case of the Burgers equation. At the left endpoint x=0x=0 the reservoir’s density is ρ0\rho_{0} and the appropriate boundary condition is the following. If ρ0≤1/2\rho_{0}\leq 1/2 then 1−ρ0≤ρ⁡(t,0)≤11-\rho_{0}\leq\rho(t,0)\leq 1 while if ρ0≥1/2\rho_{0}\geq 1/2 then ρ0≤ρ⁡(t,0)≤1\rho_{0}\leq\rho(t,0)\leq 1. Likewise, at the right endpoint x=1x=1 the reservoir’s density is ρ1\rho_{1} and the boundary condition is the following. If ρ1≤1/2\rho_{1}\leq 1/2 then 0≤ρ⁡(t,1)≤1/20\leq\rho(t,1)\leq 1/2 while if ρ1≥1/2\rho_{1}\geq 1/2 then 0≤ρ⁡(t,1)≤1−ρ10\leq\rho(t,1)\leq 1-\rho_{1}.

VII.2 Large fluctuations

We discuss first the case of periodic boundary conditions. As for the case of driven diffusive system, we want to compute the probability of a space-time fluctuation of the density and current. Due to the singular behavior of the hyperbolic evolution, there are two different large deviations regimes. In order to violate the continuity equation in (192) we need to apply an external field over a macroscopic part of the system. On the other hand if we consider a solution to (187) with shocks, we can violate the entropy condition in (192) (which allows only increasing shocks) by applying a field localized on the shocks. In terms of the microscopic dynamics, consider a high density region We describe only the probability of fluctuations violating the entropy condition in (192) which are, so to speak, much less improbable and the relevant ones for the computation of the quasi-potential. For such fluctuations the density and current are directly related. Since we do not violate the continuity equation (187), once we specify the fluctuation ρ\rho of the density the current will be given by χ⁡(ρ)\chi(\rho). The corresponding action functional has been derived in [83, 129]. The answer is amazingly simple: in order to violate the entropy condition we need only to pay the corresponding entropy cost. The subtle point is to decide which is the correct entropy to use. Note in fact that the entropy condition in (192) does not depend on the function hh: if it holds for some convex hh (gg is then given by (191)) then it holds for all convex hh. In order to find the correct choice of hh we need to go back to the small viscosity approximation (190). At this level the physical entropy hh is selected by the Einstein condition h′′​(ρ)=D⁡(ρ)/χ⁡(ρ)h^{\prime\prime}(\rho)=D(\rho)/\chi(\rho). For the exclusion process D=1D=1 so that hh is the equilibrium free energy ff, i.e.,

h⁡(ρ)=f⁡(ρ)=ρ​log⁡ρ+(1−ρ)​log⁡(1−ρ).h(\rho)=f(\rho)=\rho\log\rho+(1-\rho)\log(1-\rho). (193)

The Jensen-Varadhan large deviation formula for this inviscid Burgers equation then reads

ℙ⁡(ρε≈ρ,t∈[T0,T1])≍exp⁡{−ε−1​I[T0,T1]​(ρ)}\mathbb{P}\big(\rho_{\varepsilon}\approx\rho,t\in[T_{0},T_{1}]\big)\asymp\exp\big\{-\varepsilon^{-1}I_{[T_{0},T_{1}]}(\rho)\big\}

with I⁡(ρ)I(\rho) finite only for ρ\rho satisfying (187) and for such ρ\rho given by

I[T0,T1]​(ρ)=∫T0T1d​t​∫01d​x​[∂tf⁡(ρ)+∇g​(ρ)]+I_{[T_{0},T_{1}]}(\rho)=\int_{T_{0}}^{T_{1}}\!dt\int_{0}^{1}\!dx\,\big[\partial_{t}f(\rho)+\nabla g(\rho)\big]_{+} (194)

where [a]+=max⁡{0,a}[a]_{+}=\max\{0,a\} is the positive part of aa, ff as in (193), and gg satisfies (191). As discussed in [26] the expression (194) can be derived from (74) by considering the limit of vanishing viscosity.

While the structure of the functional II in (194) is very different from the case of driven diffusive systems of Section IV, the time reversal symmetry of Section II.3 holds also in this case. Since we are considering periodic boundary conditions, the total mass m=∫01d​x​ρ​(x)m=\int_{0}^{1}\!dx\rho(x) is conserved. The quasi-potential is then

V⁡(ρ)=∫01d​x​[f⁡(ρ)−f⁡(m)].V(\rho)=\int_{0}^{1}\!dx\,\big[f(\rho)-f(m)\big].

Since the time reversed dynamics can be realized by inverting the external field, the adjoint hydrodynamics is obtained by replacing χ⁡(ρ)\chi(\rho) with −χ⁡(ρ)-\chi(\rho) so that

I[T0,T1]∗​(ρ)=∫T0T1∫01d​x​[∂tf⁡(ρ)−∇g​(ρ)]+.I_{[T_{0},T_{1}]}^{*}(\rho)=\int_{T_{0}}^{T_{1}}\!\int_{0}^{1}\!dx\,\big[\partial_{t}f(\rho)-\nabla g(\rho)\big]_{+}.

It is now simple to check that (19) holds also in the hyperbolic regime, i.e.,

V⁡(ρ⁡(T0))+I[T0,T1]​(ρ)=V⁡(ρ⁡(T1))+I[−T1,−T0]∗​(θ​ρ).V(\rho(T_{0}))+I_{[T_{0},T_{1}]}(\rho)=V(\rho(T_{1}))+I_{[-T_{1},-T_{0}]}^{*}(\theta\rho).

We now discuss the large deviations asymptotics in the presence of boundary reservoirs. Since the boundary condition for the hyperbolic evolution (192) discussed in the previous Section can be in formulated as entropic conditions at the boundary, we need to add to the Jensen-Varadhan functional (194) the boundary terms that take into account the total entropy production at the boundary. For the exclusion process, these terms have been computed in [26] by considering the limit of vanishing viscosity. They have the form

I[T0,T1](0)​(ρ)=∫T0T1d​t​s(0)​(ρ⁡(t,0),ρ0)I[T0,T1](1)​(ρ)=∫T0T1d​t​s(1)​(ρ⁡(t,1),ρ1)\begin{split}I^{(0)}_{[T_{0},T_{1}]}(\rho)=\int_{T_{0}}^{T_{1}}\!dt\,s^{(0)}(\rho(t,0),\rho_{0})\\ I^{(1)}_{[T_{0},T_{1}]}(\rho)=\int_{T_{0}}^{T_{1}}\!dt\,s^{(1)}(\rho(t,1),\rho_{1})\end{split}

where ρ0\rho_{0}, ρ1\rho_{1} are the densities of the boundary reservoirs and the functions s(0)s^{(0)}, s(1)s^{(1)} are explicitly given in [26]. Accordingly, the full rate function is

I[T0,T1]​(ρ)=I[T0,T1]bulk​(ρ)+I[T0,T1](0)​(ρ)+I[T0,T1](1)​(ρ)I_{[T_{0},T_{1}]}(\rho)=I^{\mathrm{bulk}}_{[T_{0},T_{1}]}(\rho)+I^{(0)}_{[T_{0},T_{1}]}(\rho)+I^{(1)}_{[T_{0},T_{1}]}(\rho) (195)

with IbulkI^{\mathrm{bulk}} given by (194).

By considering the variational problem (76), i.e., V(ρ)=infI(−∞,0](ρ^)V(\rho)=\inf I_{(-\infty,0]}(\hat{\rho}), with the constraint ρ^​(0)=ρ\hat{\rho}(0)=\rho, for the action functional (195), the formulas for the quasi-potential of the boundary driven asymmetric exclusion process derived in [48] by exact computations on the microscopic ensembles can be obtained within the MFT formalism. We refer to [6], for the details of such computations that, as there discussed, can be generalized to higher space dimensions and to the models satisfying the symmetry χ⁡(ρ)=χ⁡(ψ⁡(ρ))\chi(\rho)=\chi(\psi(\rho)) for some decreasing ψ\psi.

VIII Microscopic models

Models have played a fundamental role in equilibrium statistical mechanics. The Ising model provided the first proof that statistical mechanics can explain the existence of phase transitions and was a main guide in the study of critical behavior. A reason for this effectiveness is the circumstance that the macroscopic behavior is, to a considerable extent, independent of the microscopic details. Hence different systems exhibit qualitatively the same phenomenology at large scales. This section requires some basic notions on probability theory and Markov processes, see e.g., [34].

Stochastic lattice gases are a collection of particles performing random walks on a lattice in continuous time and interacting with each other. These particles are to be considered indistinguishable. Accordingly, the microscopic state is specified by giving the occupation number in each site of the lattice. The effect of the interaction is that the jump rates depend on the local configuration of the particles, i.e., on the occupation numbers of the nearby sites. For non-isolated systems we model the effect of the reservoirs by adding creation/annihilation of particles at the boundary. The effect of an external field is modeled by perturbing the rates and giving a net drift toward a specified direction.

As basic microscopic model we consider a stochastic lattice gas in a finite domain, with an external field, and either with periodic boundary conditions or with particle reservoirs at the boundary. The dynamics can be informally described as follows. Associated to each lattice site there is an independent Poisson clock of parameter depending on the local configuration. When the clock rings, a particle jumps from this site to a neighboring site. In the case of particle reservoirs, superimposed to this dynamics, at the boundary particles are created and annihilated at exponential times.

Fix Λ⊂ℝd\Lambda\subset{\mathbb{R}}^{d} and, given ε>0\varepsilon>0, let Λε=Λ∩ε​ℤd\Lambda_{\varepsilon}=\Lambda\cap\varepsilon{\mathbb{Z}}^{d} its discrete approximation. The microscopic configuration is given by the collection of occupation variables η⁡(i)\eta(i), i∈Λεi\in\Lambda_{\varepsilon}, representing the number of particles at the site ii. We denote by Ωε\Omega_{\varepsilon} the space of all possible configurations. The microscopic dynamics {ηt}t∈ℝ\{\eta_{t}\}_{t\in{\mathbb{R}}} of the configuration of the system is formally specified in terms of its infinitesimal generator LL, defined as follows. Let f:Ωε→ℝf:\Omega_{\varepsilon}\to{\mathbb{R}} be an observable, then

𝔼⁡(f⁡(ηt+h)|ηt)−f⁡(ηt)=(L​f)​(ηt)​h+o⁡(h),{\mathbb{E}}\big(f(\eta_{t+h})\big|\eta_{t}\big)-f(\eta_{t})=(Lf)(\eta_{t})\,h+o(h)\,, (196)

so that the expected infinitesimal increment of f⁡(ηt)f(\eta_{t}) is (L​f)​(ηt)​d​t(Lf)(\eta_{t})\,dt. Recall that 𝔼{\mathbb{E}} denotes the expectation over trajectories on the configuration space. The transition probability of the Markov process ηt\eta_{t} is then given by the kernel of the semi–group generated by LL, i.e.

pt​(η,η′)=et​L​(η,η′).p_{t}(\eta,\eta^{\prime})=e^{tL}(\eta,\eta^{\prime})\,. (197)

We can rewrite the full generator LL as follows

L​f​(η)=∑i,j∈Λεci​j​(η)​[f⁡(σi​j​η)−f⁡(η)]+∑±,i∈Λεc±i(η)[f(σ±iη)−f(η)],\begin{array}[]{l}\displaystyle{Lf(\eta)=\sum_{i,j\in\Lambda_{\varepsilon}}c_{ij}(\eta)\big[f(\sigma^{ij}\eta)-f(\eta)\big]}\\ \displaystyle{+\sum_{\pm,i\in\Lambda_{\varepsilon}}c^{\pm}_{i}(\eta)\big[f(\sigma_{\pm}^{i}\eta)-f(\eta)\big]\,,}\end{array} (198)

where σi​j​η\sigma^{ij}\eta is the configuration obtained from η\eta letting one particle jump from ii to jj, σ±i​η\sigma_{\pm}^{i}\eta are the configurations associated to the creation or annihilation of a particle in site ii, and ci,j​(η)c_{i,j}(\eta), ci±​(η)c^{\pm}_{i}(\eta) are the corresponding jump rates. We denote by ∂Λε\partial\Lambda_{\varepsilon} the interior boundary of Λε\Lambda_{\varepsilon}, i.e. the collection of sites i∈Λεi\in\Lambda_{\varepsilon} at distance ε\varepsilon from ε​ℤd\Λε\varepsilon{\mathbb{Z}}^{d}\backslash\Lambda_{\varepsilon}. The cases when the rates ci±​(η)c^{\pm}_{i}(\eta) are zero except for i∈∂Λεi\in\partial\Lambda_{\varepsilon} correspond to conservative bulk dynamics, with a hydrodynamic equation as in (5). In these cases, creation and annihilation of particles at the boundary describe the interaction with the external reservoirs. Models with non-zero creation/annihilation rates ci±​(η)c^{\pm}_{i}(\eta) also in the bulk correspond to reaction-diffusion equations, an example being (155).

A physical state of the system corresponds to a probability distribution PP (ensemble) on the configuration space Ωε\Omega_{\varepsilon}. A state is invariant (stationary) under the dynamics if

∑η∈ΩεP⁡(η)​et​L​(η,η′)=P⁡(η′).\sum_{\eta\in\Omega_{\varepsilon}}P(\eta)\,e^{tL}(\eta,\eta^{\prime})=P(\eta^{\prime}). (199)

Namely, if we distribute the initial condition η\eta according to PP, then the distribution of ηt\eta_{t}, at any later time t≥0t\geq 0, is again PP. A necessary and sufficient condition for a state PP to be invariant is

EP​(L​f)=0for all observables ​f,E_{P}\big(Lf\big)=0\quad\textrm{for all observables }f, (200)

where EPE_{P} denotes the expectation with respect to PP.

All the models that we consider are irreducible, i.e. there is a strictly positive probability to go from any configuration to any other. In this case, according to general results on Markov processes, the invariant state is unique and it coincides with the limiting distribution of the system when t→∞t\to\infty.

If the generator LL satisfies the detailed balance condition with respect to some distribution PP, namely

EP​(g​L​f)=EP​(f​L​g),E_{P}(gLf)=E_{P}(fLg)\,, (201)

for all observables f,gf,g, then PP is necessarily an invariant state. In such a case the process is said to be time reversal invariant. This terminology is due to the following fact. Let ℙη{{\mathbb{P}}}_{\eta} be the probability distribution on the space of paths {ηt}t≥0\{\eta_{t}\}_{t\geq 0} with initial condition η0=η\eta_{0}=\eta, and let ℙ{{\mathbb{P}}} be the stationary process, i.e., the distribution on the space of paths with initial configuration η0\eta_{0} distributed according to the invariant state PP. Since PP is invariant, the distribution ℙ{\mathbb{P}} is invariant with respect to time shifts. We can thus regard ℙ{\mathbb{P}} as a distribution on paths defined also for t≤0t\leq 0. This probability distribution is invariant under time reversal if and only if the detailed balance condition (201) holds. Indeed, if ϑ\vartheta is the time reversal, i.e., (ϑ​η)t:=η−t(\vartheta\eta)_{t}:=\eta_{-t}, we have that ℙ∘ϑ{\mathbb{P}}\circ\vartheta is the stationary Markov process with generator L∗L^{*}, the adjoint of LL with respect to PP, and condition (201) is precisely the condition that L∗=LL^{*}=L.

An equivalent form of the detailed balance condition (201) is as follows

P⁡(η)​c​(η,η′)=P⁡(η′)​c​(η′,η),P(\eta)c(\eta,\eta^{\prime})=P(\eta^{\prime})c(\eta^{\prime},\eta)\,, (202)

for all configurations η,η′∈Ωε\eta,\eta^{\prime}\in\Omega_{\varepsilon}. In this equation c⁡(η,η′)c(\eta,\eta^{\prime}) is the transition rate from the configuration η\eta to η′\eta^{\prime}, which can be either a jump rate ci​j​(η)c_{ij}(\eta), if η′=σi​j​η\eta^{\prime}=\sigma^{ij}\eta, or a creation/annihilation rate ci±​(η)c_{i}^{\pm}(\eta), if η′=σ±i​η\eta^{\prime}=\sigma^{i}_{\pm}\eta.

When the unique invariant state does not satisfy the detailed balance condition (202), the corresponding process is not time reversal invariant. Time reversal invariant processes correspond to equilibrium thermodynamic states. The converse is not necessarily true: there can be microscopic models not invariant under time reversal corresponding to equilibrium macroscopic states [63, 64, 7, 65]. This is not surprising: going from the microscopic to the macroscopic description there is loss of information.

Next, we describe in some detail some of the most studied microscopic models, which allow a detailed mathematical analysis. They are microscopic counterparts of the macroscopic models discussed in Section V.

VIII.1 The simple exclusion process

The boundary driven simple exclusion process, on a domain Λ⊂ℝd\Lambda\subset{\mathbb{R}}^{d}, is defined letting particles move according to independent simple random walks, with the exclusion rule that there cannot be more than one particle in a single lattice site (hard core interaction). This gives a kind of classical Pauli principle. It is appropriate to remark that the simple exclusion process is a special case of the Kawasaki spin dynamics [86]. This is a conservative dynamics that satisfies detailed balance with respect to a Gibbs distribution. The simple exclusion process corresponds to the case of a constant Hamiltonian.

According to the exclusion rule, the space of all possible configurations of the system is Ωε={0,1}Λε\Omega_{\varepsilon}=\{0,1\}^{\Lambda_{\varepsilon}}. In terms of the generator (198) this corresponds to the following choice of the bulk jump rates:

{ci​j​(η)=η⁡(i)​(1−η⁡(j))​ for |j−i|=ε,ci​j​(η)=0​ otherwise .\left\{\begin{array}[]{l}\displaystyle{\vphantom{\Big(}c_{ij}(\eta)=\eta(i)(1-\eta(j))\,\,\text{ for }\,\,|j-i|=\varepsilon\,,}\\ \displaystyle{\vphantom{\Big(}c_{ij}(\eta)=0\,\,\text{ otherwise }\,.}\end{array}\right. (203)

The interaction with the boundary reservoirs is described by creation and annihilation rates ci±​(η)c_{i}^{\pm}(\eta) for i∈∂Λεi\in\partial\Lambda_{\varepsilon}. Let λ⁡(x)\lambda(x) be the chemical potential of the boundary reservoirs (it is a continuous function on a neighborhood of ∂Λ\partial\Lambda). The corresponding creation/annihilation rates are as follows

{ci−​(η)=η⁡(i)​∑j∈∂Λεo​(i)11+eλ⁡(j)​ for ​i∈∂Λε,ci+​(η)=(1−η⁡(i))​∑j∈∂Λεo​(i)eλ⁡(j)1+eλ⁡(j)​ for ​i∈∂Λε,ci±​(η)=0​ otherwise,\left\{\begin{array}[]{l}\displaystyle{\vphantom{\Big(}c_{i}^{-}(\eta)=\eta(i)\sum_{j\in\partial\Lambda^{o}_{\varepsilon}(i)}\frac{1}{1+e^{\lambda(j)}}\,\text{ for }\,\,i\in\partial\Lambda_{\varepsilon},}\\ \displaystyle{\vphantom{\Big(}c_{i}^{+}(\eta)=(1-\eta(i))\sum_{j\in\partial\Lambda^{o}_{\varepsilon}(i)}\frac{e^{\lambda(j)}}{1+e^{\lambda(j)}}\,\,\text{ for }\,\,i\in\partial\Lambda_{\varepsilon},}\\ \displaystyle{\vphantom{\Big(}c_{i}^{\pm}(\eta)=0\,\,\text{ otherwise,}}\end{array}\right. (204)

where ∂Λεo​(i)\partial\Lambda^{o}_{\varepsilon}(i) denotes the set of all sites at distance ε\varepsilon from ii outside of Λε\Lambda_{\varepsilon}. Observe that the rates at the corners of Λε\Lambda_{\varepsilon} differ as there are more neighbors.

The model is clearly irreducible, hence, as explained above, there is a unique invariant state PP satisfying (200), corresponding to the limiting distribution of the system. When the chemical potential of the boundary reservoirs is constant, λ⁡(i)=λ\lambda(i)=\lambda for all i∈Λεi\in\Lambda_{\varepsilon}, the detailed balance condition (202) holds. The corresponding stationary state is given by the product distribution

P⁡(η)=∏i∈Λεeλ​η​(i)1+eλ.P(\eta)=\prod_{i\in\Lambda_{\varepsilon}}\frac{e^{\lambda\eta(i)}}{1+e^{\lambda}}\,. (205)

On the other hand, when the chemical potential λ⁡(i)\lambda(i) at the boundary is not constant, the model is not time reversal invariant and the stationary ensemble is not product.

VIII.2 The zero range model

In the zero range model there is no bound on the number of particles which can occupy the same site, hence the space of all possible configurations of the system is Ωε=ℕΛε\Omega_{\varepsilon}={\mathbb{N}}^{\Lambda_{\varepsilon}}. The dynamics is defined letting a particle interact only with the other particles present in the same lattice site. The interaction can be either attractive or repulsive. The bulk jump rates are:

{ci​j​(η)=g⁡(η⁡(i))​ for |j−i|=ε,ci​j​(η)=0​ otherwise.\left\{\begin{array}[]{l}\displaystyle{\vphantom{\Big(}c_{ij}(\eta)=g(\eta(i))\,\,\text{ for }\,\,|j-i|=\varepsilon\,,}\\ \displaystyle{\vphantom{\Big(}c_{ij}(\eta)=0\,\,\text{ otherwise.}}\end{array}\right. (206)

where g:ℕ→ℝ+g:\,{\mathbb{N}}\to{\mathbb{R}}^{+} is a function such that g⁡(0)=0g(0)=0 and g⁡(k)>0g(k)>0, k≥1k\geq 1, describing the type of interaction. In particular, the choice of linear function g⁡(k)=α​kg(k)=\alpha k corresponds to the ideal gas (independent random walks). Also in this model the boundary creation and annihilation rates are associated to the chemical potential λ⁡(x)\lambda(x) of the reservoirs, which, as before, is a continuous function on a neighborhood of ∂Λ\partial\Lambda. The boundary rates are

{ci−​(η)=g⁡(η⁡(i))|∂Λεo​(i)| for ​i∈∂Λε,ci+​(η)=∑j∈∂Λεo​(i)eλ⁡(j)​ for ​i∈∂Λε,ci±​(η)=0​ otherwise,\left\{\begin{array}[]{l}\displaystyle{\vphantom{\Big(}c_{i}^{-}(\eta)=g(\eta(i))\,\big|\partial\Lambda^{o}_{\varepsilon}(i)\big|\,\,\text{ for }\,\,i\in\partial\Lambda_{\varepsilon}\,,}\\ \displaystyle{\vphantom{\Big(}c_{i}^{+}(\eta)=\sum_{j\in\partial\Lambda^{o}_{\varepsilon}(i)}e^{\lambda(j)}\,\,\text{ for }\,\,i\in\partial\Lambda_{\varepsilon}\,,}\\ \displaystyle{\vphantom{\Big(}c_{i}^{\pm}(\eta)=0\,\,\text{ otherwise,}}\end{array}\right. (207)

where |∂Λεo​(i)||\partial\Lambda^{o}_{\varepsilon}(i)| denotes the cardinality of the set ∂Λεo​(i)\partial\Lambda^{o}_{\varepsilon}(i), recall (204).

If the function gg grows fast enough, there is a unique invariant state PP satisfying (200). The peculiarity of this model is that, for arbitrary chemical potential λ⁡(x)\lambda(x), the invariant distribution is a product distribution. It has the following form:

P⁡(η)=∏i∈Λε1Z⁡(φ⁡(i))​φ​(i)η⁡(i)g⁡(η⁡(i))!,P(\eta)=\prod_{i\in\Lambda_{\varepsilon}}\frac{1}{Z(\varphi(i))}\frac{\varphi(i)^{\eta(i)}}{g(\eta(i))!}\,, (208)

where g⁡(k)!=g⁡(k)​g​(k−1)​…​g​(1)g(k)!=g(k)g(k-1)\dots g(1), and Z⁡(φ)=∑k∈ℕφkg⁡(k)!Z(\varphi)=\sum_{k\in{\mathbb{N}}}\frac{\varphi^{k}}{g(k)!}. The function φ:Λε→ℝ+\varphi:\,\Lambda_{\varepsilon}\to{\mathbb{R}}^{+} solves the discrete Laplace equation

Δε​φ​(i)=∑|j−i|=ε(φ⁡(j)−φ⁡(i))=0,\Delta_{\varepsilon}\varphi(i)=\sum_{|j-i|=\varepsilon}(\varphi(j)-\varphi(i))=0\,, (209)

with boundary condition φ⁡(i)=eλ⁡(i)\varphi(i)=e^{\lambda(i)} for lattice sites ii immediately outside of the boundary. Also in this case, when the boundary chemical potential is constant λ⁡(i)=λ\lambda(i)=\lambda for all i∈∂Λεoi\in\partial\Lambda_{\varepsilon}^{o}, the detailed balance condition (202) holds, the solution to (209) is constant φ=eλ\varphi=e^{\lambda}, and (208) describes an equilibrium state.

VIII.3 The Glauber+Kawasaki model

We consider here a Glauber+Kawasaki model for which the conservative part of the dynamics is given by the same rates (203) as in the exclusion process, while the non conservative part of the dynamics (198), associated to the creation and annihilation rates ci±​(η)c_{i}^{\pm}(\eta), extends over all sites ii of the domain Λε\Lambda_{\varepsilon}. In general, the creation and annihilation rates ci±​(η):Ωε→ℝ+c_{i}^{\pm}(\eta):\,\Omega_{\varepsilon}\to{\mathbb{R}}^{+} are functions, translation invariant, depending only on the value of the configuration η\eta on sites j≠ij\neq i at distance at most k​εk\varepsilon form ii (kk is a fixed positive integer). When the site ii is near the boundary, the rates ci±​(η)c_{i}^{\pm}(\eta) will also depend on the value of the chemical potential of the reservoirs.

For simplicity, we write an explicit formula for the creation and annihilation rates only on the torus, i.e. when Λ=[0,1]d\Lambda=[0,1]^{d} with periodic boundary conditions. Let τi\tau_{i} be the shift operator on the configuration space Ωε\Omega_{\varepsilon}, defined by [τi​η]​(j)=η⁡(j−i)\left[\tau_{i}\eta\right](j)=\eta(j-i). Then

{ci+​(η)=(1−η⁡(i))​b​(τ−i​η)ci−​(η)=η⁡(i)​d​(τ−i​η)\left\{\begin{array}[]{l}c^{+}_{i}(\eta)=(1-\eta(i))b(\tau_{-i}\eta)\\ c^{-}_{i}(\eta)=\eta(i)d(\tau_{-i}\eta)\end{array}\right. (210)

where the functions b⁡(η)b(\eta) and d⁡(η)d(\eta), associated to the “birth” and “death” of particles, only depend on the occupation numbers η⁡(j)\eta(j) for sites jj at distance at most k​εk\varepsilon from the origin.

Recall that any product Bernoulli distribution

Pp​(η)=∏i∈Λεpη⁡(i)​(1−p)1−η⁡(i)P^{p}(\eta)=\prod_{i\in\Lambda_{\varepsilon}}p^{\eta(i)}(1-p)^{1-\eta(i)} (211)

(cf. (205)) is time reversal invariant for the conservative part of the dynamics. Hence, PpP^{p} will be time reversal invariant with respect to the full dynamics provided that

d⁡(η)b⁡(η)=1−pp\frac{d(\eta)}{b(\eta)}=\frac{1-p}{p} (212)

for all η∈Ωε\eta\in\Omega_{\varepsilon}. Indeed, (212) guarantees that the detailed balance condition (202) holds also for the non conservative part of the dynamics. Therefore, if d⁡(η)/b⁡(η){d(\eta)}/{b(\eta)} is constant in η\eta, the stationary state PP is as in (211), where pp is uniquely determined by (212). When d⁡(η)/b⁡(η)d(\eta)/b(\eta) is not constant, the corresponding stationary state PP is, in general, not invariant under time reversal and not product.

VIII.4 The Kipnis-Marchioro-Presutti model

The Kipnis-Marchioro-Presutti (KMP) model [88], originally proposed as a simple solvable model of heat conduction, does not fit exactly in the general framework outlined above and we need to modify the notation accordingly. We discuss this model only in the one-dimensional case.

This model describes a linear chain of harmonic oscillators with a random exchanges of energy between nearest neighbors and possibly heat baths at the boundary sites. As usual, let Λ=(0,1)\Lambda=(0,1) be the macroscopic domain and Λε=Λ∩ε​ℤ\Lambda_{\varepsilon}=\Lambda\cap\varepsilon\mathbb{Z} be the corresponding discrete chain. In each lattice site i∈Λεi\in\Lambda_{\varepsilon} there is an harmonic oscillator and we call (q⁡(i),p⁡(i))(q(i),p(i)) its canonical coordinates so that its energy is Hi​(q⁡(i),p⁡(i))=q​(i)2+p​(i)2H_{i}(q(i),p(i))=q(i)^{2}+p(i)^{2}. The oscillators are mechanically uncoupled, i.e. the total energy is H=∑iHiH=\sum_{i}H_{i}, but the dynamics has a stochastic term which induces an interaction. More precisely, on the bonds (i,i+ε)(i,i+\varepsilon) there are independent Poissonian clocks. When the clock across the bond (i,i+ε)(i,i+\varepsilon) rings, we compute the energy E=Hi​(q⁡(i),p⁡(i))+Hi+ε​(q⁡(i+ε),p⁡(i+ε))E=H_{i}(q(i),p(i))+H_{i+\varepsilon}(q(i+\varepsilon),p(i+\varepsilon)) and redistribute the canonical coordinates of the two oscillators uniformly to new values (q′​(i),p′​(i)),(q′​(i+ε),p′​(i+ε))(q^{\prime}(i),p^{\prime}(i)),(q^{\prime}(i+\varepsilon),p^{\prime}(i+\varepsilon)) chosen uniformly on the surface Hi​(q′​(i),p′​(i))+Hi+ε​(q′​(i+ε),p′​(i+ε))=EH_{i}(q^{\prime}(i),p^{\prime}(i))+H_{i+\varepsilon}(q^{\prime}(i+\varepsilon),p^{\prime}(i+\varepsilon))=E. On the boundary sites there are other two independent Poissonian clocks. When a clock rings at a boundary site i∈∂Λεi\in\partial\Lambda_{\varepsilon}, choose the new value of the coordinates (q′​(i),p′​(i))(q^{\prime}(i),p^{\prime}(i)) according to the following rules forgetting the old configuration (q⁡(i),p⁡(i))(q(i),p(i)). Sample a value of the energy EE according to an exponential distribution of parameter λ⁡(i)\lambda(i) and let (q′​(i),p′​(i))(q^{\prime}(i),p^{\prime}(i)) be uniformly distributed on the surface Hi​(q′​(i),p′​(i))=EH_{i}(q^{\prime}(i),p^{\prime}(i))=E.

A peculiar feature of this model is that the local energies HiH_{i} have a closed Markovian evolution. In the sequel, we shall denote by η⁡(i)∈ℝ+\eta(i)\in\mathbb{R}^{+} the energy of the oscillator at site i∈Λεi\in\Lambda_{\varepsilon} and describe formally their evolution. Observe that from a statistical mechanics viewpoint these are indeed the relevant quantities. Let us define for p∈[0,1]p\in[0,1]

[σpi,j​η]​(k)={η⁡(k)if​k≠i,j,p⁡(η⁡(i)+η⁡(j))if​k=i,(1−p)​(η⁡(i)+η⁡(j))if​k=j.\left[\sigma_{p}^{i,j}\eta\right](k)=\left\{\begin{array}[]{ll}\eta(k)&\textrm{if}\ k\neq i,j\,,\\ p(\eta(i)+\eta(j))&\textrm{if}\ k=i\,,\\ (1-p)(\eta(i)+\eta(j))&\textrm{if}\ k=j\,.\end{array}\right.

and for s∈ℝ+s\in\mathbb{R}^{+}

[σsi​η]​(k)={η⁡(k)if​k≠i,sif​k=i.\left[\sigma_{s}^{i}\eta\right](k)=\left\{\begin{array}[]{ll}\eta(k)&\textrm{if}\ k\neq i\,,\\ s&\textrm{if}\ k=i\,.\end{array}\right.

For this model the general formula (198) has to be substituted by

L​f​(η)=∑i,j∈Λε,|i−j|=ε∫01d​p​[f⁡(σpi​j​η)−f⁡(η)]+∑i∈∂Λε∫0+∞dsλ(i)e−λ⁡(i)​s[f(σsiη)−f(η)],\begin{array}[]{l}\displaystyle{Lf(\eta)=\sum_{i,j\in\Lambda_{\varepsilon}\,,|i-j|=\varepsilon}\int_{0}^{1}\!dp\,\big[f(\sigma_{p}^{ij}\eta)-f(\eta)\big]}\\ \displaystyle{+\sum_{i\in\partial\Lambda_{\varepsilon}}\int_{0}^{+\infty}\!ds\,\lambda(i)e^{-\lambda(i)s}\big[f(\sigma_{s}^{i}\eta)-f(\eta)\big]},\end{array} (213)

where λ⁡(i)\lambda(i) are the temperatures of the boundary thermostats. The generator in (213) describes a stochastic evolution in which every pair of nearest neighbor sites after an exponential time redistribute the sum of their energies between the two sites in a uniform way. This mechanism preserves the total energy of the system. At a boundary site ii after an exponential time the energy is replaced by the value of an exponential random variable of parameter λ⁡(i)\lambda(i).

If λ⁡(i)=λ\lambda(i)=\lambda for both boundary sites, then the model is time reversal invariant. The corresponding equilibrium state PP is given by the following product distribution on (ℝ+)Λε\left(\mathbb{R}^{+}\right)^{\Lambda_{\varepsilon}}

d​P​(η)=∏i∈Λελ​e−λ​η​(i)​d​η​(i).dP(\eta)=\prod_{i\in\Lambda_{\varepsilon}}\lambda e^{-\lambda\eta(i)}d\eta(i). (214)

On the other hand when λ⁡(i)\lambda(i) is not constant the model is not time reversal invariant, the invariant state is not product, and an explicit representation is not known (except for the case of a single oscillator [16]).

We refer to [79] for a variant of this model in which part of the energy is dissipated.

VIII.5 Weakly asymmetric models

We now show how to modify the stochastic models described above in order to take into account the action of an external vector field. Let F:Λ→ℝdF:\Lambda\to\mathbb{R}^{d} be a vector field, describing the force acting on the particles of the system. When the system goes from the configuration η\eta to the configuration σi,j​η\sigma^{i,j}\eta, the work done by the force field FF is

Fi,j=∫[i,j]F⋅𝑑l,F_{i,j}=\int_{[i,j]}F\cdot dl\,, (215)

where [i,j][i,j] is the oriented segment from ii to jj (which has length of order ε\varepsilon). The perturbed rates are defined by

ci,jF​(η)=ci,j​(η)​eFi,j/2.c^{F}_{i,j}(\eta)=c_{i,j}(\eta)e^{F_{i,j}/2}\,. (216)

When |i−j||i-j| is of order ε\varepsilon, then the work (215) is of order ε\varepsilon and we have

ci,jF​(η)=ci,j​(η)​(1+Fi,j2)+o⁡(ε).c^{F}_{i,j}(\eta)=c_{i,j}(\eta)\big(1+\tfrac{F_{i,j}}{2}\big)+o(\varepsilon)\,.

If F=−∇HF=-\nabla H is a gradient vector field, then Fi,j=H⁡(i)−H⁡(j)F_{i,j}=H(i)-H(j), and equation (216) becomes

ci,jF​(η)=ci,j​(η)​e[H⁡(i)−H⁡(j)]/2.c^{F}_{i,j}(\eta)=c_{i,j}(\eta)e^{[H(i)-H(j)]/2}\,. (217)

For the KMP model the net amount of energy flown across the bond (i,j)(i,j) when the configuration η\eta is transformed into σpi,j​η\sigma^{i,j}_{p}\eta is given by (1−p)​η​(i)−p​η​(j)(1-p)\eta(i)-p\eta(j). The perturbed dynamics on the bond (i,j)(i,j) is defined by

∫01d​p​e[(1−p)​η​(i)−p​η​(j)]​Fi,j/2​[f⁡(σpi,j​η)−f⁡(η)],\int_{0}^{1}dpe^{\left[(1-p)\eta(i)-p\eta(j)\right]F_{i,j}/2}\left[f(\sigma^{i,j}_{p}\eta)-f(\eta)\right]\,, (218)

where in this case Fi,jF_{i,j} is the work done per unit energy.

Observe that Fi,jF_{i,j} in (215) is of order ε\varepsilon. Namely, on the microscopic scale the external field is small with the scaling parameter. This is the reason for the name weakly asymmetric. The case in which Fi,jF_{i,j} in (216) is of order one corresponds to asymmetric models. In this case the hydrodynamics is given by hyperbolic conservation laws and not by driven diffusive equations. We refer to [87] for periodic boundary conditions and to [5] for the case of models with reservoirs.

VIII.6 Empirical density and current

In order to pass from a microscopic model to the corresponding macroscopic system, it is convenient to introduce some intermediate quantities, called the empirical density and the empirical current.

The empirical density associated to the configuration η∈Ωε\eta\in\Omega_{\varepsilon} is defined as

ρε​(η,x)=εd​∑i∈Λεη⁡(i)​δ​(x−i),\rho_{\varepsilon}(\eta;x)=\varepsilon^{d}\sum_{i\in\Lambda_{\varepsilon}}\eta(i)\delta(x-i)\,, (219)

where δ⁡(x−i)\delta(x-i) is the delta distribution concentrated at site ii. It gives a positive distribution on the domain Λ\Lambda, describing the local densities of particles. It is equivalently defined by

∫Λd​x​ρε​(η,x)​f​(x)=εd​∑i∈Λεη⁡(i)​f​(i),\int_{\Lambda}dx\,\rho_{\varepsilon}(\eta;x)f(x)=\varepsilon^{d}\sum_{i\in\Lambda_{\varepsilon}}\eta(i)f(i)\,, (220)

for a continuous function f:Λ→ℝf:\,\Lambda\to{\mathbb{R}}.

The empirical current is associated to a trajectory ηt\eta_{t}, t∈[0,T]t\in[0,T], of the particle system on the configuration space. Denote by NTi,jN^{i,j}_{T} the number of particles that jump from ii to jj in the time interval [0,T][0,T]. At the boundary, for i∈Λεi\in\Lambda_{\varepsilon} and j∈∂Λεo​(i)j\in\partial\Lambda_{\varepsilon}^{o}(i), NTi,jN^{i,j}_{T} is the number of particles leaving the system at ii by jumping to jj (annihilation), while NTj,iN^{j,i}_{T} is the number of particles entering the system in ii jumping from the reservoir site jj (creation). The difference QTi,j=NTi,j−NTj,iQ^{i,j}_{T}=N^{i,j}_{T}-N^{j,i}_{T} is the net number of particles flowing across the oriented bond (i,j)(i,j) in the time interval [0,T][0,T]. The instantaneous current d​Qti,j/d​tdQ^{i,j}_{t}/dt is thus a sum of δ\delta–functions localized at the jump times across the unoriented bond {i,j}\{i,j\} with weight +1+1, respectively −1-1, if a particle jumps from ii to jj, respectively from jj to ii. The empirical current is defined as

jε​(η,t,x)=εd​∑{i,j}(j−i)​δ​(x−i)​d​Qti,jd​t,j_{\varepsilon}(\eta;t,x)=\varepsilon^{d}\sum_{\{i,j\}}(j-i)\delta(x-i)\frac{dQ^{i,j}_{t}}{dt}\,, (221)

where the sum is over unoriented bonds {i,j}\{i,j\} such that |i−j|=ε|i-j|=\varepsilon. Note indeed that the product (j−i)​d​Qti,jd​t(j-i)\frac{dQ^{i,j}_{t}}{dt} is symmetric with respect to the exchange of ii and jj. The empirical currents jεj_{\varepsilon} is a distribution on Λ×[0,T]\Lambda\times[0,T] with values in ℝd{\mathbb{R}}^{d}, describing the local flux of particles. It is equivalently defined by

∫0Td​t​∫Λd​x​jε​(η,t,x)⋅F⁡(x,t)=εd​∑(i,j)∑k=1NTi,j(j−i)⋅F⁡(i,τki,j),\begin{array}[]{l}\displaystyle{\int_{0}^{T}\!dt\int_{\Lambda}\!dx\,j_{\varepsilon}(\eta;t,x)\cdot F(x,t)}\\ \displaystyle{=\varepsilon^{d}\sum_{(i,j)}\sum_{k=1}^{N^{i,j}_{T}}(j-i)\cdot F(i,\tau^{i,j}_{k})\,,}\end{array} (222)

for a continuous vector field F:Λ×[0,T]→ℝdF:\,\Lambda\times[0,T]\to{\mathbb{R}}^{d}. In the above equation τki,j\tau^{i,j}_{k}, k=1,…,NTi,jk=1,\dots,N^{i,j}_{T}, denote the times at which particles jump from site ii to site jj. In (222) the sum is over oriented bonds (i,j)(i,j) such that |i−j|=ε|i-j|=\varepsilon.

In the one-dimensional case, recalling the definition (174) of the average total current 𝒬ε,T{\mathcal{Q}}_{\varepsilon,T}, by choosing F=1F=1, we get

𝒬ε,T=ε2T​∑iQTi,i+ε.{\mathcal{Q}}_{\varepsilon,T}=\frac{\varepsilon^{2}}{T}\sum_{i}Q^{i,i+\varepsilon}_{T}\,.

From the previous formula one can deduce the relationship between 𝒬ε,T{\mathcal{Q}}_{\varepsilon,T} and analogous quantities considered in [24, 44, 3, 1].

VIII.7 Hydrodynamic limits

The models introduced in the previous subsections have a non trivial scaling limit under a diffusive rescaling. Since the lattice size is ε\varepsilon this corresponds to speed up the dynamics multiplying the transition rates by ε−2\varepsilon^{-2}. The basic formula we will use is

Nti,j=ε−2​∫0tci,j​(ηs)​𝑑s+Mti,j.N^{i,j}_{t}=\varepsilon^{-2}\int_{0}^{t}c^{i,j}(\eta_{s})ds+M^{i,j}_{t}\,. (223)

Formula (223) is derived by classic arguments in the theory of Markov processes, see e.g. [33]. Given the configuration ηt\eta_{t} at time tt, the expected value of the increment Nt+d​ti,j−Nti,jN^{i,j}_{t+dt}-N^{i,j}_{t} is ε−2​ci,j​(ηt)​d​t\varepsilon^{-2}c^{i,j}(\eta_{t})dt. The last term Mti,jM^{i,j}_{t} thus describes the microscopic fluctuation (in probabilistic language, it is a martingale). From (223) we get

Qti,j=ε−2​∫0tqi,j​(ηs)​𝑑s+M~ti,j,Q^{i,j}_{t}=\varepsilon^{-2}\int_{0}^{t}q^{i,j}(\eta_{s})ds+\tilde{M}^{i,j}_{t}\,, (224)

where

qi,j​(η)=ci,j​(η)−cj,i​(η)q^{i,j}(\eta)=c^{i,j}(\eta)-c^{j,i}(\eta) (225)

is the mean instantaneous current across the bond (i,j)(i,j), and M~ti,j\tilde{M}^{i,j}_{t} is a fluctuation term, which plays the same role as Mti,jM^{i,j}_{t} does in (223).

The models we introduced in the previous sections are of gradient type. This means that there exists a function h⁡(η)h(\eta), depending on the configuration η\eta only through a finite number of lattice sites, such that

qi,j​(η)=h⁡(τi​η)−h⁡(τj​η),q^{i,j}(\eta)=h(\tau_{i}\eta)-h(\tau_{j}\eta), (226)

where, as before, τi\tau_{i} denotes the shift on Ωε\Omega_{\varepsilon}.

For the simple exclusion process we have h⁡(η)=η⁡(0)h(\eta)=\eta(0), while for the zero range model we have h⁡(η)=g⁡(η⁡(0))h(\eta)=g(\eta(0)). The construction for the KMP model is slightly different and Qti,jQ^{i,j}_{t} represents the net amount of energy flowing across the bond (i,j)(i,j) in the time interval [0,t][0,t]. The mean instantaneous current appearing in formula (224) in this case becomes

qi,j​(η)=∫01d​p​([σpi,j​η]​(j)+[σpj,i​η]​(j)−2​η​(j)).q^{i,j}(\eta)=\int_{0}^{1}dp\Big(\left[\sigma^{i,j}_{p}\eta\right](j)+\left[\sigma^{j,i}_{p}\eta\right](j)-2\eta(j)\Big)\,. (227)

From (227) we deduce that (226) still holds with h⁡(η)=η⁡(0)h(\eta)=\eta(0).

In order to discuss the hydrodynamic behavior, we first observe that the definition of Qti,jQ^{i,j}_{t} implies the discrete continuity equation

ηt(i)−η0(i)=−∑j:|j−i|=εQti,j.\eta_{t}(i)-\eta_{0}(i)=-\sum_{j\,:\,|j-i|=\varepsilon}Q^{i,j}_{t}. (228)

In view of (224), we can rewrite this equation as

ηt​(i)−η0​(i)=−ε−2∑j:|j−i|=ε∫0tdsqi,j(ηs)+fluctuation\begin{split}\eta_{t}(i)-\eta_{0}(i)=&-\varepsilon^{-2}\sum_{j\,:\,|j-i|=\varepsilon}\int_{0}^{t}ds\,q^{i,j}(\eta_{s})\\ &+\mathrm{fluctuation}\end{split} (229)

Consider now a test function ψ:Λ→ℝ\psi\colon\Lambda\to\mathbb{R}. By integrating (229) in space we deduce

∫Λd​x​ψ​(x)​ρε​(ηt,x)−∫Λd​x​ψ​(x)​ρε​(η0,x)=εd∫0tds∑ih(τiηs)[ε−2∑j:|j−i|=ε(ψ(j)−ψ(i))]+o⁡(1)\begin{split}&\int_{\Lambda}\!dx\,\psi(x)\rho_{\varepsilon}(\eta_{t};x)-\int_{\Lambda}\!dx\,\psi(x)\rho_{\varepsilon}(\eta_{0};x)\\ &=\varepsilon^{d}\int_{0}^{t}\!ds\sum_{i}h(\tau_{i}\eta_{s})\left[\varepsilon^{-2}\sum_{j\,:\,|j-i|=\varepsilon}\left(\psi(j)-\psi(i)\right)\right]\\ &\;+o\left(1\right)\end{split} (230)

where we used (226) and a discrete integration by parts. The term o⁡(1)o(1) represent the space integral of the fluctuation in (229). It vanishes as ε→0\varepsilon\to 0 as the random variables Mti,jM^{i,j}_{t} have mean zero and are almost independent for different bonds. Observe that the term inside square brackets in (230) is a discrete version of the Laplacian of ψ\psi; namely,

ε−2∑j:|j−i|=ε(ψ(j)−ψ(i))=Δψ(i)+o(1).\varepsilon^{-2}\sum_{j\,:\,|j-i|=\varepsilon}\left(\psi(j)-\psi(i)\right)=\Delta\psi(i)+o\left(1\right). (231)

As already mentioned, both for the exclusion and the KMP processes condition (226) holds with h⁡(η)=η⁡(0)h(\eta)=\eta(0). In these cases, by taking the limit ε→0\varepsilon\to 0 and denoting by ρ⁡(t,x)\rho(t,x) the limit of ρε​(ηt,x)\rho_{\varepsilon}(\eta_{t},x), (230) yields directly

∫Λd​x​ρ​(t,x)​ψ​(x)−∫Λd​x​ρ​(0,x)​ψ​(x)=∫0td​s​∫Λd​x​ρ​(s,x)​Δ​ψ​(x)\begin{split}&\int_{\Lambda}\!dx\,\rho(t,x)\,\psi(x)-\int_{\Lambda}\!dx\,\rho(0,x)\,\psi(x)\\ &\quad=\int_{0}^{t}\!ds\int_{\Lambda}\!dx\,\rho(s,x)\,\Delta\psi(x)\end{split}

which is the weak formulation of the heat equation

∂tρ=Δ​ρ.\partial_{t}\rho=\Delta\rho.

This is the hydrodynamic equation for both the simple exclusion and the KMP processes. Namely, for these models D⁡(ρ)=1D(\rho)=1.

For the zero range process we have instead h⁡(η)=g⁡(η⁡(0))h(\eta)=g(\eta(0)). Therefore, (230) yields directly a closed equation for the density only in the case g⁡(k)=kg(k)=k, corresponding to independent particles. In order to derive the hydrodynamic equation we need a mathematical formulation of the local equilibrium assumption. The basic idea is the following. Fix a point i∈Λεi\in\Lambda_{\varepsilon} and consider a macroscopically small, but microscopically large, neighborhood B⁡(i)B(i) of ii. Since the total number of particles is locally conserved, on the macroscopic time scale, the system in B⁡(i)B(i) is essentially in the homogeneous equilibrium state corresponding to the average density in B⁡(i)B(i). Therefore, we can replace h⁡(η)h(\eta) with the corresponding ensemble average.

In order to compute this average, we describe the equilibrium states PρP^{\rho} of the zero range process. These are product distributions of the form (208) with φ⁡(i)\varphi(i) constant and equal to the solution of

ρ=φ​Z′​(φ)Z⁡(φ).\rho=\varphi\frac{Z^{\prime}(\varphi)}{Z(\varphi)}\,. (232)

Let

Φ⁡(ρ)=EPρ​(g⁡(η⁡(0))).\Phi(\rho)=E_{P^{\rho}}(g(\eta(0)))\,.

In view of the previous discussion, in (230) we can replace

εd​∑ih⁡(τi​ηt)​Δ​ψ​(i),\varepsilon^{d}\sum_{i}h(\tau_{i}\eta_{t})\Delta\psi(i)\,, (233)

by

εd​∑iΦ⁡(1|B⁡(i)|​∫B⁡(i)ρε​(ηt,x)​𝑑x)​Δ​ψ​(i),\varepsilon^{d}\sum_{i}\Phi\left(\frac{1}{|B(i)|}\int_{B(i)}\rho_{\varepsilon}(\eta_{t};x)dx\right)\Delta\psi(i)\,, (234)

where |B⁡(i)||B(i)| denotes the volume of B⁡(i)B(i). We refer to [87, 124] for the (quite technical) proof of this statement.

Since B⁡(i)B(i) is macroscopically infinitesimal, by taking the limit ε→0\varepsilon\to 0 in (230), we derive the weak formulation of the non-linear diffusion equation

∂tρ=Δ​Φ​(ρ),\partial_{t}\rho=\Delta\Phi(\rho)\,, (235)

which is the hydrodynamic equation for the zero range process. We conclude that for the zero range process D​(ρ)=Φ′​(ρ)D(\rho)=\Phi^{\prime}(\rho).

We discuss now the hydrodynamic scaling limit of the empirical current. In order to obtain a microscopic expression for the mobility we consider the case of weakly asymmetric models. Recalling (215), for such models (224) holds with (225) replaced by

qi,j​(η)=ci,jF​(η)−cj,iF​(η)=ci,j​(η)−cj,i​(η)+12​[ci,j​(η)+cj,i​(η)]​Fi,j+o⁡(ε)=h⁡(τi​η)−h⁡(τj​η)+12​[ci,j​(η)+cj,i​(η)]​Fi,j+o⁡(ε)\begin{split}&q^{i,j}(\eta)=c^{F}_{i,j}(\eta)-c^{F}_{j,i}(\eta)\\ &\quad=c_{i,j}(\eta)-c_{j,i}(\eta)+\frac{1}{2}\big[c_{i,j}(\eta)+c_{j,i}(\eta)\big]F_{i,j}+o\left(\varepsilon\right)\\ &\quad=h(\tau_{i}\eta)-h(\tau_{j}\eta)+\frac{1}{2}\big[c_{i,j}(\eta)+c_{j,i}(\eta)\big]F_{i,j}+o\left(\varepsilon\right)\end{split} (236)

where we used the gradient condition (226) for the rates without external field.

For the KMP model, using (218) and (227), we instead get

qi,j​(η)=η⁡(i)−η⁡(j)+13​(η2​(i)+η2​(j)−η⁡(i)​η​(j))​Fi,j+o⁡(ε)q^{i,j}(\eta)=\eta(i)-\eta(j)+\frac{1}{3}\Big(\eta^{2}(i)+\eta^{2}(j)-\eta(i)\eta(j)\Big)F_{i,j}+o\left(\varepsilon\right) (237)

Let G:[0,T]×Λ→ℝdG\colon[0,T]\times\Lambda\to\mathbb{R}^{d} be a test vector field. Recalling the definition of the empirical current (221), by using (236) and writing the sum over unoriented bonds as 1/21/2 the sum over oriented bonds we get

∫0td​s​∫Λd​x​jε​(η,s,x)⋅G⁡(s,x)=εd∫0tds∑ih(τiηs)[ε−12∑j:|j−i|=ε(G(s,i)−G(s,j))]+εd−12∫0tds∑i∑j:|j−i|=ε12[ci,j(η)+cj,i(η)]Fi,jG(s,i)+o⁡(1)\begin{split}&\int_{0}^{t}\!ds\int_{\Lambda}\!dx\,j_{\varepsilon}(\eta;s,x)\cdot G(s,x)\\ &\;=\varepsilon^{d}\int_{0}^{t}\!\!ds\,\sum_{i}h(\tau_{i}\eta_{s})\Big[\frac{\varepsilon^{-1}}{2}\sum_{j\,:\,|j-i|=\varepsilon}\left(G(s,i)-G(s,j)\right)\Big]\\ &\;+\frac{\varepsilon^{d-1}}{2}\int_{0}^{t}\!\!ds\,\sum_{i}\sum_{j\,:\,|j-i|=\varepsilon}\frac{1}{2}\big[c_{i,j}(\eta)+c_{j,i}(\eta)\big]F_{i,j}G(s,i)\\ &\;+o(1)\end{split} (238)

where the term o⁡(1)o(1) is due to the fluctuation in (224).

Observe that

ε−12∑j:|j−i|=ε(G(i)−G(j))=∇⋅G(i)+o(1)\frac{\varepsilon^{-1}}{2}\sum_{j\,:\,|j-i|=\varepsilon}\left(G(i)-G(j)\right)=\nabla\cdot G(i)+o(1) (239)

and, since Fi,jF_{i,j} is of order ε\varepsilon,

ε−12∑j:|j−i|=εFi,jG(i)=F(i)⋅G(i)+o(1).\frac{\varepsilon^{-1}}{2}\sum_{j\,:\,|j-i|=\varepsilon}F_{i,j}G(i)=F(i)\cdot G(i)+o(1). (240)

We now define in general

Φ⁡(ρ)=EPρ​(h),χ⁡(ρ)=12​EPρ​[ci,j+cj,i]\Phi(\rho)=E_{P^{\rho}}(h),\qquad\chi(\rho)=\frac{1}{2}E_{P^{\rho}}\left[c_{i,j}+c_{j,i}\right] (241)

where PρP^{\rho} denotes the homogeneous equilibrium state with density ρ\rho. By the same local equilibrium argument discussed before, we get that the right hand side of (238) converges as ε→0\varepsilon\to 0 to

∫0tds∫ΛdxΦ(ρ)∇⋅G+∫0tds∫Λdxχ(ρ)F⋅G\int_{0}^{t}\!ds\int_{\Lambda}\!dx\,\Phi(\rho)\nabla\cdot G+\int_{0}^{t}\!ds\int_{\Lambda}\!dx\,\chi(\rho)F\cdot G (242)

which is the weak form of

J(ρ)=−∇Φ(ρ)+χ(ρ)F=−Φ′(ρ)∇ρ+χ(ρ)FJ(\rho)=-\nabla\Phi(\rho)+\chi(\rho)F=-\Phi^{\prime}(\rho)\nabla\rho+\chi(\rho)F

that is (6) with D​(ρ)=Φ′​(ρ)D(\rho)=\Phi^{\prime}(\rho) and χ⁡(ρ)\chi(\rho) as in (241).

In the case of the exclusion process, ci,j​(η)+cj,i​(η)=η⁡(i)​(1−η⁡(j))+η⁡(j)​(1−η⁡(i))c_{i,j}(\eta)+c_{j,i}(\eta)=\eta(i)(1-\eta(j))+\eta(j)(1-\eta(i)) so that χ⁡(ρ)=ρ⁡(1−ρ)\chi(\rho)=\rho(1-\rho). In the case of the zero range we have ci,j​(η)+cj,i​(η)=g⁡(η⁡(i))+g⁡(η⁡(j))c_{i,j}(\eta)+c_{j,i}(\eta)=g(\eta(i))+g(\eta(j)) so that χ⁡(ρ)=Φ⁡(ρ)\chi(\rho)=\Phi(\rho). For the KMP model the equilibrium state is a product of exponential distribution so that, using (237), we can deduce χ⁡(ρ)=ρ2\chi(\rho)=\rho^{2}.

When the condition (226) does not hold, the model is called non gradient. In this case the deduction of the hydrodynamic equation is more complicated. Referring to [87] for the detail of this derivation, we mention that in the general case the diffusion coefficient is linked to the microscopic dynamics by a Green-Kubo formula, see [124, II.2.2].

We discussed the hydrodynamic limit without considering the boundary terms. At the boundary there is a Glauber dynamics speeded up by a factor ε−2\varepsilon^{-2} that keeps fixed the density at a value determined by the local chemical potential of the external reservoirs [60].

VIII.8 Large fluctuations

In this section we derive, for models satisfying the gradient condition (226), the fundamental formula (11). For simplicity, we restrict to models without external field.

We need an expression for the relative distribution of two stochastic particle systems. Since these processes can be constructed using independent Poisson processes, we start by giving the relative distribution of two Poisson processes. More precisely, consider two Poisson processes with parameters depending on the value NtN_{t} of the process. The first one has parameter c⁡(Nt)c(N_{t}) and the second one is obtained from the first with a time dependent perturbation and has parameter c⁡(Nt)​eF⁡(t)/2c(N_{t})e^{F(t)/2}. Then the ratio between the two ensembles on the time window [0,t][0,t] is, see [12, App. A],

d​ℙd​ℙF|[0,t]=exp{∫0t[c(Ns)eF⁡(s)/2−c(Ns)]−12∑kF(τk)},\begin{split}\frac{d\mathbb{P}}{d\mathbb{P}^{F}}\Big|_{[0,t]}=&\exp\Big\{\int_{0}^{t}\left[c(N_{s})e^{F(s)/2}-c(N_{s})\right]\\ &\quad-\frac{1}{2}\sum_{k}F(\tau_{k})\Big\},\end{split} (243)

where the τk\tau_{k} are the jump times.

Consider a macroscopic fluctuation (ρ⁡(s),j⁡(s))(\rho(s),j(s)) in the time window [0,t][0,t] of the empirical density and current satisfying the continuity equation. In order to estimate the probability of this fluctuation we introduce an external field FF such that (ρ⁡(s),j⁡(s))(\rho(s),j(s)) becomes typical, that is its probability is close to one as ε→0\varepsilon\to 0. The external field FF that we need to introduce is obtained solving the equation

−D(ρ)∇ρ+χ(ρ)F=j.-D(\rho)\nabla\rho+\chi(\rho)F=j. (244)

The ratio between the distributions of the original particle system and the one obtained with the perturbation FF in the time window [0,t][0,t] can be computed by using (243). Recalling (215), we get

d​ℙd​ℙF|[0,t]=exp{∫0tds∑|i−j|=εε−2ci,j(ηs)(eFi,j​(s)/2−1)−12∑|i−j|=ε∑k=1Nti,jFi,j(τi,jk)}.\begin{split}&\frac{d\mathbb{P}}{d\mathbb{P}^{F}}\Big|_{[0,t]}=\exp\Big\{\int_{0}^{t}\!ds\sum_{|i-j|=\varepsilon}\varepsilon^{-2}c_{i,j}(\eta_{s})\left(e^{F_{i,j}(s)/2}-1\right)\\ &\qquad\qquad-\frac{1}{2}\sum_{|i-j|=\varepsilon}\sum_{k=1}^{N^{i,j}_{t}}F_{i,j}(\tau^{i,j}_{k})\Big\}.\end{split} (245)

Recalling (222), the second term at the exponent above is equal to ε−d​12​∫0td​s​∫Λd​x​jε⋅F\varepsilon^{-d}\frac{1}{2}\int_{0}^{t}\!ds\int_{\Lambda}\!dx\,j_{\varepsilon}\cdot F. By expanding up to second order eFi,j​(s)/2e^{F_{i,j}(s)/2}, using the antisymmetry of Fi,j​(s)F_{i,j}(s) with respect to i,ji,j and the gradient condition (226), we rewrite the first term as

ε−d∫0tdsεd−2∑i∑j:|j−i|=εci,j(ηs)[12Fi,j(s)+18Fi,j(s)2]=∫0tds∑i{h(τiηs)ε−24∑j:|j−i|=ε[Fi,j(s)−Fj,i(s)]+ε−2∑j:|j−i|=ε12[ci,j(ηs)+cj,i(ηs)]18Fi,j(s)2}≈ε−d∫0tds∫Λdx{12Φ(ρε)∇⋅F+14F⋅χ(ρε)F}\begin{split}&\varepsilon^{-d}\int_{0}^{t}\!ds\,\varepsilon^{d-2}\sum_{i}\sum_{j\,:\,|j-i|=\varepsilon}c_{i,j}(\eta_{s})\Big[\frac{1}{2}F_{i,j}(s)+\frac{1}{8}F_{i,j}(s)^{2}\Big]\\ &=\int_{0}^{t}\!ds\,\sum_{i}\Big\{h(\tau_{i}\eta_{s})\frac{\varepsilon^{-2}}{4}\sum_{j\,:\,|j-i|=\varepsilon}\big[F_{i,j}(s)-F_{j,i}(s)\big]\\ &+{\varepsilon^{-2}}\sum_{j\,:\,|j-i|=\varepsilon}\frac{1}{2}\big[c_{i,j}(\eta_{s})+c_{j,i}(\eta_{s})\big]\frac{1}{8}F_{i,j}(s)^{2}\Big\}\\ &\approx\varepsilon^{-d}\int_{0}^{t}\!ds\int_{\Lambda}\!dx\,\Big\{\frac{1}{2}\Phi(\rho_{\varepsilon})\nabla\cdot F+\frac{1}{4}F\cdot\chi(\rho_{\varepsilon})F\Big\}\end{split}

where we used local equilibrium as in the previous section, see in particular (241) for the microscopic definition of the transport coefficients. Since FF satisfies (244) we finally deduce that

d​ℙ|[0,t]d​ℙF|[0,t]≈exp{ε−d∫0tds∫Λdx[12(j−jε)⋅F−14F⋅χ(ρε)F]}.\begin{split}\frac{d\mathbb{P}|_{[0,t]}}{d\mathbb{P}^{F}|_{[0,t]}}&\approx\exp\Big\{\varepsilon^{-d}\int_{0}^{t}\!ds\int_{\Lambda}\!dx\,\Big[\frac{1}{2}(j-j_{\varepsilon})\cdot F\\ &\qquad-\frac{1}{4}F\cdot\chi(\rho_{\varepsilon})F\Big]\Big\}.\end{split} (246)

We now estimate the probability of the fluctuation (ρ⁡(s),j⁡(s))(\rho(s),j(s)), s∈[0,t]s\in[0,t]. We write

ℙ⁡((ρε,jε)∼(ρ,j))=𝔼F​(d​ℙ|[0,t]d​ℙF|[0,t]​1(ρε,jε)∼(ρ,j)),\begin{split}\mathbb{P}\Big(\left(\rho_{\varepsilon},j_{\varepsilon}\right)\sim(\rho,j)\Big)=\mathbb{E}^{F}\left(\frac{d\mathbb{P}|_{[0,t]}}{d\mathbb{P}^{F}|_{[0,t]}}{\boldmath 1}_{\left(\rho_{\varepsilon},j_{\varepsilon}\right)\sim(\rho,j)}\right),\end{split} (247)

where 1A\boldmath 1_{A} denotes the indicator of the set AA. By using (246) and the fact that under the perturbed distribution (ρε,jε)≈(ρ,j)(\rho_{\varepsilon},j_{\varepsilon})\approx(\rho,j) we finally get

ℙ⁡((ρε,jε)∼(ρ,j))≈exp{−ε−d14∫0tds∫ΛdxF⋅χ(ρ)F]}\begin{split}&\mathbb{P}\Big(\left(\rho_{\varepsilon},j_{\varepsilon}\right)\sim(\rho,j)\Big)\\ &\qquad\approx\exp\Big\{-\varepsilon^{-d}\frac{1}{4}\int_{0}^{t}\!ds\int_{\Lambda}\!dx\,F\cdot\chi(\rho)F\Big]\Big\}\end{split} (248)

which, in view of (244), concludes the proof of the fundamental formula.

In the case in which one considers only the fluctuations of the density, as in Section IV.1, formula (248) has been first obtained in [89] for the exclusion process.

As for the hydrodynamic limit, we discussed the large deviation asymptotic without considering the boundary terms. At the boundary there are independent Glauber dynamics speeded up by ε−2\varepsilon^{-2} so that the asymptotic probability to observe a density fluctuation on a region Γ⊆∂Λ\Gamma\subseteq\partial\Lambda of the boundary is of the order e−ε−(d+1)​|Γ|e^{-\varepsilon^{-(d+1)}\left|\Gamma\right|} which is much smaller than e−ε−de^{-\varepsilon^{-d}}. The fluctuations whose probability is exponentially small in ε−d\varepsilon^{-d} have therefore the values of the density at the boundary fixed by the reservoirs.

VIII.9 Quasi-potential and relative entropy

We consider two states of a system and establish a connection between the quasi-potential VV and the relative entropy between the corresponding ensembles.

This connection is readily established in equilibrium. For simplicity, consider the case of lattice gases without external field and constant chemical potential, i.e. the case of homogeneous equilibrium states. The Gibbs distribution on the volume Λ\Lambda is

PΛλ​(η)=1ZΛ​(λ)​exp⁡{−HΛ​(η)+λ​∑i∈Λη⁡(i)},P^{\lambda}_{\Lambda}(\eta)=\frac{1}{Z_{\Lambda}(\lambda)}\exp\Big\{-H_{\Lambda}(\eta)+\lambda\sum_{i\in\Lambda}\eta(i)\Big\}, (249)

where HΛ​(η)H_{\Lambda}(\eta) is the energy of the configuration η\eta, λ\lambda is the chemical potential, and ZΛ​(λ)Z_{\Lambda}(\lambda) is the grand-canonical partition function. Recall that we have included the dependence on the temperature in the Hamiltonian. According to the standard postulates of statistical mechanics, the pressure pp is given by

p⁡(λ)=limΛ↑Zd1|Λ|​log⁡ZΛ​(λ),p(\lambda)=\lim_{\Lambda\uparrow{\boldmath Z}^{d}}\frac{1}{|\Lambda|}\log Z_{\Lambda}(\lambda), (250)

and the free energy per unit volume ff is obtained as the Legendre transform of pp,

f⁡(ρ)=supλ{ρ​λ−p⁡(λ)}.f(\rho)=\sup_{\lambda}\big\{\rho\lambda-p(\lambda)\big\}.

The relative entropy S⁡(ν|μ)S(\nu|\mu) of the probability ν\nu with respect to μ\mu is defined by

S⁡(ν|μ)=∫d​P​d​νd​μ​log⁡d​νd​μ.S(\nu|\mu)=\int\!dP\>\frac{d\nu}{d\mu}\log\frac{d\nu}{d\mu}. (251)

Observe that if we choose μ\mu as the uniform probability then S⁡(ν|μ)S(\nu|\mu) is the Gibbs entropy.

Fix two chemical potentials λ0\lambda_{0} and λ1\lambda_{1}. We claim that

limΛ↑Zd1|Λ|​S​(PΛλ0|PΛλ1)=[f⁡(ρ¯0)−f⁡(ρ¯1)−λ1​(ρ¯0−ρ¯1)],\lim_{\Lambda\uparrow{\boldmath Z}^{d}}\,\frac{1}{|\Lambda|}S\big(P_{\Lambda}^{\lambda_{0}}\big|P_{\Lambda}^{\lambda_{1}}\big)=\big[f(\bar{\rho}_{0})-f(\bar{\rho}_{1})-\lambda_{1}(\bar{\rho}_{0}-\bar{\rho}_{1})\big], (252)
